EXPULSION OF JUDGE CATRON From Ten
NEssEE.-The Louisville Journal, of August
18th, gives the annexed particulars relative
to the expulsion of Judge Catron from
Nashville, Tennessee:


One day last week the Vigilance Committee
of Nashville waited upon Judge Catron, and in
formed him that he must either resign his office
of Judge or leave the State, and asked him
which he would do. The Judge was not prepa-
red to render an answer. The Committee gave
him twenty-four hours to decide upon his course,
letting him understand that if at the end of that
time he should neither have resigned nor left
Tennessee, they would take his affairs into their
own hands-meaning that they would eject
him by whatever force might be found neces-
sary. Within the twenty-four hours the old
man took his departure from Tennessee, leav-
ing his aged wife behind him, as she was too
sick and feeble to be removed. We heard of
him in this city on Friday or Saturday, but did
not see him. We presume that he is still in
this vicinity.

headline:
Internal Scheme to Poison the State

 Volunteers at Jefferson City
article:
The Examiner gives the following de- tails of this diaboIical attempt at wholesale murder, which has been briefly referred to in our colums

 A negro woman who resides in the vi. cinily of the bakery at which the bread for the volunteers al Jefferson City Is baked, informed some of our citizens that a cer- tain white man living here, had made pro- posas to her to poison the troops by pla- cing arsenic in the flour of which the bread is baked, stating to her as an ln- ducement that Frank Blair would then come here and set all the negroes free.

 A plan was at once set to catch the gentleman, with such evidence as would convict him. The woman was told to make an appointment to meet him again that night, which she did, and when the hour arrived, number of our most respec- table citizens were so placed around the house, as 10 overhear what was said with in. The man conversed freely with the woman, stating his.whole plan and object. He said he had been disappointed that day in getting the poison from St. Louis, but that man would certainly be up the next day with 1t.

 When she demurred to the plct as too dangerous, he argued with her 10 show how easy it could be done without detec- ton, her vicinity and access to the bakery giving her ample opportunity of putting poison into the flour without being known. Having heard sufficient evidence to insure the scoundrel secured. He proved to be man named Amos Cope, who-has been in this city for some months. He came here with his family, last winter, from Kansas, in destitute circumstances, and has been employed since then as a labor CT, his wife taking in washing to aid in their support. He was member of the Home Guard, recently formed, and is said to have been useful and efficient. He has been supposed to be a quiet inofensive man, and is generally regarded in this matter as the hired tool of more designing mlsCreantS.

 Of course, when the discovery of the diaboical plot was made known, the troops here were greatly exasperated, and were with difficulty restrained from summary execution of the miserable wretch. But fortunately better counsels prevailed, and the law will be allowed to take its course. The man is now in jail and strongly guar ded. There can be no doubt of his con- viclion, as the evidence against him is pos tive and overwhelming.

The trial of Burdue, for the murder of
Moore, came off early in the summer of 1851,
in the District Court of Yuba county, before
Judge G. N. Mott, now of Marysville. Jesse
o. Goodwin, Esq, aided, / think, by William
Walker, OF Nicaragua notoriety, acting as
prosecutors, and f. L. Aud, Esq, for the de-
fense. The jury empanneled to try the
cause was composed of the most intelligent
and respectable men of the county, and
everything denoted that the prisoner would
have fair and impartial trial. The excite
ment was intense among the people of-Marys
vile, for every man, or nearly every man,
believed the prisoner to be the notorious
Jim Stewart. A Vigilance Committee had
been organized there, and determination
expressed by more than one person connect
ed with that organization, that if by any
means the jury acquitted the defendant, he
should be hung.


When the case was called, an effort was
made by the attorneys for defendant to have
the trial postponed, but all efforts of this
sort were in vain. The outside pressure was
too great. The fiat of guilty had been de-
creed against the prisoner, and nothing had
to be done but to convict him, in accordance
with the forms of law.


The trial began. From the commence
ment to its close, the whole effort on the
part of the prosecution, was to identify the
prisoner as Stewart; for every body was we'll
satisfied that Stewart was the guilty party.
The efforts of the defendants counsel were.
to satisfy the jury that the prisoner was not
Stewart, and to prove an abb Hosts of
witnesses who had been summoned from
Fosters Bar, were called upon to identify
the prisoner, and more than two thirds of
'all those examined on that point testified
unequivocally that the prisoner was Stewart.
Judge Stidger, Nehemiah and Ezra Dodge,
and one or two others of the Fosters Bar
witnesses, including the writer, testified as
uaequivocaly that the prisoner was not
Stewart.


1t is not my purpose TO give the entire
testimony elected pro and con at Burdue's
trial, but as portion of the testimony went
directly to the point of the prisoners guilt,
it will be necessary to give it here.


Rawley, Wilson, Captain Vim. Dobbins and
Malcomson, testified as at the former exam
inaton. A man named Shaundown, testi-
fed that he was intimately acquainted with
Jim Stewart that they had been partners in
mining, ate at the same table, and slept to-
gether under the same blankets for several
months that he knew Stewart as we'll as he
did any man living; that he could not be
mistaken as to his identity that the man
before .iim on trial was Jim Stewart that
he was as certain of that fact as he was that
the sun rose and set. In answer to oues-
tions, he said Jim Stewart had certain in
delible ink marks upon his hands, and de-
scribed them as follows: A small star be-
tween the finger and thumb of the left hand,
rather dim; q circle or ring around the Sec
ond finger of the right hand, and also a deep
cash or cut made through the end of the
second finger of the right hand, thus form
ing a club finger, or a double finger at the
end He enumerated several other marks
upon the person of Stewart, and strange to
relate, when the prisoner held up his hands
before the court and jury, every mark sworn
to by the witness were found upon them just
as they were described by the witness.
Here was truth positive-conclusive at least
to the minds of the jury, as well as the
court and bystanders, and this evidence
sealed the prisoners fate.


The evidence given for the defense could
not counteract the effect of Shaundown S
testimony, for although all who were exam
ined testified that if Stewart had indelible
ink marks upon his hands, they had no
recollection of them, but that he might have
had them for aught they knew to the con-
trary. The evidence given by the Fosters
Bar Justice was positive and unequivocal,
and in direct opposition to more than forty
persons who had testified before him. He
gave full description of Jim Stewart, of his
size, color of his hair, shape of his head,
body, legs, and, in fact, every part of his
person; compared him with the prisoner,
and pointed out the difference between
Stewart and Burdue, even to the shape of
the nose, color and expression of the eyes,
color of beard, &c. He also said that he re-
inembered distinctly that Jim Stewart had a
defect on one of his fingers, occasioned by a
cut; that the first joint was stiff &C. He
denied that Stewart had an injury of the
second finger of the right hand, as described
by Shaundown, and stated positively that
the prisoner was not tue Jim Stewart of
Fosters Bar Nehemiah Dodge also testified
positively that the prisoner was not Stewart.
So did George Prescott, a former partner OF
Stewards. Ezra Dodge, and a few Others
called for the defense, testified more eau
tiously. They said there was strong re-
semblance between Stewart and the prisoner,
but they did not believe that the prisoner
was Stewart, &c.


Eventually the case was given to the jury
and in due time verdict of guilty was rem
dered. The excitement among the outsiders
was intense, for it was feared the testimony

await his sentence, which was to be given in
one week thereafter.


The prisoner was therebpon taken totjail,
where, on the following day. ], in company
with the Fosters Bar Justice, visited him.
The prisoner was much detected. In con-
versation with the Judge, he gave detailed
statement of his tribulatons and persecu-
tions, and closed by avowing himself inno-
cent of every crime imputed to him. He
said he did not care to live any longer, as
life had become burden to him that if he
had escaped from this charge, still he would
have to be immured in the walls of the pen
itentiary for IA years, for a crime he was as
innocent of as he was of the murder of
Moore. He wept bitterly on bidding US
good bye" and called upon the good God
who ruled all things well to bless the Judge
for the efforts made to save him.


On the following day Judge s., together
with number of others, including the
writer, returned to Fosters Bar, arriving
there in the evening of the same day. On
the night of our arrival, or rather before day
on the following morning, Judge Stidger,
was aroused from his slumbers by person
who had come in post haste from Marysville,
with a message from the Secretary of the
Vigilance Committee at that city, announc-
ing to him that the person supposed to be
the veritabe Jim Stewart had been arrested
at San Francisco, and was in the hands of
the Vigilance Committee; that it was the
desire of the Committee at Marysville that
Judge S. should proceed directly to San
Francisco for the purpose of identifying
Stewart, and if possible save Burdue. Judge
s. Immediately started for San Francisco via
Marysville, taking George Prescott with him.


AS | was not connected with any of the
scenes which followed, can not as an eye
and ear witness. describe them Conse-
quently, to close the history of this Eurdue
case properly, must resort to facts connect
ed with Stidger and Prescotts trip to San
Francisco, as detailed to me by both parties.


They told NE that on their arrival at
Marysvlle, on the day they left Fosters,
they found the entire city in a complete
hum of excitement, and thousand different
rumorS in circulation respecting the party
arrested at San Francisco that hundreds of
men who had formerly joined in the hue and
cry against Burdue were now anxious to
save him, and urged them to go on to San
Francisco and see the man under arrest;
that on the following morning they took
stage for Sacramento, and before they reached
that city met the stage bound for Marysviile
with Mr. Wm Hawley on board, who in
formed them that they need go no further,
as he had seen Jim Stewart hung by the
Vigilance Committee the day before, &c. lie
said, among other things, that he was now
satisfied of his mistake in swearing that
Burdue was Stewart, as he did at the trial
of Burdue.


Notwithstanding this information, the
parties continued their journey and arrived
at San Francisco about eleven o'clock that
night. They Immediately ascertaned that
the man they wished to see had been hung,
as Mr.. Hawley had stated, the day before,
and that in all probability be had been given
to the doctors As it was too late ut night
to make the Investigations required, they
concluded to delay matters until the follow
ing morning.


Early in the morning they set themselves
to work, and ascertaned that the body of
the man who had been hung was buried on
the evening of their arrival, and not given
to the doctors, as reported. On learning
this fact, they proceeded to the Mayor OF the
city, c. Brenham, Esq, and obtained from
him an order authorizing the exhuming of
the body Of the executed man. In accord
ance with the order, the parties procured a
carriage and took with them the Mayor, and
several gentlemen connected with the press,
proceeded to the graveyard, where the sex
ton was in waiting and had the body taken
up and examined. They recognized the dead
body before them as that of Jim Stewart.
They made thorough examination of his
hands, and strange to relate not a single
n.ark sworn to by Shaundown was found on
either of them The third finger Of the
right hand had the marks as testified to by
the Fosters Bar Justice, and it was the only
mark upon his fingers.


Having satisfied themselves that jim Stew
art was dead and buried, they returned to
Marysville, where they filed in the District
Court an affidavit of the facts herein set
forth. On receiving the affidavit, an appli-
cation for new trial in behalf of Burdue
was made by his counsel, and granted. A
nolle prosequi was entered by the Court, and
Burdue ordered to be returned to the Sheriff
of San Francisco county. He was so re-
turned.


During the time Stewart was in the hands
of the Vigilance Committee, Janson, who
had been knocked down with slung shot,
as detailed il these "reminiscences, visited
him at the rooms of the Committee He
testified before the Committee that the man
before him was the one who committed the
deed, and that the man in the Yuba county
Jail was not the person. When Burdue was
returned to San Francisco, a motion in his
behalf was made to the District Court that
had passed sentence of IA years imprison-
ment on him, for a new trial, which was
granted, a nolle proseqm entered by the court,
and Burdue was thereupon discharged


Stewart, previous to his execution, made
a confession in which he confessed himself
guilty of all the crimes alleged against Bur-
due.


To THE EDITOR This ends my reminis-
cences, so far as they relate to the Stewart
and Burdue matter. | might detail to you
the Providental circumstances which led to
Stewards arrest, but fear to trespass upon
your columns.

 Commander Lloyd B. Newell, U. s. A., shot himself to-day in the Merchants hotel.

 A schooner loaded with provisions, des- tined for Savannah, Ga, was seized by the police in the Delaware river.

 10000 men are drilling in this city.

 NEW YORK. April 27.-Gen. Butler has planted battery upon the heigths opposite Annapolis.

 The United States sloop of war Pawnee is at Washington.

 A large number of Virginians are in this city, having been driven away from their homes because they refused to take the oath of allegiance to Virginia.

 Governors Hicks of Maryland and Letcher of Virginia, have proposed jointly to Lincoln to guarantee the safety of the capital. Lincoln declined.

 An escaped North Carolinian says the secessionists in that State are carrying everything before them--driving off all now sympathizers with their movements, and threatening to hang exGov. Gilmer, who persistently y resists secession.

 HARRrsBURa, April 27.-The forces at Harper's Ferry believe Beauregard to be in Richmond with 1000 troops and provi- sions going to Baltimore.

 BosroS, April 27.--The harbor is being closed against shipments for the aid or comfort of the Confederate States.

 Concord dispatches say Ex.President Pierce has gone to Philadelphia and Bal timore on mission of mediation at the request of Ingersoll.

 NEW YORK, April 27.--G. N. Harney, who was returning from St. Louis. to Washington by order of the secretary of war, has been arrested at Harper's Ferry and carried to Richmond.

 RICHMOND. April 27.-It is reported here that dispatch has been received from Secretary Cameron, asking if he would be protected in coming to this city to ask an armistic of sixty days. A number of Un- ion flags have been raised in the western section of this State.

 BALTIMORE, April 27.-The Notifications on the Virginia coast near the approach to Norfolk. and Portsmouth are advancing ra paidly The entrance to Norfolk harbor still remains obstructed Efforts are being made to raise the frigates Merrimach, Ply mouth and another war vessel. It Is thought the attempt will prove successful. A dis. patch dated Alexandria, Va, the 22d inst, says that the 7th New York regiment was literally cut to pieces between Annapolis and Marlboro by the Maryland troops.

 CAIRO, April 27.-The steamer C. E. Hillman from St. Louis to Nashville was abandoned by her officers, and found to contain 1000 kegs of powder and other contraband articles. Southern passengers here report troops raising at Memphis and other points to proceed by railroad through Columbus, Ky, to attack Cairo from the opposite side of the river. The steamer J. D. Perry from St. Louis to Memphis was brought to, nothing contraband was found and she was allowed to proceed.

 CHICAGO, April 27.-25,O00 stand of arms have been removed from the St. Lous arsenal to Springfield, Illinois.

 PrRRYvrLLE, Mp., April 27.--It is re- ported that the Virginians have seized the schooners Gen. Knox, Geneva and Victoria of Maine. The crews have been sent out of the State.

 HAnRrspuRe, April 27th.-Large num- bers of virginians, mostly from Fairfax county are arriving here--refnsing to take the test oath. They report 15,Ooo armed men in Virginia.

 Perfect security is felt in Washington. Provisions are plenty. The ship Pawnee Is safe.

 NEW YORK, April 27.-The government has chartered several more steamers, and commissioned Senator Wilson to obtain guns for the defense of Annapolis and get ten more regiments from Massachusetts.

 HARRISBURG, April 27.--It is reported here that an attack was made by Marylan- ders on Hanover Village, York county, Pa.. on Tuesday, occasioned by great stam- pede of negroes-whole families were cros- sing into Pennsylvania. Great fears were felt of the departure of all the slaves of the border counties.

 SECESSION IN MISSOURI.

 WARSAW, Mo-, April 27.--Great south ern rights meeting here--resolutions were adopted favoring immediate secession, and requesting the Governor to repel any at- tempt of the administration to march troops through Missouri for the purpose of making war on the southern States or to reinforce the forts and arsenals, also com plimenting the Governor for refusing to send Lincoln the quota of troops called for.

spondents at New York, in calm, dispassion-
ate manner, expressing regret that trouble

ters-much to his surprise. In the meantime

tee. who presented him with a pile of letters,

ed his position he gave him list of all his
correspondents in New York, and charged
him to call upon every one of them and assure
them that his letters meant nothing You
see," said be, the character | have been

the fool | made myself to appear There are

article:
we give the sentiments .the prominence Of this column that all shades of public opinion may be fully and freely displayed.

 To THE UNION MEN OF LIrcHFIELD.- Freedom of speech and of the press has been, in theory at least, the pride and boast of our Country-of our whole Country. In practice, we of the North, with here and there an exception, have allowed the unrestrained discussion of all subjects, limited only by the law, and we have justly complained that for many years past this freedom of speech and discussion has been denied in the Southern portion of our Country, and at- Councils and that persons accused of entertain ing certain prescribed opinions have been sub- iected to all sorts of indignity and odfum, and in many cases knocked down, whipped, tarred and fathered, imprisoned, and even put to death without the form of legal trial, and without any other evidence of guilt than the mere suspicious efa Vigilance Committee or a Mob.

 While condemning these acts, let us not be guilty of like intolerance. Let us be consis- teut in the application of the principle of free speech, and refrain from threatening or attempt ing to intimidate those of our misguided fellow citizens whose feelings are on the side of the Southern seceders and rebels. Allow them the full expression of their opinions let them rejoice over the U61eaL O1 Lue uOVcAA"Cut lOICCo lCI them even raise the Secession flag if they choose. They will ere long find that they are their own worst enemies. In thus doing, they subject them selves to the pity or scorn of the loyal and pat. riotic, and when this conflict is past they will hide from the public gaze unless they are as de- void of shame as of patriotism.

 These remarks have been elicited on account of occurrences the past week in Litchfeld. It is greatly to be regretted that in this orderly and law loving community both order and law should be broken by attempts to suppress the utterance of Secession sentiments or Secession rejoicings This is all wrong. It tends to keep up or create bitterness of feeling among neiighbors and friends which is scarcely less to be dreaded than war itself. No good ever comes of prescription. The cry of persecution is raised for those who are the subjects of it, and a sympathy excited in their behalf which causes reaction in their favor. The true course is to let them "alone in their glory!" Besides Union men can afford to be liberal and lenient. Their cause is just; their triumph ultimately certain.

 A NEW YORK REPUBLICAN.

 Milton, July 29th, 1861.

 While we give hearty and cordial assent to most of the sentiment and expression of opinion in the above communication, we may take the oc- casion that offers to frankly state single point n which we differ from our correspondent

 He argues well that "mob' is calculated to De reused to the point of overturning both law md order, and that the cry of "persecution" is asily raised by those who, rejoicing over the de- eat of our Governments forces and who give ut erance to rebelous sentiments, ,are loud for free lom of speech, and cry, like the rebels, to be alet alone."

 ,artook not at all of the character of |" mob" or nob-law, or were like them only at least in point ,fnumbers, in unanimity of sentiment, and in a firm determination that these reasonable, seces- ion utterances had gone quite far enough. Some # our best and most prominent citizens, either y encouragement or actual participation, gave favor to the move. An almost unanimous public sentiment was firmly fixed, and a long suffering people were fully determined that something must be done, if it could be done quietly ant de- gently, to effectually express public feeling, and to save ourselves from the disgrace and stigma of eherishing nest of traitors and disunionists in our midst. Everything that was done was done decently and in order; no outrages were commit ted, none offered, for the purpose of forcing re. csntation, or of frightening traitors into submis sion. Only such as were knovn to have given utterance to denunications of our government and our cause were visited no disgrace was offered to these, unless it is disgrace to an American citizen living in Litch6eld, under the protection ofthe laws and the government of our Country, to acknowledge or to wave our country's flag Only these were waited upon at all, and because others were willing to make such concession to sentiment as to raise the American standard of their own accord, they ought not to have the ere. dit of being terrified into so doing, but that they did SO from the purest patriotic motives. At least so we wish to think of them and their elev. enth hour repentance.

 Other occurrences" which might perhaps be construed to partake of "mob-law" were owing, in one case, to most cowardly and brutal attack upon one of our citizens, and in the other to the uncalled for, impertinent, and dastardly crime of taking down the American flag from the roof of house which the perpetator did not inhabit, and with which he had nothing to do-the auth. ors of both which outrages were dealt with much more lenienty than they would have been by any other course, and which the sentiment of a com munity pronounces just and right.

 The visitations have now ended as quietly as they were begun, and if from the occurrences any and all who feel disposed to rejoice in our reverses and sheer at and bewail the triumphs of cause which is to save our country and preserve from anarchy are satisfied that it is wise in this law-abiding community to hold discreet tongue in their heads, we are sure no one will be better satisfied with the result than a New York Republican," or good men everywhere here and throughout the Country.

 At all events let us hope that the lesson will not be mis-improved, since those who are base enough to talk treason, to cheer for Beauregard's army in the hearing of those who have sons and brothers fighting in the great cause, and to gloat over any reverse or slaughter of our sons and brothers, are far better restrained by little wholesome fear of an instant expression of popu. lar indignation, than they are by words merely or the scorn of the loyal and patriotic"

article:
but when there is an uprising against the
authority Of State, and the State Govern
ment asks for Federal aid to put down the
insurrection, it is considered that it is the
duty of the Federal Government to grant
such aid. And how would this aid be
granted? 1t would be granted, we answer,
by sending out Federal troops to assist the
State Government in putting down the in-
surrection, We will cite case in point. as
showing how this subject was recently view
| ed in this State. During the excitement
caused BY The uprising of the Vigilance Com
mittee in 1885, Governor Johnson sent Com
missioners to Washington, to ask that the
Federal Government interfere to put down
the Committee. The aid was not sent, be-
cause it was considered unnecessary. The State
Government believed that the Federal Gov
Government never denied its own right to
interfere if the occasion required it. These
Commissioners on their return from Wash
ington, asked pay from the State for going
upon the mission upon which they were sent
by the Governor. We believe the question
as to whether they are to be paid, is not yet
settled. A good deal has been said about
the matter, but nobody has raised the ques-
tion as to the right of the Federal Govern
ment to aid State Government if occasion
requires it, in putting down insurrection
against the State. Those who opposed the
measure for the paying of the Commissioners,
did SO upon the ground that the doings of the
Vigilance Committee ld not constitute an
occasion demanding Federal interference and
they also opposed it. and chiefly too, upon
the ground that the Governor alone had not
the legal right to send the Commissioners, but
that he ought to have called the Legislature
together that being the power to decide as
to whether the Federal aid should be asked
for or not. We will not pretend to say how
many there are, who advocated the paying
of those Commissioners, and who are now
olamorous for the secession doctrine of State
rights. Will they say now that a State being
sovereign, the Federal Government has no
right TO send troops into State to protect
the State laws? If so, they have changed
their minds considerably of late. If the
Federal Government cannot send an armed
force into State if necessary, to protect
the State authority, of course it would have
been nothing but folly to ask the Federal
Government to interfere in such a manner.
Now, what is this secession doctrine of
estate rights worth? There is an uprising
of portion Of the people of the State-the
State authorities say it is an insurrection and
call upon the Federal GoYe"pment for help,
and nobody denies the right of the State to
ask for help or the right of the Federal Gov
ernment to grant it if it deems it necessary.


Now we ask, if the Federal Government
has the right to send an armed force to pro-
tect the authority of State threatened by
citizens Of that State, has it not the right to
protect its own laws by force if necessary,
when menaced or set at naught by the peo-
pie of a State2 If, as the secessionists a.
lege, a State is 50 sovereign and so independ-
ent of the Union that the Federal laws can
only be enforced in n State by the consent of
the State, they cannot, Of course, claim that
the Federal Government has the right to
interfere to protect the laws of a State when
menaced by citizens of that State The Federal
Government is certainly as Independent of a
State, as State is of the Federal Govern
ment, and if the Federal power cannot be
used to protect its own property and uphold
its laws in State, it surely cannot be used
to protect the property and authority of an
individual State


This secession doctrine Of Estate rights" is
palpable fallacy and it is strange kind of
logic which leads men to deny that the pos
session of property gives the right to protect
it. A strange kind of logic it is, which
teaches the seeessionists that they can seize
on Federal property. and that a war must
follow If the Federal Government attempts
to protect that property. A strange kind of
logic it is which makes them say that any
State can at any time dissolve its connection
their doctrine Of state rights"-a doctrine
which means, ave will do as we please
this is their motto in plain English, and it
would appear to nmbody their idea of the
privileges derived under q Republic. Are
they tired of Republic? Do they grow
weary of the growing American power and
American fame "a fame and power which
arose from Union in the American Revolu-
ton, and the growth OF which can only cease
in dismemberment of the Union? Has it CONS
to this, that the doctrine of Estate rights
has lead men to advocate not merely the se-
ccssion of State, but also to allege that the
seeding State should maintain her seperate
government through the aid of some mon
archiai power2 A weak State indeed would
that be, which, having withdrawn from the
Union. would ask for the fostering care of
monarchy and yet, we are told that this is
an idea of the State rights secessionists. Veri-
ly this secession doctrine Of "State rights" is
not only papable, but a very dangerous
fallacy.

headline: Pacific RepublIc in San Francisco.
article:
We hear from several sources that the
people of San Francisco are almost unani-
mously in favor of Pacific Republic. The
vote Of that city at the last election is con-
elusive evidence that large portion of the
inhabitants have no objections to living un-
der Lincoln's administration, and the feel
ing which has of late grown up there must
be attributed to some cause disconnected
with politics. From what we can learn, the
property holders and business men of San
Francisco have got the absurd idea into
their heads that the establishment Of Pa
ciGc Republic would greatly improve the
business, and increase the prosperity of the
city Ia addition to this, San Francisco,
like all commercial towns, contains large
floating population, who are always ready
to advocate any measure likely to produce
excitement and trouble, in hopes that some
thing may turn up for their benefit. These
causes combined, have probably had the et-
feet to build up pretty strong Pacific Re-
public party at the Bay.


There is a rumor floating around to the
effect that an organization has been perfect
ed, having for its object the seizure of the
Custom House and the fort at the entrance
to the harbor, as preliminary step towards
the formation of an Independent govern
ment the seizure to be made as soon as in
telligence reaches California of fighting
having commenced at the East. There may
be no truth in the report, but the lengths
to which revolutionary measures were car
ried in that city by the Vigilance Commit
tee in 1856, should be a warning to the Of
fcers at the fort to be prepared for every
possible emergency. The foreigners who
ranged themselves under the Vigilance ban
ner, would make excellent tools for design
ing men to inaugurate revolutionary
movement.


One thing is certain, San Francisco can
not influence the interior. That was tried
in 1856 without effect. The people of the
interior are quite we'll cOntented to remain
in the Union at least until the troubles at
the East are settled and If any revolution
airy measures are attempted at the Bay,
they will be put down.

The witness alluded to was named NAL
comson, an Irishman by birth and packer
by occupation" He was engaged in packing
goods from Marysville to Downieville He
testified that on the night preceding the
murder, he camped with his train only
few yards distant from the spot where Moore
fell that he arose early in the morning and
found two of his mules missing-one gray
and the other a black that the atmosphere
was quite hazy, and the sun not yet up; that
he looked around for his missing mules near
the camp, and, not finding them, walked
down the road towards Dobbins' house look
ing for them that not finding them, he
returned to his camp and ate his breakfast;
that by this time the sun was up, and the
daziness of the atmosphere dispeled that
in looking around, he saw, to the north of
the road, about two hundred yards distant,
two animals, one gray and one black:
which be supposed were his; that he went
to them and discovered they were horses
and not mules, and that there was another
horse, a sorrel, there also. Seeing these
animals picketed out, excited his wonder, and
he glanced around for the owners; that he
soon discovered, in sort of brush house,
three men, two of whom appeared to be
asleep, while the third was sitting in the
doorway watching the movements OF the
witness; that he went up to this man and
asked him whether he had seen any stray
mules that morning. On receiving an an
swer ia the negative, he asked the stranger
what he was doing there. He replied, "hunt-
ing stray animals" Malcomson also testified
that he then returned to his camp, saddled
up one of his mules and rode down the road
towards Marysville, passing Dobbins' Ranch.
Not finding or hearing of his mules, he re-
turned to his camp; that when within few
hundred yards of the spot, with his vision
obstructed by small intervening hill, he
heard gun-shot in the direction of his
camp. He rode slowly until he got to the
top of the hill, and then looked around to
discover from whence the report came, but
SAW no one He then descended to the fiat
where his camp was situated, and as he ap-
preached it, he saw three men coming from
the right hand or south side of the road,
cross it, and pass towards the brush house
where he had seen the animals and men at
an earlier hour of the morning. He gave
an accurate description of the men said
one had double -barreled shotgun on his
shoulder, and another pair of saddle-bags,
which appeared to be weighty, and that the
men came from the direction of the ravine
in which Moore's body had been found. He
closed his statement by saying that he did
not know Jim Stewart, never having seen
him in his life; did not know whether the
prisoner was Stewart or not; but this he did
know, that the man who talked with him at
the brush house and the one before him,
were one and the same person and that the
prisoner was that man ; he could not be
mistaken in his identity.


A lengthy cross-examination followed,
without in the least vitiating Malcomson' s
testimony; and soon after the examination
closed.


In summing up, the Justice said, among
other things, that he was not called upon to
decide whether the prisoner before him was
or was not James Stewart; that if his guilt
or innocence depended upon his identity as
Stewart, he should feel it his duty to dis
charge him that although numerous wit
nesses had testified and identified the prison
er as Stewart, he (the Justice) felt sure they
were mistaken. But, said he, am not called
upon to decide that point. / am sitting here
as an examining magistrate, to determine
whether there is sufficient evidence to war
rant me in holding the defendant to answer
to higher court for the crime OF murder.
This is the question for me to determine,
and however much / may feel disposed to
believe the prisoner innocent, duty, as we'll
as my oath of Office, compel me to decide in
accordance with the evidence. Therefore,
taking the testimony of Mr.. Wilson and Mr..
Rawley both of whom swear they never saw
Jim Stewart, but that the prisoner is the
identical man whom they saw at the Ranch
buying provisions, powder, shot, etc., a few
days before the murder, and the testimony
of Malcomson, who swears positively to the
identify of the prisoner as the man he saw
near the scene of the murder on the morn
ing of its occurrence, he must commit the
sprisoner to the Jail of Yuba county to await
gnis trial for the murder of Moore.

EXPERIENCE OF AN ANDRoscoGGIN Boy IN
ALABAMA.-Alden Moulton, son of Joel Moul-
ton, OF Greene, who has been at work in
Alabama, at a place q miles from Mobile,
during the past six months, arrived in town re-
Gently, and gives an interesting account Of his
experience among the chivalry. He was en-
gagged with several other Northern men in
cutting wood for a Southerner, and being
encamped some distance from settlements, the
party were not molested until Sunday morning
May 18th. At that time they were visited by
a vigilance committee from Mobile, who order
ed Moulton and the other Northerners to leave
within twelve hours, and then tied up their
employer Ia Southerner) and whipped him for
retaining Northern men in his service Moul-
ton left at once with what little be could obtain
from his employer, but failed to get more than
$50 of his wages. He passed through North
ern Alabama and Western Tennessee without
being stopped, and safely reached the United
States camp at Cairo. At all points South
ern troops were drilling and active war prep
aratioDs were going on. There were however.
many Union men in all parts of the South, who
are forced to maintain prudent silence.


The best part of Moulton's story remains to
be told When he reached Cairo, he found
the identical Southerner, who had heen his
employer and as such had been fogged, in
camp at Cairo. and actually enlisted in the
United States Army. On Moultons express
ing surprise at this, the late Southerner ex-
planned by declaring that he made up his mind
to give full payment and interest for the fog
ging which his Southern friends had bestowed
upon him.-Leriston (Me) Journal.

headline: A Rcminiscenee-case OF Berdue.
article:
A writer in the last number Of the San
Juan Press, gives lengthy account Of the
trial and conviction Of Berdae. at Marys-
vile. in the summer of 1851, for the mur-
der of a man named Moore. II was one of
the most extraordinary cases of mistaken
identity on record. The real murderer was
one Jim Stewart, who in some respects bore
striking resemblance to Berdue, which
led to the arrest of the latter at San Fran
cisco, for an assault with nteut to murder
"a crime committed by Stewart. He was
fully identified as Stewart, and under that
name was convicted and sentenced to four
teen years Imprisonment, and then sent to
MarysviIle TO be tried for the murder OF
Moore. There was no question that Stew
art had murdered Moore, and on the trial
the whole effort Of the prosecution was to
identify the prisoner as Stewart, while the
defense endeavored to convince the jury
that be was not the person. A large num-
ber of witnesses were summoned from Fos-
ter's Bar, where the murder was committed,
nearly all of whom swore positively that
the prisoner was Stewart, while five or
six swore that he was not the man. The
jury, however, brought in o verdict of gull
ty, and the prisoner was remanded to the
custody of the Sheriff, to await bis sentence.
A few days after his conviction, the real
murderer, Stewart, was arrested in San
Francisco, aud having confessed bis crimes,
was hung by the Vigilance Committee. A
new trial was then granted Berdue, and he
was released on the motion of the prOsecut-
ing attorney. He was then taken to San
Francisco, and in similar manner released
of the charge for which he had been con-
victed in that city.


During bis incarceration and trials, Ber-
due, as may we'll be imagined, suffered the
most intense agony. Soon after his arrest
at San Francisco, the crime with which be
was charged was of such an aggravated
character, that an attempt was made by the
Vigilance Committee to rescue him from
the authorities and hang him at once. His
prison was surrounded for many hours by
an infuriated populace, clamorng for bis
life, and it is said that his agony of mind
was so great that he lost thirty pounds of
flesh in twenty-four hours. The excitement
in Marysville was nearly as great aud it
is probable that his conviction in both
places was owing, in great measure, to
threats of mob, and the prejudice against
the real criminal.

At meeting of the citizens of Prairie county, at Brownsville, on Monday, May 27th, 1861;

 On motion, JOHN w. ADAMS was called 10 the chair and J. c. MoRRILL appointed secretary.

 R. s. Can't, Esq, explained the object of the meeting to be 10 take into consider ation the action of the citizens of Pigeon Roost township in hanging three negroes and a white man, who had planned an in- surrection.

 Also, the issuing of bonds by the Coun- ty Court of Prairie county, for military purposes, was taken into consideration, and it was suggested that bonds be issued in sums of $50, in ordersthat the means may be more efficiently used.

 On motion of R. s. Can't, Esq, in was RESOLVED, That the action of the citizens of Pigeon Roost township in the investigation of a contemplated servile instruction in that neighhorhood, and the execution of the guilty parties, is hereby fully approved, and that we, the citizens of the county of Prairie, hereby pledge ourselves to share the responsibility of that action with the Vigilance Committee at Hickory Plain, and to sustain them in that action as far as in our power. On motion, Resolved, That the issuing of bonds by the County Court be reduced to $50, instead of the sums heretofore designated. On motion, Resolved, That the Commission CTS have the power through the County Court, to raise the amount of interest on the bonds to as high as 10 per cent.

to search for the criminals who lurk about
the city.

From the Dublin Irishman May H.
| This American war fills us with pain anC
| disgust, such as We have no words to convey

and South who now thirst for one-another'

And for what2 The ambition of few
INSCRIPTIONS demagogues the fanaticism o

Our sympathies are still with the South
we confess. Not that we have any othe
feeling for slavery, the curse of America
than one of aborrence but because we be
| leve the South has been forced into thi
quarrel by the arrogance and fanaticism of
faction in the North.


Yet-shall we frankly confess it ?-ou
sympathy with the Southerns has been des
perately shaken since we last wrote. Why
Simply then, because we have, in the mean
time, found the leading newspapers in Eng
land defending that side of the quarrel.


A friend Or two have already taken US tC
task for what we said on this subject las
week They have accused us of backing UP
slavery, of siding with the masters of the
poor Negro, and all that. That have ear.
nestly protested that we are in the wrong

we were "leetle" in the wrong last week
But understand. We have nothing to re-
tract on the "nigger" question: we have nc
apology to make for supposed advocacy Of
slavery. The one single reason why we
think we were not altogether in the right is
this: we find the organs Of England on the
same side.


When England takes part with the South,
she can have no possible good object in view.
When sho loudly backs up the seeded States
she must have discovered that the integrity
of the Union was inimical to her piratical
power. Therefore, though the South seem.
to have been right in this quarrel, we confes:
to pang of terror and ALARM when we find
our enemy-the enemy of humanity-Eng
land-backing up the quarrel of the South
erners.


When we Irish are side by side with
England in any quarrel, we must be in the
wrong. 1t is the natural instinct Of our race
to hate the English side and take the other
and if the southern States of America have
England for their hacker, they must look OIL
it as Il thing of fate to have Ireland for theil
foe.


The special organ of English opinion-thc
Times-sides with the Southerns and talks
of sending ships to keep their coasts clear
of course. that cotton may be still freely eX-
ported. And the English government does
send ships of war into the Gulf of Mexico
accordingly, The smaller fry follow in the

astonlshed p when we find what processes to
be the organ of English Catholics---a period
ical called the Rambler-Lacllin up the
SOuth with in md iprr fo
ventlY for their success over the North And
on what ground? Because, as the Rambler
openly declares, the great Republic of the
United States was the one great rival OF
England on the high seas-an "arrogaat
rival, to He hated and abhorred-and SO this
blessed Christian journal expresses its earnest
hope that the said Republic may be broken
up, the arrogant rival destroyed, and the
pirate flag of England be free to float tri-
umphant over the oceanl


We confess we were not prepared for this
startling view of the question and since we
have read these English pronunciamentos our
sympathy with the Southern States mas re-
ceived a dreadful blow.


In taking side or any quarrel, England
can only have her own base and selfish de-
signs in view These designs are essentially
opposed to the best interest of humanity.
The Southerners may have right on their
side eriginally--as we believe they have; but
when England hvors their quarrel, then
such an enormous amount of wrong-diretul
unmitigated wrong-is leagued with them as
almost utterly obliterates their right, and
leaves the overwhelming balance Of justice
on the other side. God pity these Sotherns
blighted by tie curse of English favor aud
support


We take the other side instinc;ively: for
our hereditary foe is over the way Whose
accepts the alliance and friendship of our foe

enemy by that very act; and We cannot

A man named Janson, the proprietor of a

Soon it was noised abroad that Jim Stew

His coactctton had been determined on at the

NEssEE-The Louisville Journal, of August
18th, gives the annexed particulars relative
to the expulsion of Judge Catron from Nash
vile, Tennessee:


One day last week the Vigilance Commit.
tee of Nashville waited upon Judge Catron,
and informed him that he must either resign
his Office fudge or leave the State, and ask
ed him which he would do. The Judge was
not prepared to render an answer. The
Committee gave him twenty four hours to de-
eide upon his cause, letting him understand
that if at the end of that time he should ne;-
ther have resigned nor left Tennessee, they
would take his affairs into their own hands
meaning that they would eject him by what
ever force might be found necessary. With
in the twenty four hours the old man took
his departure from Tennessee, leaving bis
aged wife behind him, as she was too sick and
feeble to be removed We heard of him in
this city on Friday or Saturday. but did not
see him. We presume that he is still in this
vicinity

DEAR SIR--I sit down to give you, in as brief manner as possible, an account of the awful condition of our country. An intended insurrection of the slaves, assisted by many white men, has been disclosed by negro. It was to have commenced oil the 4th of July. and was not disclosed un- til the night of the 2d. I went up to Liv- ingston. On the Sd and 4th the excite ment exceeded any thing l ever saw. l joined company and assisted in taking se- veral white men and negroes. A steam doctor, by the name of Cotton, was com uander-n-chef. We took him and deli vered him at Livingston, on the night of the 3d. We also took Doctor Saunders, formerly of Summer county, Ten, and one other. Saunders was a steamer. A court of twelve men were appointed to examine and pronounce sentence. Cotton and Saun- ders aud the third person, whose name forget, were hung on the 4th, and 9 negroes, at the same time. We have taken IT men, whose names Cotton gave up under the gallows. They are trying them at Living ston. One was hung yesterday, at Dr. Deans, "a steamer.) Cotton stated that there were number of steam doctors con- cerned, but he could not reeollect their names. Col. Perkins, of Madison, and q party of men went down on Big Black, on the night before last, to take man by the name of Sharkey, a rich planter. In try ing to take him in his house, he killed Per- kns, and wounded one other badly, and wounded two horses mortally. Sharkey's hand was shot the moment he fired the first gun, which killed Perkins. He then fired his pistols with his left hand, and re- treated and made his escape.

 l went down at the head of five men on yesterday morning, and found sharkey, and took him and delivered him at Clinton. have been the leader of small party, ne- yer more than men. have taken three prisoners, all of whom are now under trial, at Clinton, before committee. l have no doubt but that all those at Livingston will be hung. have not time to give you the particulars at present. 1t Is certain that this country has been ii q critical sit uation. (Plan.) Cotton was to commence at Battles Bluffs and proceed to Livingston, thence 10 Vernon. thence to Clinton, thence tO VdChSOut tiltiG u lOD tHC bdHh5 thCuCO to Raymond, thence to Port Gibson, thence to Natchez. It was as well planned as It could have been. Ii is believed from Cot ton's confession, that there are some hun- dreds of whites engaged. have not slept two hours in the twenty-four for six days and nights, and have been on horse back more than four-fifths of the time. You may judge that am not in a condition for writing. have to hurry to Clinton this morning, and sent to q neighbor to get a horse, and concluded, while waiting, to write you line. l will give you tho rough account in few days. THE SAN FRANCISCO ELECTION.
article:
THE SAN FRANCISCO ELECTION.


A few weeks ago Gen. Estell an
nounced in the assembly chamber, that
no man who sympathised with the vig-
lance committee would ever again be
elected to the legislature from San
Francisco. The democratic portion of
the assembly, with one or two excep-
tions, confessed their faith in the pre-
diction, and leading democrats through
out the state received and reiterated the
words of the great oracle as truth. At
the time the General made his grand
speech, nobody expected that the mat
ter could be tested before next fall;
and it was expected that, by that time,
the remembrance of the vigilance COM
mittee would be pretty much effaced
from the public mind, and buried be-
meath thoughts of other and fresher is
sues. So that, apparently, there was
but little risk in assuming the character
of prophet, because the truth of the
prophecy would, in all probat ility, new
er be determined.


But alas for these soothsayers, they
were put upon their trial too soon. Had
they placed the date Of the events
which they foretold far off in the future,
they might possibly have escaped a
conviction of imposition. Had they
said that twenty, or ten, or even five
years hence, no man would be elected
on the vigilance issue, they would have
placed themselves in a safe position.
But no : they supposed that anything
which they promulged in the name of
democracy, would be received as gos-
pei !; and SO they must needs proclaim
that the "reaction" had come - that
vigilance was already unpopular, even
at the very. scene of its triumphs - and
that never again in San Francisco
would one of its friends be elected.


Mr.. Tilford inflicted terrible blow
upon his anti-vigilance friends, when he
resigned his seat in the senate. But he
had pressing interests to attend to at
Washington. Important federal posi-
tions were to be filled on the Pacific,
and host of political beggars had al
ready gone to the national capitol. He
was forced, however reluctantly, to fol-
low them in order that his graceful
manners and pleasing address might
have their due influence upon the in
coming administration. A special elec-
ton was called to choose his successor
Here, then, was an unexpected oppor
tunity of proving the truth or falsehood
of what these braggarts had been say
ing. The issue was fairly and squaroly
that of vigilance and anti-vigilance. -
The forces were vigorously and loudly
rallied on either side. Jones was the
candidate of the so-called claw and Or
der" party, with the strength of the
democratic name in his favor; Wood
worth was the candidate of the vigil
antes, supported by no other party, or
combination whatever. The election
came off on the gath, and Woodwork
was elected by a majority of fifteen Aum-
dred and ninety eight.


We suppose now that these buster
ing towards will let this vexed question
of vigilance rest. We hope that the
miserable braggartism which they were
afraid to exhibit before the last general
election, but which they have been so
prolific of since, has now been settled
by little wholesome fear. By the fan
tastic tricks which they have cut over
what they supposed to be dead body,
they have aroused for moment, the
sleeping giant, and with single move
of his powerful arm, he has thrown them
from him, frightened and trembling
We rather think they'll let him sleep
hereafter.


We hope that this senseless persecu-
ton of the vigilance committe will here
end. Its honest opponents must now
see, that, whatever there was right or
wrong about it, it was a movement of
the people was sustained by the peo-
pie and will be sustained by the peo-
pie, as long as the agitation of it lasts.
Those who conscientiously oppose it.,
say that it affords precedent which
will endanger the future stability of
government. Why then, we ask, do
you endeavor to keep the precedent
continually before the public mind +! 1t
cannot be to punish the offenders, for
they, if any there be, are the sovereign
people, and who is to be the hangman

the first can be filled by Senator, the sec
ond one has no duties to perform but what
might easily be effected by contract, and as
for the third and last named officer the Sec
re'ary of State, could fill his place as we'll as
not.


These Offices are all provided for in the
constitution and are each of them referred
to in two or more sections, which harmon
ise with each other.


Now it is true you may reduce the saar-
les to these places, until they will no longer
be desirable, and then to the scandal of the
state they will fall into the hands of persons
who will use them for purposes of bribery
and gain.


1t is also provided that, there shall be
elected, an attorney for the people, who by
way of compliment to the usage in other
States, is styled District Attorney, although,
he is but county officer.


The duties of this Office may be discharg
ed by any lawyer who is worthy the conf
dence of the community as an attorney
and is purely of business nature. Often it
happens one attorney is a good criminal
lawyer, whilst another is more expert in civil
business;-the two qualities are seldom COM
bined in the same person. When elected
he holds bis Office for a fixed period, and is
responsible only to the people at large, in
stead of moving under the watchful eyes of
a board OF Supervisors with full power to
employ and discharge as best suited the in
teress they represent


If any one can give good reason why
counties should transact their business differ
ant than prudent citizen does his private
affairs; we have not heard it. In our poor
judgement this office should be abolished,
notwithstanding it has been sanctioned by
long usage There was time in the his
tory Of the English people, when party spirit
ragged intoerably, when the executive power

murder, the best and most blameless citizens;
and the people established for themselves as
barrier between themselves and this tyrany
the Grand Jury and provided that none
should be obliged to answer for an infamous
or felonious charge, unless by indictment
found by this jury.


This was right and proper in the time it
was needed; it was step in advance, and

as body are no more nor less, than head

article:
The opposition press are making themselves
quite pleasant under the impression that they
can induce the people to believe that the
Democratic party has taken stand upon
and against the Vigilance movement Of last
spring. In proof Of this they cite the action
of the Legislature on the vote of Dr. Scott
and Father Gallagher, and the vote on the
resolution of Mr., Stafford on the abuse by
Estell ofthe privilege question:" s (


We might as we'll accuse the American
party Of the crime of embezzement because
of the conduct of Treasurer Bates The
question has never been even debated in any
party council Of the Democrats of the State
at large, and because men from the noun
taius choose to misrepresent the sentiments
Of their constituency upon this subject they
would make that constituency responsible for
this assumed reflection of opinion. .nvd'


The rantngs of these representatives do
not reflect the decision of the people upon
this subject, for the very excellent reason
that they have never passed upon the ques-
ton, as a political body. When the Demo
cracy make Cen Estell and the State Jour
nal their mouth pieces, we will consider the
charge as having some sembance of truth,
at present their enunciations are no more
like the honest shout of our stout legions,
than is the sound of tin whistle like that
Of the trumpet of Gabriel. If the party as
such, has taken any stand whatever, it is
against admitting this local quarrel to be-
come a party issue.


The Republican element of the Vigilance
Committee in San Francisco, endeavored to
have it (the Committee) espouse their cause;
the Young Mems Democratic Club" took
up the glove. and if certain of the members
of the Legislature choose to make themselves
the tools of that Club, it does not thereby
become Democratic ISSUE The State Jour
nal advocates the cause Of the Steam Naviga-
ton Company, and the Legislature has neg
lected thus far TO check its power to impose
upon the pubic-does the Democracy for
that reason declare itself supporter of
monopoly corporations When men assum


ing to be Democrats occupying any position,
illustrate by their acts, a true sense of the
living sentiment of Democracy, then those
acts will bird the members of the party,
otherwise one may look for dissensions in
the ranks, and new combinations to spring
forth from the dissatisfied elements. In the
mean time we shall labor for harmony among
the Democracy, that our efficient organiza-
ton may be of advantage to the public, and
shall not use the term ''recreant Democrat"
without just cause.

DREADFUL STORM AND SuIpwREcKs.-On
Sunday morning Jan. 10th, commenced the
severest storm at the northeastern part of
the United States known for many years.
1t extended over the eastern, middle and
western States, and as far south as Virginia.
and continued with but little abatement Of
violence until Monday at midnight. Snow
fell to an average depth of two feet, and in
some places drifted to the height of fifteen
feet. All the railroads were blocked, and
the mails stopped.


The cold throughout this storm was in
tense, and many persons were frozen to death
in the roads. So encountered were the roads
that on the 2st January, when the eastern
mail arrived at New Haven, Connecticut
the conductor there refused to send on train
to New York. There were great many
passengers for California, who were deter
mined to be in New York in time for the
seamer-which they could not have been if
the train had laid over; consequently, there
was a row, and the passengers broke open
the place where the conductor had conceal
ed himself, and forced him to start the
train.


On the coast the storm was most disastrous
The brig Emcline, from tbs West Indies,
went ashore at Barnegat on Sunday broke
to pieces, and all hands perished. Several
other vessels were wrecked or driven to sea
In Massachusetts Bay the most damage was
done to shipping. We have accounts of
more than Il dozen wrecks in the vicinity of
Boston. The ship Orrissa from Calcutta,
was wrecked on Cohastetts Beach, and the
mate and three seamen drowned. Bark
1edesco from Cadiz, Captain Patterson, was
wrecked at Swampscot, near Lynn, and all
hands perished. Ship California from Sur
imam, and bark New Empire, from Mobile,
were wrecked on Cohassett Rocks; crews
saved in life boats. Bark 4. G. Cothraa,
from Apalachicola, went ashore at Race
Point; crew saved. Several smaller craft
were also wrecked at various points in the
Bay, and others were driven to sea from
their moorings. Owing to the disarrange-
ment of many of the telegraphs and the
stopage of the railroads, our information as
yet is from but limited extent of the sea
coast.

 Yesterday morning at 10 o'clock, the vicinity of the corner of Vine and Fourth streets was the scene of intense excitement. most bloody affair took place, which resulted Tn United States Deputy Marshal John C. Elliot being mortally stabbed by a runaway slave from Kentucky, and the slave being shot. THE OWNERSHIP OF SHE SLAVES AND THEIR

 ESCAPE.

 The particulars of the affair are as follows: About seven years ago Col. c. A. Withers, of Covington, Ky, (Superintendent of the Gov ington and Lexington Railroad, purchased from his nephew slave woman, whose husband was owned by a gentleman in the immediate neighborhood. The purchase was made solely with view of preventing the separation of the slaves as the Colonel's nephew was about to locate in Missouri. Two years afterwards the owner of the slave man died, and his son, be- coming heir to the estate, desired to dispose of the man by sending him to the south and offer ing him for sale. Col. Withers again came toward and prevented the separation of man and wife by purchasing the husband

 He located the pair in good house, we'll and conveniently furnished, and treated them in the most kind manner, as every one acquant- ed with the Colonel will testify that nothing but the milk ofhuman kindness flows through his veins." Recently the managers and agents of the underground railroad have been tamper ing with the slaves, and on Saturday evening, June 10th, they made their escape. 1t is well known that there is regularly or ganized vigilance committee of the under ground railroad directors in this city, and in fact, in all the northern and most of the south ern cities A member of their lawless lnstltu- ton, becoming, no doubt, disgusted with his unen viable position, exposed the affair of the running off of Col. Wither's slaves and gave the necessary information last week as to their whereabouts. A meeting of the vigilance com mittee was held on Friday, and money raised to run the slaves off at twelve o'clock last night.

 WHERE THE SLAVES WERE sECRETED. From the information obtained, it was as. certained that the slaves of Col Withers, whose names are Irwin Broadus and Angeline Broa- dus, were secreted in room No. IS, in Taft's building on Vine street, just above Fourth, ad- joining the Gazette office. This room was oc- cupied by Wm. A. Conolly, one of the elit0r, of tue Cincinnat, Duly Commercial. Conolly resided with his family few miles from the city on the line of the Cincinnati, Ham, ilton and Dayton railroad, but his business in the city required his attepyion at night, and | this room was his headquarters He formerly published little seven by nine sheet of rank abolition character, but it died from lack of patronage, after short existence. It was de- voted to scurility and the abuse of respectable citizens. Recently Connolly has occupied his time in pointing out thieves to our policemen, and in every instance he has proved himself an expert in the business. During the railroad celebration he had three thieves arrested, and his testimony in the police court convicted them.

 THE CAPTURE, sTABBING AND SHOOTING.

 The room of Conoly was closely watched during Friday night, and at ten o'clock yester . day morning United States Deputy Marshals Juo. k. Anderson, B. P. Churchill, John c. Elliott, J. K. Love- Jas. Woodward and E. B. Carty, having the proper official documents proceeded to make the arrest. In order to pre- vent the escape of the slaves over the roof of the adjoining buildings Mir. Woodward was stationed on the roof of the house at the trap door, having gained access from house two doors of. The officers went up stairs to the | room and one of them knocked at the door; no response being given, Mr. Elliott clambered up to the transom window over the door, and, looking in, remarked that they were there, for he saw their dinner" Forcing his body par taly through the transom, he saw the parties in d small room adjoining, and exclaimed " here they are.' He then endeavored to get into the room, but instantly fell back on the floor, upon his feet, and said he was stabbed. Marshal Anderson then endeavored to kick the door in, but not succeeding, grasped an old bed post near by and burst it open. At this mo- ment a shot was fired at the negro, who was standing fronting the door, knife in hand. He fell to the floor, and after short scuffie, in which he fought desperately, the knife was wrenched from his hands and he was pnioned. In the meantime Mr. Elliott had gone down stairs, and was assisted to the office of the United States Marshal, on the opposite corner, when it Was discovered that he had received two wounds ohe of most serious nature in the left breast near the shoulder and flesh cut upon the inside of the left arm, at the el- bow

 The slaves were conveyed to the Marshal's office also, and on examination the negro Irwin was found to be shot in the abdomen. Medi- cal assistance was immediately procured, Dr. Blackman attending Mir. Elliott and Dr. Dan lrdge the slave.

 The wounds made upon Mr. Elliott were in- tiictei by the dirk of a cane, and, owing to its narrow breadth, it was an impossibility to probe the wound to any extent The blade of the dirk was found to be covered with blood to the length of over eight inches. Internal hem orrhage eusued from the breast wound; but Dr. Blackman expressed the opinion that it was not necessarily fatal, although of very dam gerous character, and depending upon the ex- tent of the hemorrhage and the direction of the dirk to It's fatality Every care and atten- ton was paid to Mir. Elliott to render him com fomabe

 The wound of the negro was in the cavity of l the stomach, but the locality and direction of the ball could not be discovered In all proba- oility it will prove fatal.

headline: A Wrong to be Righted.
article:
The Union Democrat regards the pro-
vision of the revenue Law requiring pop
erty holder to pay taxes on all that he may
have in his possession, regardless of the in
debtedness that may be standing against him
as unj Just and onerous upon tax payers. In
the way Of illustration, it says:


"An energetic, business man will build a
house at cost of eight or ten thousand dol
lars, giving mortgage on it, at or before
completion, for three thousand; at the ap-
pointed time, if an honest man, he will be
assessed for the eight or ten thousand dollars
as the case may be, and the mortgage will,
at the same time, pay his taxes on the three
thousand. Thus the three thousand dollars
pays double tax.


This species of injustice has existed for
years, and it is high time the law were
amended in that particular. Should the
next legislature Judge any modification nee
cessary in the present law, We hope this i'm
portant item may not be overlooked. Tax
payers should be assessed for what they are
worth-neither more or less. After making
a fair return of their property, their Just
indebtedness should be allowed as an offset
The decrease in the revenue under such a
rule, would, we believe, be more imaginary
than real, nssmueh as it is generally cred
tied that scores of our citizens shirk true
assessment as the law stands now. A thor
ough and impartial assessment would, we
are satisfied, more than compensate for any
loss the revenue might sustain by virtue of
such an amendment. Added to which we
should, as community, have the satisfaction
Of knowing that every dollar collected would
not only be Legal, but just"

John Everson, pump manufacturer, was shot in the left breast, just above the nipple, by man named John Able, well known to this community as gambler.

 The provocation, we learn, was, that Everson asked Able to pay him an amount of money which The (Able) had borrowed from him whereupon Able commenced abusing Everson, and finally drew pistol and shot him. This occurred in front of the Worsham House, and in the presence of a number of gentlemen. Mir. Everson died almost immediately. Able was arrested and carried to the calaboose, large and indig- nant crowd following after him, intent upon summary punishment.

MUSTANG AND ANTELOPE HUNT.

BY THE EDITOR.
article:
Last Thursday we left HornltoS IN company
with the Hon. William j. Howard, on visit TO
his Rancho, situated some five miles south of
this town, on Burns Creek. The rancho en-
braces within its boundaries the very beaut-
full valley of Buena Vista, through which runs
the Creek, and around which the graceful hills
of the Pelone lift their gentle slopes. Fronting
the valley on the south appears the, bold tow
er-ke front of the Court House Rock-rising
up out of the top of an oval hill and stand
ing prominent to view before the gaze of the
admiring visitor. A capacious adobe building
furnishes pleasant retreat for the attendants
on the rancho from the summers heat-while
well, at convenient distance from the house, af-
fords water of most pure and excellent quality
to satisfy the thirst Of the industrious laborer or
the passing stranger. Near the road stands a
very large Corral built Of rock taken from a
neighboring sandstone quarry, which affords
most admirable slabs for building purposes


Higher up the valley is seen the barley field,
embracing within its ditched fence some two
hundred acres of land, the soil of which readily
produces all kinds of grain and vegetables


Long before reaching the house we passed
many cavey-yards of horses, guarded by In
dians, and quietly feeding along the margin
of the stream. Stroling towards evening TO
very large garden in which every descrip-
ton of vegetables were growing, we reached
the Indian Rancheria and saw the squaws
and children busy engaged in cleaning
wheat and barley in wooden battiers. Mr..
Howard and brother have some fifty or sixty
Indians in charge on his Rancho, most of whom
have been reared under their immediate care,
and for which It seems to us he should receive
a compensation from government. The males
were absent attending to the various duties Of
the farm, and the squaws seemed to eye us
with glance of curiosity. The Indians ap-
peared healthy and contented, and were dress
ed after the American fashion. After pleas
ant nights repose we arose next morning to
witness the preparations in progress for the
hunt. Shortly after breakfast, various bands
of horses were driven into the corral, and then
began the sport Of lassooing. Old mares and
young studs, colts, mules and Indians, were
all hudded together in one promiscuous crowd,
until the sweeping swing of the lasso put the
band in motion, and then the corral was filled
with dust and noise. One after another Of the
animals selected for the chase were captured
with the larrette and drawn away from the
throng and securely staked beyond the reach
of the band Of horses that were shortly to be
driven out of the corral The horses secured,
and the cavey-yard again turned loose to free
dom, the sport of mounting the young colts by
the Indians began to attract attention. Many
of the colts had never before been mounted,
and we expected to behold some lofty tumbling
and awful pitching-nor were we disappointed
in our expectations. A belt was bucked
around the backs of the horses, sufficiently
loose to admit the knees of the riders, and a
rope halter was tightly drawn around the nose
of the wild and timid animals. The squaws,
young and old, left their quarters to witness
the prowess of their ambitious sons, and stim


ulated the young equestrians by cheers and
praises. And well did these young bucks
need encouragement, for such pitching, such
rearing, such a biting and snorting and a
twisting, never was beheld since the formation
of the kingdom of hoss-dom. No sympathy
was manifested by the Indians for their COM
panions when thrown in the air by some af
frighted animal-the girls laughed at their
mishaps, and mocked at their misfortunes


When cast to the ground with force sufficient
to kill an ordinary white man, the Indian
would quickly spring from the dust, pull the
blind over the colts eyes, adjust his blanket
and his strap, and then re-mount, when the
same occurrence would again be witnessed,
and as heartily laughed at by the delighted
toomen Indians All things being soon made
ready for the start, the Indians set off at
gallop for the Mariposa Creek, driving the pack
mules or leading extra horses for the chase,
Directing our course towards Montgomery's
Ranch, we bade the hills adieu and with hasty
speed soon reached that gentlcman's abode
and were regaed with some cool and delicious
melons, and after witnessing some graceful
feats of his noble stallion, we again turned the
heads of our stecds towards the plains.


Bear Greek was soon crossed by us, and be-
fore an hour had elapsed steaming gallop had
brought us to the Lone Willow encampment
on the Mariposa Creek The Indians with the
pack mules and led horses had arrived some
two hours before us, and we found the colts
all staked out and wood collected for the eve

Another letter from Nicaragua.


As it is desirable to publish everything
calculated to throw light upon the condi-
tion of Gen. Walker, we give the follow
ing, which appeared in the Placer Press of
Saturday, December 9th:


VIRGIN BAY, Dec. 3, 1856.


Dear Hawhins After voyage of
twelve days, [ find myself thus far on my
homeward voyage We had fine pleasant
weather on the voyage Being detained
for short time at this place, the head
quarters Of Walker, [ have embraced the
opportunity to send few lines of gossip
from this Interesting locality. On the
Sd ult., Costa Rican sloop-of-war, carry
ing a crew of one hundred and twenty men
and an armament of thirteen guns, en-
tered the harbor of San Juan. In the
afternoon Walkers small sloop, the Gran
ada, ran out and engaged her. After
about two hours fighting, they succeeded
in blowing up the Costa Rican About
forty prisoners were taken, most of whom
have since died, and the balance are badly
burned with powder.


At San Juan we found that Walker had
seized two hundred mules belonging to the
Transit Company. There were only wagons
sufficient to convey about fifty passengers;
the balance had to walk. At several
places along the line we saw trunks lying
upon the ground, broken open. Every
half mile couple of soldiers are stationed
on the road. At the Half Way House
they were dying off rapidly with the
cholera


Almost every one Of Walkers men
met asked me for money to buy bread!
stating that they had not tasted particle
of that article for three weeks Some
had been without food for days at a time
Three-quarters of pound of beef per day
is the only ration furnished to the troops
[ have not yet seen single healthy look
ing individual in the country John G..
Eubank, our former Deputy Sheriff, died
of cholera, at Granada, on Monday last
Walker has been compelled to abandon
Granada and burn the town, and has been
fighting against 900 Costa Ricans, with
a starved squad of 500 men, for the last
ten days.


Hennesy (banished by the Vigilance
Committee) is in command Of Granada.
Girls. Lilly and Mike Brannigan are here
The former knocked down one of our
passengers at San Juan. This class of men
constitute the leaders of this marauding
expedition.


Two months ago Walker had l 800 men;
they have dwindled down to $50 In that
time they have fought twenty battles but
the greater number have died with the
cholera.


The natives are almost to a man against
Walker. Those who express themselves
in favor. of him are held in subjection
through fear. Conversation with those
likely to possess the best knowledge of
Walkers true position, satisfies me that he
cannot hold out more than six weeks longer
at the furthest.


Only seventy recruits came out with us
from San Francisco, and not two hundred,
as has been reported.


Where [ took breakfast this morning, a
soldier came in with an order from the
officer in command, stating that he wanted
the boards of which the floor was com
posed for co6ins. The landlord refused to
give them up, upon which the soldier left,
saving that he should return and take
them


All the soldiers are cursing the day they
came to this God-forsaken land, and the
natives are held in such abject subjection
that they dare not call their lives their
own. The beautiful country" SO much
talked of, [ have not yet seen; it IS GER
tainly not upon the route Travelled by US.
IF you have any desperadoes IN Placer
that you desire to be rid of, send them
here. If they are not shot, disease will
soon dispose of them. Escape is impossl-
BILE. Death is stamped upon the counte-
nance of every man who has been here
two months.
