headline: Governors Message.
article:
above document from a synopsis that was
published in the Californis american of
Thursday. After the Introductory remarks,
the Governor alludes to the Vigilance Com
mittee question in justification of his own
course in relation to that matter and in re-
viewing the history OF that body, very prop
erly concludes that their evident design was
the overthrow of our government.


His views in relation to the Indian Res
ervation system are in consonence with those
of Gov. Bigler, which were in favor of the
removal of the Indians beyond the limits of
the State


The message sets forth in an elaborate
manner the condition Of our State finances
and goes to show that the amount of cash in
lhe treasury on the lst of January, was
$2l2 ,404 o. Then comes statistical ac-
count of our monetary affairs, among which
it is shown that the expenditures over the
receipts since the State was organized are
$4,13l,12 81. After deducting the amount
of cash in the treasury from what is shown
to be our present debt, the amount owed by
the State is $3,777 ,054 "A.


After lengthy manifest of our affairs, the
Governor suggests that the Legislature pass
an act legalizing the State Indebtedness and
recommending other measures for bettering
our present condition of financial embar-
rassment, urging the necessity of more strin-
gent measures in the collection of taxes, and
also recommends that the assessors be paid
per entdgc instead of per diem, there
by making it their interest to increase the
amount of revenue collected He thinks
the foreign miners tax should be so reg
ulated as to give larcer proportion to
the State, and advises revision of the
present license laws. He also is in favor of
an income tax, exempting certain amount
therefrom, say $1,000 per annum, the tax to
be levied on all officers, State, Municipal &C.
He also recommends certain measures rela-
tive to what is known as the Civil Fund


In relation to the nor. payment of the Ju-
ly interest by default of Palmer, Cook s. Co..
he merely expresses himself as sorry it hap.
pened and hopes like calamity will not oc-
cur again, AMI declares himself satisfied with
the manner in which the commissioners con-
Quoted the war debt business


The Message strongly recommends the
submission of proposition to the people to
call convention for revising the State Con-
stitution He is also in favor of granting
protection to those who have purchased
swamp and overtiowed lands and suggests the
repeal of the laws prohibiting their sale ,and
with regard to school lands, recommends
their immediate selection and occupancy
The State Library is represented as in a
very hourishing condition. An inspection
of the affairs of the Insane Asylum is ad-
vised. The laws relating to attachments
insolvents, sole traders, homesteads, and di
vorces, he thinks should be amended, also
the present laws regarding interpretations of
towns and cities, and of rents, be remodeled.
The expediency of making the Offices of No
taries Public elective, is urged upon the at
tention of the Legislature. He likewise is
in favor of change in the election laws and
and urges the passage of a registry law, ,and
the erection of house of refuge for young
criminals, and favOrs the abolition of the
States Prison Directors, and advises an in
spection of the State Printing laws. He rec
ommends more efficient military laws, and
suggests that the mortgage act be amended
so as to include steamboats,, and stocks OF
incorporated companies


The message concludes with few para
graphs in favor of urging upon the general
government the Pacific Railroad, and in the
meantime. the construction Of an emigrant
wagon road, lined with suitable military
posts, from this State to the valley of Mis-.
sissippi.

 to beg, steal, spy for burglars and on thelr own account practice those vices which cannot be named in respectable language; five thousand great and small gamblers prey upon the credu- lous and the infatuated, standing all day at the doors of their dens in Broadway, as we'll known in nerson and profession as the Mayor himself; ten thousand lazy, drunhS-, 4L;~..:~,, ort-boys, SWlII-Doys, killers, roughs, and rowdies of other names, lounge on rum cursed corners of the streets ,mak- ing day disgusting, night hldeous, and travel dangerous to all who can be sus- pected of having responsibility or mon ey; thousands of emigrant swindlers, mock auctioneers, lottery dealers, ool- icy packers, pickpockets, hall theives, burglars, wharf-rats, area-sneaks, pimps and yampyres, practice their knaverieS as openly and with as little fear of punishment as though they were engaged in the most virtuous and legitimate of human pursuits. headline: Emigration TO California.
article:
There are several companies making pre-
parations to start on that long and teadious
trip from this section. 1t seems from some
cause or other that emigration have stopped
to some extent to the land of gold. We see
by late accounts that the gold mines holds
out faithful and yields in great abundance
We are somewhat struck with surprise to
know from what cause emigration is checked,
unless it is from the blasting effects of the
late Vigilance Committee. 1t is, however,
enough to astound the hospitality and honor
of any country. Its Unconstitutional efforts
aud lawless productions are spread forth to
the world at large. Even old England in
her great bosom of tyranny were never SO
corrupt and base in her oppression and aris
tocratic principles as that of the Vigilance
Committee. 1t has cast the dark cloud of
contempt upon her golden soil, and cause
the emigrant to look to the future, and lay
down his golden proclivites, and come to the
conclusion to stay at home where law and
civility is regarded as the only emblem by
which country can prosper and become
great. But, however, California is great
country, and would be still greater if it were
not for bad legislation and bad laws, but law
does not exist there however. There is one
kind of law and that is, the strongest party
and the meanest men dictate such laws as
suits their own purpose and convenience. If
country can become great under such admin.
istration, we would like to know in what way
We hope that her character will be redeemed
and cast upon the throne of greatness.

Our citizens are aware that trouble has.
commenced at Fort Scott, in Bourbon coun-
ty. By the latest accounts we learn the
following particulars, which call for the
prompt action of all true lovers of freedom.
For some time past the Rufians of Bourbon
county have annoyed the Free State settlers
under pretended legal authority. Their
horses, cattle, corn and hogs have been ia
ken under one pretence and another, and at
last a large number of writs have been OBJ
lained, under the Rebellion act, which the
Territorial Legislature has repealed. The
settlers formed a Vigilance Committee for
their own protection, and proceeded to try
several persons for stealing. No excessive
punishment was inflicted, but the men who
were known to have stolen hogs, ETC., were
sentenced to return them or similar proper
ty Ten days since, the Free State men
were gathering under the command of Ma


ior Abbott, of the Wakarusa. The Rev.


Mr.. Stewart and two others, while out on
the scout, were taken prisoners and carried
into Fort Scott. Next day Capt. Balm, of
the Little Usage, was sent out to see what
had become of Stewart and his companions.


They approached Barnesville, about eight
miles from the Fort. Here Balm was ac-

pursued, and the Ruffians succeeded in cap
turing five of the company. There are now
eight of the Free State men in the hands of
these hell-hounds. It was mistake on the
part of Capt. Balm, who is a brave and gal
liant man, in not retreating in more orderly
and soldierly manner On Wednesday,
about noon, seventy of the Rufians, headed

compensation was made to the Free State
men for damages, to withdraw his men,
Little demanded their unconditional surren-
der, which was peremptorily refused, and
the truce declared at an end by Abbott
whenever the Rufians advanced. Both
parties retired. Abbott had forty men,
but eight of whom had Sharpe's rifles. He
posted his men in the cabin and behind
| trees Little detached twelve men to the
right and twelve to the left, and advanced
with the main body. The boys fred. Mar
shall Little was severely wounded, one man

No one was injured in the Free State COM
pany. The Rufiians retreated behind an
adjacent house, and tie firing was continued
/ for an hour, when the Rufians retreated,
cursing one another for being cowards.-

| Free State men being short of provisions

tty, bearing orders from Gen. Lane. He

times wrong now unfolding the cor

headline:
New Abolition Movement in Massachu'
setts-Arming of the Nigger Worship
article:
We copy the following strange article
from the New York Herald. We only
hope that the statements therein made are
rather the result Of the exaggeraton which
characterizes the statements of the journal
from which we quote, or Of desire to
lay before its readers startling narratives.
The present may be regarded indeed as the
age of secret societies. The late Know
Nothing party gave an impetus to move
ments Of this kind which it will take years
: of sober and calm reflection to counteract
When we read of Vigilance Committees
and armed negro associations, the conclu-
sion rises unbidden that the experiments of
self government is failure, and that even
our boasted enlightenment is not suffi-
cent for the maintanance of Republi-
can Institutions. The train of reflections
which tho following article prompt are suffi-
cient to make the patriot weep. Here it is.


"We entertained hope that the recent
abolition anniversary meetings would throw
some further light on certain Massachu-
setts association, to which our attention has
been attracted for some time past. But,
save the vauntng invitation of General
Wentworth Higgnson for convention of
slaves to assemble publicly in the City Hall
of Worcester, we heard no direct illusion
either to the association or its power. That
invitation alone, however-giving the pro-
poser credit for the usual abolition sanity-is
proof positive that he must have spoken with
some secret authority to render the invitation
sefe and the persons of the invited secure; and
of the nature Of the league which lies behind
this invitation. we are now enabled to give
some details that will prove, we think, de-
serving Of very serious consideration.


"We do not allude to the Boston Wig
ilance Committee or its auxilares, but to a
secret society, elaborately organized, drilled,
disciplined and trained to the use Of arms.
The true title Of this society we are not at
liberty to divulge; but as its members have
adopted for their flag one OF the old symbols
of New England, we may call it by the
name in general use among its members
the Pine Tree League


"Strictly speaking, this league is not Of
an abolition character; its one sole and OK
elusive aim is the notification, in Massachu-
setts, of the Fugitive Slave law. All other
issues and objects it ignores, and politics
whether national, State or municipal-are
forbidden to be discussed within its gather
ipgs. Thus having no patronage to bestow,
mere politicians avoid it, and only those
ultra zealots are at home in its ranks who
are willing to do duty and make sacrifices
in support of an abstract principle.


"This society is divided into two orders
or classes-technicall known as assistants
and Athletes-the former comprehending
the new members and those whose senti.
ments are least advanced. The Athlete are
selected by ballot from the Assistants, and
SO exclusive is the organization that one
black ball. or vote in the negative, defeats
candidate; and none are eligible unless
fully prepared to adopt, to its utmost extent,
the motto of the association, which is Every
thing for the Cause To the adoption of
this motto we believe the elected have to
swear; but on this point our informant is not
certain.


'The Athletes are drilled in small COM
panies, once, twice, and in some places thrice
each week, not only to the old-fashioned
use Of the musket and bayonet, but in all
the modern and improved accomplishments
of the French chasseur. To these purely
military exercises is added a novel one
perhaps the most efficient for the purposes
had in view that could he invented;-it is
called the yalking-stick dill. The arms
for this exercise are cudgels Of all shapes and
kinds-gold- needed canes, hickory sticks, and

headline: Our Senatorial Candidates.
article:
Our Senatorial Candidates.


The Senatorial candidates nominated by the
Democracy at Yankee Jim's, are evidently not
such as suit the editor of the Placer Press If we
Judge from the manner in which he opens out on
them in his last issue. Democratic nominations
never suit the editor-he constantly enters his
protest against them, until it has become fixed
fact that in this particular he s not to be satisfied
The better the nominations the more our friend
Is disposed to growl and had be failed to offer bis
annual complaint we would have been led to be-
lieve that the convention had blundcred badly in
its work. But we are saved any misgivings-the
Press finds fault, which is positive assurance that
our ticket is "all right" and one eminently wor-
thy the support of the people.


With prophetic vision, the editor sees in the
nomination Of J. II. Baker, cause for resurrccting
the feuds Of the Democracy in this county in 64,
and that a few hundred Democratic votes will be
cast against him as "evidences of the distinguish
ed consideration with which they cherish the re-
collections of the past" With the editor "the
wish Is father to the thought" and it would be
all the more gratifying to him if his wor swould
prove true.


But Mr. Baker was opposed to the acts OF the
Vigilance Committee, and herein we have one
great cause of the editors dissatisfaction; and
being dissatisfied he does Mr.. Baker rank injustice
in saying that had he been in the last Legislature
"he would have stood manfully shoulder to shoul-
der, with Gen. Estell and cracked his voice with
shouts of delight and applause at the furious
TRADE Of obscene dcnunciation of Viglanceism,
which fell from the lips of that celebrated old
scamp" That 'obscene denunciation" was far
from meeting the approval and Endorsement OF
Mr.. Baker, or of any Democrat who desired the
preservation Of lecorum in our Legislative halls.
The editor may have been satisfied that the filthy
TRADE should have been delivered, in the hope
that in the future it would be a good political
nut to crack. Query-does the editor of the
Press remember the time she stood manfully
shoulder to shoulder" with that same celebrated
old scamp Gen. Estel, in the Know Nothing
State Convention in 1855. That was claimed to
be a convention Of reformers, men who were
going back to the "purer days Of the Republic"
Estell at that time was the editor of the central
organ of Kuow-Nothingism and was recognized
as leading spirit and exemplar of the principles
Of that party. Has the Press so soou forgotten
one of their ilustrious champions. tits true Es
1el is no credit to any party, but we submit that
his recent admirers should not turn so coldly from
him.


J. II. Baker, is gentleman in every way quail
fed to fill the responsible position OF Senator;
has liberal requirements, is familiar with the af
fairs of the State and county, is an old resident,
l. l.. .,,tar l., =,
strict integrity and morality Of characterize will
receive such an Endorsement from the Democracy
as will convince all Of the high estimation in
which he is held, aud will make an efficient and
honest legislator, in the councils of the State.


10 coming { o speak Of James Anderson, the can
didate for the short term, the editor of the Press
poses his lance and goes in full tilt, as ii to de-
molish his old political antagonist at a single
dash. We have read remarks of similar import
in regard to Mr. Anderson in the Press two years
ago-they were harmless then and will prove of
equal force at the present time. Mr.. Anderson
has outlived all the silly charges that have been
made against him from time to time, and to-day is
one Of the most popular men in the county. As
one evidence Of this, he was nominated by the
Democratic Convention by aeclamatou-h having
opponent; aud still further proof will be in his
election by sweeping majority at the coming
election. The twaddle about an Auburn clique,
and Mr.. Anderson's identification with it, is a
stale, senseless, and thread-bare subject. Such
talk is decidedly fat.


The editor of the Press failed TO inform his
readers of fact which We suppose be will read-
ly admit, that James Anderson possesses 10 an
eminent degree the qualities of u legislator; that
he is fearless, honest, and Independent in the ad-
vocacy of that which he believes right, and that
as Senator his course would reflect honor upon
himself and constituents


If our cotemporary desires to swell the majority
Of Messrs Anderson and Baker, we would advise
him to give them the benefit Of a few more notices
of the same sort.

os..1. ON the vigilance Resolution.
article:
I'm the last day OF the session OF the DeIno-
.r.te Convention, the Committee on resolutions
having made their report. Mr.. P. T. Herbert, of
M.ripOsa county presented as a minority report
IN. following resolutions:


P,.Olred, That the perpctuity Of our Demo-
cratic form of government, is based upon the
resnect of the people for the laws they them
selves create.


R,,cRred. That inasmuch as under our form of
government all power comes from the people,
and constitutions and laws are but the express
lions of the popular will, therefore the late vio-
latIon of our Constitution and laws, by por-
tion Of the people organizing themselves into
armed bodies and exercising legislative Judicial
and executive functions, is direct reputation
Of the principles upon which our government is
Sounded. and can but tend to debase us in the
estimation Of the people Of other countries, and
postpone the day when = Republican form OF
government will be the one only known among
civilized nations.


A motion was made TO lay Mr.. Herbcrt's res
olution on the table. which was strenuously
opposed by that gentleman who denounced the
Vigilance Committee and Black Republicans in
unmeasured terms, and complimented, in
handsome manner, Mr.. Nugent, of the San
Francisco Herald, for his independent course
during the troublous time Of 1885,


Mr. Porter, of Calaveras, contended that the
resolutions were q minority report, and could
not be summarily disposed Of, as contemplated
by the motion.


Mr.. Anderson, of Nevada SAID that from the
frst he had been opposed to the actions of the
Vigilance Committee, and WIS so still. But he
thought tho introduction Of such resolution
uncalled for and impolitic.


Mr. Hawks, of San Francisco, in lengthy
speech argued that the resolution involved
great national question of the utmost impor-
lance to this State and Nation. He did not
wish to shower down curses or anathemas on
the heads of those who appeared most promi-
nent in the bloody scenes enacted last year in
San Francisco, for many of them he thought
were far less deserving of censure than some
who kept in the background and pulled the
wires. He would leave the latter to the gnaw-
lngs of their own concencss. and sure he was
sheir pillows would be haunted by visions Of
their victims. He did not believe that Demo-
cracy had fallen SO low as TO fear taking the
responsibility, making the issue and meeting it
boldly in the face. Support Of the Constitution
and laws had always been cardinal virtue
among true Democrats, and he believed such
was still the case among California Democrats.
Mr.. Hawks, in the course Of his remarks, refer
red to the Democratic party Of San Francisco,
who, in the hour Of tribulation, when seemingly
deserted by their brethren throughout the State,
were not dscouraged--dd not fall into apathy
but buckled OIL their armor, marched forward
in solid phalanx and gave James Buchanan
majority in their own city and county.


Mr.. Lee, of Ell Dorado, opposed the passage
of the resolution. The question was purely
local one, and only interested San Francisco.
He knew residents of FL Dorado county, Demo-
Gratis from their cradles, who had aud still did
eympathz. with the Vigilance Committee, aud
lie knew that the Democracy of the men to whom
he referred was unimpeachable, The speaker
had always opposed the Committee, but as the
country is now quiet and the people generally
showa willingness to obey the laws, he thought
the agitation Of the Vigilance question unnec-
sssary. The fact that this convention has nom
mated John Il. Weller for the Gubernatorial
chair, sufficiently proves that the Democratic
party, or a majority of them, are opposed 10
that organization. As he thought the adoption
OF the resolution would inevitably split the
party, he should consider himself in duty bound
10 oppose its adoption.


Mr. Hoge, of San Francisco. said hc could
not sit silently and not take part in discussion
such us he had Just heard. The resolution
rested and should rest not only OH the platform
Of the Democratic party. but on that of oil re-
publican governments He was pleased TO see
that the Chief Magistrate Of the nation had an
hounced and proved himself determined to put
down all such reasonable organizations, found
ed for the purpose of setting at defiance the laws
and institutions OF their country. The Black Re
Fai,licans of Cincinnati and the "Plug Uglys"
at Washington had felt the strength Of the fede-
raj arm and the points OF bayonets in the hands
of u. S. troops. Mr. Buchanan has announced
himself opposed to the actions of the Vigilance
Committee and shall this convention, forsooth,
delay to endorse heartily the opinion of a Dem
oeratc national administration? This Vigilance
Committeesm stinks in the nostris of honest
men. The organization is base commngling
of every ism aud element that ever strove to
defeat the Democratic party or crush its prn-
ciples. The Vigilance Comnittce hung four
nen---every one of whom were Democrats!
They arrested three hundred and cighty-fve
others. Every Black Republican among them
was discharged. Who will now say it is not
Black Republican organization?


Mr.. Van VOORHEES, opposed the resolution On
the ground that the merits Of the question
should be confined to San Francisco. He did
not wish Wings aud know Nothings to under
take to teach him what was Democracy. He
ha1 never voted any other than Democratic
ticket, but was nevertheless always willing to
receive with open arms persons who wished
for the first time to join the great national
Democratic party


Mr.. Hawks rose to explain. The gentleman
(Mr. Van Voorhies) had seen proper to animad-
vert on his course 1t was true he had been
born and educated Whig bat when that party
ceased to exist, he committed the cgregious
error Of joining the Know NOthings. He had,
during the last campaign, endeavored to atone
for his misstep by stumping the State for Bu-
chanan and should continue to be Democrat
SO long as he believed that due respect for the
laws Of the country was a distinguishing eea-
ture of that party.


Mr.. Campbell of Sierra, offered the following
substitute for Mr.. Herbert's resolution:


Resolved, That the Democracy of California
will ever support the Constitution and laws of
their State, and of the United States and will
ever use their utmost endeavors to preserve as
sacred and inviolate that priceless legacy Of our
fathers contained in the Bill Of Rights and the
writ Of habeas corpus


Mr.. Whiteside, of Yuba, also offered substi-
tute. which was declared out of order.

A Mass Convention of the Free State
party of Pottewatomie county was held
on the 9th inst, at Rockingham, in said

chair, and L. r. Palmer appointed Secre-
tary.


On motion of E. NJ. Squares, a COM

lutions, expressive of the sentiment of
the Convention.


E. NJ. Squares, DR.. Adams and Charles
Jenkins were appointed said committee,
who retired, and after having had the
subject under consideration, reported the
following


RESOLVED, That we believe the most
speedy and sure way to redress our wrongs
is through the medium of the Territorial
Legislature.


Resoluea, That we believe the true pol
icy of the Free State party is to secure all
the Territorial offices possible at the Oc-
tober election.


Resolred, That sound policy does not
dictate further adherence to the Topeka
Constitution or State organization; but
we recommend that the next Legislature,
after repeating all obnoxious laws, should
proceed to enact such other laws as may
be necessary for the future government of
the Territory.


Reso1ued, That this Convention appoint
vigilance committee, whose duty it
shall be to secure as large vote as pos
sible at the October election; also to call
delegate convention to make our county
nominations, and transact such other bus
mess as usually devolves upon such COM

The all absorbing topic of public conve rsa.

Whether there be any truth in such wild

Atidavits favorable to him, the honest but false
logic of Judge Shattuck, man possessing in

Character, the testimony Of a lady at the Inter,

Manufactured favorable incidents, are put in

hers and elsewhere with q profase hand, to
create favorable public sentiment.


With the Vigilance Committee, all this is
clearly understood, und will be disregarded
At distance it may be efectual in making
some converts. Meanwhile the public at large

alton, will have weight--great weignt-in the

ded the statements of the Vigilance parties in

coming necessary for correct decision.


For the arduous labors, the unwearied ex.
ertions, and many hours OF close, patient atten
tion by night and by day, devoted to this case.
the Vigilance Committee are entitled to credit
In an organization like this, representing every
interest, and every nook and corner of the city,
gathering information from such multitude

comes more thoroughly canvassed than by any
other court. Our citizens therefore, have con.
hdence, that whatever may be the fate of Ter.
ry, it will arise from a candid consideration Of

en- n,asse, and we have temporary govern

article:
CrrObOrating Evidence Of the Nominating


of J. G. Fremont by Palmer, Cook & Co.


The subjoined extract is taken from letter
written, says the True Californian, by dis
tinguished citizen of the District of Colum-
bia to a gentleman in San Francisco, and
published in that paper.


The writer was in San Francisco at the
breaking out of the difficulties in May last.


1t seems the finger marks Of Palmer, Cook

ruin of California State credit, is strongly Y

the rounds Of the papers headed "Fremont

ble:-


WASHINGTON, July Is, 1856.


Affairs in California are creating consid-
cradle interest here, and the majority is deci-
dedly favor of the action of the Vigilance
Committee Its necessity and objects are
generally understood and appreciated, and the
only fear entertained is, that possessing un
limited power, it may abuse it. But of this
| have no fear, and impress many with my
opinion. The political horizon presents an
exceedingly lowering and variegated appear
ance. Party spirit never run higher and
fanaticism anticipates that the hour of
triumph has come. The feeling that per-
vades the North western, Northern and New
England States, is startling to every Unionist
and supporter of the Constitution. The demon
of fanaicsm is loose and emboldened by the
folly Of Brooks, and the ruffianism of Herbert
he appears to be sweeping away in his course
all of the wisdom, sense and conservatism that
have clung to these regions. What think
YOU in California of the nomination Of
remont? 1t took men by supprise was at
first received with laugh Of derision; but as
sisted by all the clap-trap Of Rocky Mountain
explorations and political ballads, it has
spread like wild-fire, and all the Northern
States are in blaze. The election of such
a man, representing such principles, would
dissolve the Union. have no fear of success
but it is the part of every American to do
his duty and | hope you and your friends
will take care of California. The Herald has
been bought, it is rumored by Joe Palmer;
and further, that the interest on the State
bonds, due on the lst of July instant, have
been used by that firm in creating public
opinion in the North and Northwest. -
told me that as early as January last, agents
was traversing Illinois and Indiana with abun-
dant funds for that purpose. Can this be
true? Has the money for the payment Of the
State bonds been deposited with Palmer,
Cook & Co.! Ifso, why did they not pay
the interest on the State bonds? This is the
second time they have failed Such laxity on
the part of the State or its agents must great
ly injure your credit abroad


The San Francisco Globe, from which we
copied the article we have alluded to, in the
steamer edition of the 10th inst, says;


"The people of California are too familiar
with all the statements contained in the arti
Gle headed "Fremont and his friends" to
need additional proofs Of their truthfulness.
Suffice it to say that although the article

month, nothing has appeared in the opposing
papers which, in the slightest degree, can
be construed into an argument tending to re-
flute the statements therein contained, unless
the letter of Able Stearns Esq, be consider
ed as ameiorating the charges. Mr.. Stearns

We are prepared to show that Mr.. Stearns'
letter threatening clear explanation is not
sufficient. We demand his statement of the
whole truth; and unless he gives US the
whole truth, we will render him assistance
such assistance as will make him sorry that
he ever permitted himself to be drawn from
his insi signifcant seclusion to bolster up
corrupt man.

 1sRpecanoe battle-ground, September B. 10 tie Editor of the Enquirer: .a

 The largest political assemblage ever con- vened Tn the west is now on the Tippecanoe battle-ground. It comprises Union men of all parties, now at work with the democracy to se- cure the continued undivided existence of our national confederacy, and to perpetuate repub- , can form of government. Their number is variously estimated at from forty to sixty thou sand, and should think fifty thousand as not exceeding the true amount. Certainly it is much the largest political gathering ever saw, and have seen many.

 The train from Lafay yette, which arrived about noon, brought at least two thousand persons, including the Hon. John c. Brecknridge, Ste phen A. Douglas, General Cass, John Van Bu- ren, Colonel Preston, James B. Clay, and other distinguished speakers.

 Immediately there was grand rush for the stand, and so eager were the masses to testify their attachment that the distinguished gentle men above mentioned were borne along almost over the heads of the crowd without voltion of their own.

 When the principle rostrum was reached there was one of the most exciting and inspir ing scenes presented which can be imagined- Almost as far as the eye could conveniently reach, on either side, was dense throng of hu- man forms, packed as closely as they could stand, with hats and bonnets off, and swinging in the air while cheer upon cheer arose so deep and loud as might have made one think the spirit of Tecumseh had entered each tree of the forest surrounding the battle ground, and with one accord the woods sent up a shout, whose slightest effect would be to re. e.animate the sleeping warriors who rested beneath the turf upon which they stood.

 The Hon. John c. Breckinridge he | ~ upon whose brow | Nature has written gcntleman,' was the first to address the assembled thou sands. He said that he regretted the necessity of having to apologize for half broken voice, but such a course the more imperative be- cause of the overwhelming size of the crowd. He had been called upon to speak again and again while en route for Tippecanoe, and that must be his excuse for the condition of his | voice.

 At this point General Cass made his appear ance upon the stand, and greeted with three times three hearty cheers ever rose from an assembage. He bowed and took a seat on the platform.

 Before proceeding further l will supply an omission which 1 had nearly overlooked, and that is in regard to the organization of the con- ventlon previous to the introduction of MT. Breckinridge to the assemblage.

 On motion of Mir. Williams, mayor of Lafav- cite, the Honorable J ohn Petit, of Indiana, was unanimously elected chairmal and after that list of vice presidents was endorsed by vote of the convention.

 Judge Petit, in taking the chair, made few remarks expressive of his appreciation of the honor conferred upon him, and of his attach ment to that Union whose preservation was now the dearest object to the hearts of every patrio. tic American citizen.

 l Mir. Breckinrldge continued his remarks, say ing that the great issues involved in the present contest rendered all merely personal considcra- tions perfectly contemptible.

 There are, said he, in this vast ass emblage which now stretches before me, thousands of Kentuckiaus who feel that they have a blood bought right to be present They re- cognize in this turf that which covers their fa- thers resting place, that of yours, men of Indiana.

 He must be blind indeed, or given over to fatal delusion, who does not see that this Union is now seriously endangered. The anmosity and ill-wil manifested by the sectional party of the north against the south might be per fectly proper were they rival nations; but, be- ing parts of one great whole, they are as unna- tural as mischievous. The geographical line which our fathers feared has been drawn across the hearts of our people, and, unless soon ob liberated, will act like canker upon the body polite

 The difference between the two great con- fictng parties of the country is unlike that ever before presented The sectional party of the north cannot succeed except by the total overthrow of society in the south, for the fif- teen States cannot, will not submit to the con- templated encroachment upon their rights of which the restriction of slavery to its present limits, without regard to the will of the people, is but the prelude

whole communities of men incur and commit,
when they attempt to defy the law, and to set
themselves up above its power.

GEORGETOWN, July 81, 1856


EDITORS ARGUS AN article in the San Francis
co Bulletin few days since, says the mountains are
ready for revolution in this State Though the
proposition is ridiculous to any thinking man, it may
be well to contradict it for while we admit that as
a part of the State we have sympathized with the
Vigilance Committee in their good work of regener-
alton in the City of San Francisco yet we deny that
we favor revolution. Our laws may be imperfect,
and our Constitution detectives but constitutional
provision is made for correcting those evs-and now
while we sympathize with the Committee in all their
acts of Equity, we desire that they should disband
without any further delay which should they do,
without any unworthy, debasing acts, they may
expect their mountain friends to oppose any legal
proceedings against them while we shall oppose with
equal frmness any appropriation of funds for their
relief


We advise the Committee to hurry through, and
to entertain no idea of revOltuon. Such a step
would be fatal to them. The people are with the
Committee as yet-but one false step will make an
instantaneous change. A VIGILANT.

execution witnessed by $4,000 people. The

dressed the audience in clear firm voice Said he
killed DR.. Randall in self defence, and prepared
for death-that he never lived a day at the end of
which he was afraid to meet his Maker Brace, on
the contrary, acted and talked like drunken man--
said he was drunk-and made nothing like state
ment, and interrupted Hetherington whilst he was
speaking. The last words Of the latter were


Il forgive all my enemies. God have mercy on


When Hetherington had got nearly through speak
ing, Brace said, turning to his companions Dry
up old fellow; you have talked enough don't keep
me here any longer. Damn it, dry up" He died

The bell Of the Committee rooms tollcd when
Brace and Hetherngton were launched into eternity
Neither suffered much. Brace scarcely moved
Hetherington moved but once.


The bodies hung thrty-fve minutes, and were
taken down by Coroner Kent.

deem it appropriate to accompany its inau-

course will be, because we have had the
conduct of the Record for the past three

article:
The Christian Advocate, of this city, has
supported theVigilance Committee since the
commencement of the organization as yigor-
ously as any of the secular papers. In the
issue of this week we find the following let
ter. addressed to the Publishing Committee
by the Rev Randall Hobart, censuring (but
in those mild terms which become n minister
of the GospeD the course pursued by the
Advocate We commend it to the attention
Of our readers:


DEAR BRETHREN Will you suffer one
who has been connected with the NJ. E.
Church for almost forty years, to address a
few lines to you, as conductors of the Adyo-
cate, relative to the course pursued by you
during the awful outbreak of popular vio-
lence in the commercial metropolis Of the
State?


g 1t cannot be matter of surprise to you
that in a state OF things so extraordinary as
now exists in our midst, good men should
differ in opinion in regard to the proper
course to be pursued; and while | would ex-
tend christian charity for right intention,
must deprecate the course you have pursued
in your paper during this excitement, cal
culated, as | conceive, to encourage lawiess-
ness and violence, that has already led to
acts that by the civilized world, will be
classed as treason, murder, piracy and rob
berry.


g am aware of the justification attempt
ed to be set up, and while | am ready to ad
nit that great evils exist, and that the
course of Justice has been perverted, yet
with all due Difference to the opinions ex-
pressed by many that | have every reason
to expect, differ widely from them, as tC
the proper remedy.


Il do not design at present to discuss
this subject. | am convinced that it would
be of no avail, that reason has not sufficiently
resumed her throne, to permit those who
have been carried away in the whirlpool Of
passion to reason calmly. But brethren
your position as the directors Of 4 Christian
journal, should be a conservative one
Where are we to look in time of storms and
amid the rage Of excited passions for words
Of calm and sober import, if not to the fol
lowers of Him, ''in whose hands was no yio-
lence: who when He was reyiled, reyiled
not again: whose voice was not heard in the
streets:" Shall our State, disgraced al
home and abroad, her laws trampled in the
dust, her highest officers tlse subjects Of in
suit and the butt Of every ribald jest, have
no sympathy from those who profess & tc
fear God and keep his commandments ::
| Has there been new revelation from Hea-
ven, since Paul exhorted, < that first of all
prayer and supplication be made for all that
are in authority:' 1t is now the eXhorta-
ton, :. let good men pray" for the mob:
But | forbear. ! took my pen to address
you "A few lines, with the faint hope that n
feeble voice mi ght be heard amid the storm
and that as Christian ministers placed in i
position 10 have some influence, you might
be induced to pour oil upon the troubled
waters, and thus secure the reward of him
who said, blessed are the peace makers, fol
they shall be called the children Of God.'
Yours, in the bonds of a peaceful gospel.


RANDALL HOBART.

headline: Democratic County Convention.
article:
In this mornings paper, will be found
call for the Democratic County Convention,
to assembled at 0roville on the Odd Of Au-
gust, for the purpose of electinS delegates
to the State Convention, and the nomlna-
ton of officers The committee in making
the call, have been unable to designate the
number of delegates to which some OF the
new precincts are entitled, because no party
vote has been given since the precincts were
established. 1t will be matter that must
necessarily be determined by the Conven-
ton. As every body seems determined to
90 for Buchanan, the committee were dis
posed to allow each precinct a representa-
ton for the whole number of votes cast at
the county seat election; but concluded to
leave the matter to be settled by the pre-
cincts and the convention.


1t is important that every precinct should
be represented in the convention. We wish
we could thoroughly impress upon the De-
mocracy the Importance of full represen-
tation. In these times, good citizens should
no longer neglect or refuse to see that pro-
per, honest and patriotic and faithful men
are selected to fill the public Offices.


Butte county is entitled to two Members
of Assembly the present year, and the IN
creasing Importance and diversified interests
of the county, as well as the State at large
demand that they should be "honest, capa-
BILE and faithful" Elect no one because he
is in favor of, or opposed to the Vigilance
Committee. Select them from the solid men
of the county. Delve into the mines, or
search over the farming interests OF the
county, and select men whose interests are
identified with the county. whose home is
in our midst, whose character, moral worth
and intelligence are known. There are such
men in the county, and it is the duty of the
Convention to bring them out. Such men
will not become the tools of politicians, nor
all them in their unholy designs of p.under.


Fellow Democrats, let US have full Con-
vention, and a fair expression of the people,
and we shall nominate good men and elect
them. Would all the counties go to work
with the determination to elect none but
men who are identified with the counties, we
should hear less of corruption-have more
Wholesome and Just laws and inagurate new
era in our State. Butte county alone can
not effect this, but we can add our mite to
the general good, and secure the services OF
honest minded honorable men if we choose
or by neglect can surrender our rights td
weak, imbecile and migratory politicians
whose only hope is plunder, and who present
themselves at every opening not guarded
by the people.

headline: The Shooting of DIR. Randall.
article:
The Town Talk, after mentioning the cir
cumstances which led to the assault upon
Dr. Randall by Hetherington, already pub
lished, says:


He returned to the city at 12 o'clock yes
! terday, in order to attend to some law busi-
ness, and at 3 o'clock wrote some instructions
in Judge Sutherland's Office, his attorney, in
order that that gentleman might proceed
that night to Benicia to attend to some law
affairs. He went thence to the s.. Nicholas
Hotel, where he arrived just previous to
o'clock. In the room were Col Gift, Judge
McCorkle, and Mr.. Taliaferro, conversing
between the desk and the window; Mr.
Casey, the proprietor of the hotel carriage,
leaning against the same; Mr.. Sheppard,
the book keeper, writing at his desk, and
Just beyond Col Bell and Mr.. Mckenzie,
State Prison Directors, and some other gen.
tlemen, one in conversation with the bar
keeper and one behind the bar.


Dr. Randall came up to the book-keeper.
who handed him two letters, remarking,
iocularly: g Doctor, | have two letters for
you, which I'll give you if you'll give me two
bits" To which the Dr. replied, in his usu
al manner, "rll see--I don't think they're
worth il - but opening one, he remarked;





the register of the hotel, which is on a swivel
on the counter, round. and wrote his name,
and afterwards read his letter, still retain
ing his position. A few seconds thereafter
Hetherington entered, and approaching the
counter seized Dr. K. by his beard, which
is very long, and said: s. Cd damn you, Eve
got you now :" at the same time twisting the
Doctor round, facing the northern wall


The DR. Immediately drew his pistol, but
before he could use it Hetherington fred
the ball passing close by Mr.. Sheppard, and
entering the wall adjoining the safe. The
residue of the affray occurred instantane-
ously: both fired, and Hetherington kept on
firing in rapid succession. The smoke CO
vered the parties, and the gentlemen in 'the
room we're panic struck-the balls whistling
around them so quickly that fears were en-
tertaned that each would be shot. DR.. Ran
dali crouched round inside of the counter,
Hetherington still firing when he got there.


Hetherington bent over the counter, and
fired his fifth and last shot at the Doctors
head the ball entering the left temple, and
lodged, as is presumed, on the base of the
brain, infcting a mortal wound Drs. To-
land and Hewlett were in immediate attend
ance, but, from the character of the wound,
recovery is impossible. DR.. Randall remain
ed insens; ble. which is gratifying, for, hang
ing between life and death by a thread, he
is cut of pain His right side was immedi-
ately paralyzed, whicn leads to the supposi-
tion that the ball lodged near the spinal
connection.


Hetherington was Immediately secured and
conveyed to the Vigilance Committee Rooms
So panic struck were all present, it was not
until Mr. Sheppards cries that Dr. Randall
was murdered the aid came forward to raise
him from the floor, and convey him, bleeding
and insensible, to an upper room.


The excitement spread outside rapidly,
the noise of the shooting causing many to
rush to the spot, and soon hundreds of in
quiring and curious persons gathered a
round, aud for hours the place was the CEN
trail point of attraction to all our citizens.


The balls, judging from the one picked
from the wall, were half an ounce in weight.
The south wall shows one shot, the north
wall, adjoining the door to the private en-
trance, another, and the east casing of the
door a third, while a fourth passed through
the desk supporting :hc register and the
book itself, within a hairs breadth of kill
ing the book keeper. Fortunately no shots
were fired to the southeast, or the gentle
men sitting there would have been shot
one at least, if not all.


Both pistols were obtained by the Vigi
lance Committee, and frtm Dr. Randall-s
only one chamber was empty. Ilethering-
tons were all discharged.


1t is represented that lIetherington has
been driven out of his mind by reverses,
particularly in regard to DR.. Randall's
transactions, he seeming to think the Doctor
desired to cheat him.

AFFAIRS IN SAN FRANcIsco.-The inau-
ence of the Vigilance Committee does not
/ appear to be very efiicacious in preventing
blooodshed in San Francisco The late an
nouncement by Telegraph of the killing of

The public mind is prepared apparently for

cisco. 1t was received almost as matter of
course 1t is fact that viii be admitted by

led them to excesses, violence and blood
shed, rather than the contrary one Of de-
terring the vicious and evil disposed from
the commission of crime.


The Committee have now been in session
two months, and have been the supreme
power in San Francisco, and we desire to
askithe public, whether crime has been di-
minished under their rule' Whether life
has been rendered moro secure un6er their
regin If so, why was Ford shot down in
the streets-why was Dr. Randall assaulted
and killed in one of the public hotels: The
particulars of the assault will be found in
another column.

Hetheriugton was in the hands of the Vigi-
lance Committee. A despatch of the 26th

quilted by the Executive Committee, and

Simultaneous with this announcement
comes another, to the effect that judy e Ter
ry has been acquitted by the Executive Com

warrant issued by the U S. Court could not

united an opportunity is offered for the

be~n The fate of Terry had not Hetbering-
ton been sent Il vctim--lkc the Ram at the

1t would almost seem that the Executive
Committee desired Il sacrifice to appease the
outside pressure, and that Judge Terry
would have been retained, had not Hcther-
ington foo ishly sacrificed himself 10y the
murder Of DR.. Randall.


To what do these things lead The law

their duty as law-abiding citizens, and mur-
der hollly stalks forth in the streets of the

and, setting aside all forms of law, attempt

power of the People Is found inadequate to

San Francisco 1t wants good citizens
men who combine and will uphold and main
tain the with power Of the People the majesty
/ of the laws.

headline: The Recent Events in San Francisco.
article:
The events Of the past eight days IN San
Francisco are Of the most extraordinary ma
ture, that ever transpired in free country.
From the tragic scene on the l+th-the
shooting of Mr.. King by Casey-until the
present moment, one fact has hurried upon
the heels of another in quick succession, thus
keeping the public mind under strain of the
most intense excitement, forbiding that calm
reflection which leads one to reliable ronclu-
sions. Knots of citizens would collect to-
gether, make up purse, and eagerly gather
from the telegraph wires the very latest ru-
1nors as they transpired at the scene Of ac-
ton. These again would spread the intelli-
gence, but little less rapidly than the tee-
graph-passing it from mouth to mouth,
until, if business was not stopped, men were
rendered less capable to transact it, by the
suspense that hung upon their feelings.


Il is great responsibility for any people
to wrest from the appointed officers the exc
cution Of the law; but it is far greater, when,
as in this country, the people are in the full
exercise OF the sovereign power and may
appoint who they please as their Judicial,
ministerial and executive officers. One may
excuse, nav, even sanction, the acts Of an
ignorant inturiated mob, goaled by starva-
ton, and insulted by protligate tyrany, as
has been the case in Europe. because those
people had no hand in making the govern
ment under which they live. The slave may
cast off his burden, and if done violently no
one blanes him.

In answer to this question, we can only
give our impressions.


The property holders and business men OF
the city-the very men most interested in
preserving and enforcing due observance OF
law in spirit and in truth, are the members
and leading spirits of the Vigilance Commit
tee. Men of property-rirh men-are never
As a body revoutionsts; strong governments
are their idols, for in their strength depends
the permanency Of property rights. We

quiet harmonious concert, without passion,
deliberately and with the most perfect order
as a mob.


The leaders are men Of intelligent discl-
plined minds; sober but determined action

characteristics of mob


Without the forms Of law they seem to be
administering it in its true spirit, and to the
satisfaction of the public-a mob acts with
out reason and in violation Of the genius OF
order.


Life and property are probably more Sc

ont-that these officers assist in the perpe
tration Of this villany, through adhesion to

We are again called upon to place upon the record

As soon as the first blow was struck Terry and

No sooner was the blow struck than a swift cour-

outside pressure, and that Judge Terry

ington foolishly sacrificed himself by the

front in the streets OF San Francisco. tire

men who combine and will uphold and main
tain the with power Of the People the majesty

MD HAMILTON gave fine serenade on
Monday last, attended 10y his associate mu-
sicians, and followed by three distinguished
gentlemen from Bidwells Bar, who all were
seen at about - o'clock to issuc from the
Lodge of the Independent Order OF uood
Fellows, known by the name of the Subter-
ranean, where they left the Deacon IN as
happy fame Of mind rs could be expected
at that witchng hour. As they proceeded
along the streets, entrancing the natives
with such " concord Of sweet sounds as IS
not often heard outside of Chinese concert,
or n Digger funeral, and drawing many Il
night cap to the windows by the power of
their melody, they discovered to their dis
NAV that one Of their party, JeemeS,
was missing. A long search was immedl-
ately instituted, and after a truitle-S waste
of much precious time, low moan was heard
and n voice family exclaiming, NlgiiantS'
be merciful . Take me off," I'm dry,
&c. Approaching the place from whence
these exclamations proceeded, the unfortu-
nate gentleman was discovered bent almost
double, over lady's clothes line What
were his feelings or his fears at this time 1t
is impossible to conjecture. Had he ever
been guilty Of a crime or even OF an indlS-
cretion, which, we may safely aver, he had
not he might have supposed himself IN the
hands of the Vigilance Committee, and suf-
ferng the fate of Cora. But the most rca-
sonablc Interpretation Of his incoherences'
was that having been Slightly saturated
with the liquids flowing from the Deacon'S
bar, he had hung himself upon the line to
dry, and now considered himself in proper
condition to receive the operation Of the
smoothing iron.


It was now found advisable by the party,
to beat an immediate retreat for the Sub
terranean, where, after refreshing their ex-
hausted powers, a beautiful song" The Lady
with the Glass Eyes was sung by the Doc
tor, amidst thunders of rapturous applause,
which concluded the ceremonies Of the morn
ing.

To the Editors of State journal:
GENTLEMEN.--I have observed an arti

the subject Of the intereeption of lettel
addressed by Gen Howard TO B. " Leigh
Esq, and the terms OF that article call iol
my reply. 1t is true that the henous erin,
seems to have been committed somewhere
for it is publicly confessed by those who ap.
pear to speak by authority, but you may
be in error when you hasten to the conclu-
sion that the crime was committed in this
city. and at my Office, However, am quite
willing, and even anxious that the facts shall
be brought out, whether they implicate this
Office or any other.


The very day on which the matter was
first made public. proceeded to investigate

or three informants up to the Executive
Committee of the Vigilance Committee, who

Besides being one of the highest criminal

gender suspicion against this Office, and ere
ate wide distrust of the whole mail system
and therefore feel it my duty, to leave
nothing undone which may tend to the de-
lection of the criminal in this case The U.
S. Statute provides


THAT if any person shall take any letter
or packet, not containing any article OF val
ue or evidence thereof, out of Post Once,
or shall open any letter or packet, which

respondence. TO PRY INTO ANOTHER'S

fender, upon conviction, shall pay for every
such offence, sum not exceeding five hun
dred dollars, and be imprisoned not exceed
ing twelve months


Finding the U. S Statute making this SO
grave and serious a matter, and myself deep
ly feeling the Importance of enforcing that
statute. | now announce that | will pay to
the party or parties who shall secure the
con nFiction OF the criminal in the case of the
letter herein spoken OF, enc hun
dred dollars.


Very respectfully


Your obedient servant,


c. l. WELLER,


Post Master.

headline: LIBERATION OF TERRY-After 81
article:
LIBERATION OF TERRY.-After six
weeks of close confinement, the Vigi-
lance Committee, on thorough exami-
nation of all the evidence for and
against their prisoner, decided to set
him at liberty, which was accordingly
done on the 7th inst.


Public sentiment had applauded the
acts of the Vigilance Committee up to
the time of Terrys liberation, and with
the exception of wild and blood thirs-
ty few, who had set their hearts on the
execution of Terry, and steeled them
against the palliating circumstances of
his case, there is general feeling Of
acquiescence in the magnanimous dispo-
sition of the distinguished prisoner by
the Committee. The general features
of the evidence against Terry were pub
lished long ago, and we early took the
ground that if such was all, and the on
ly evidence against him, he was not
worthy he-dnom> ~ excited populace
had designed for ism. And before we
gave a blind sanction to all the acts OF
the Vigilance Committee, or gave them
a carte blanche for ourselves, we desir-
ed to be fully satifed that the members
ofthe Committee were men ofiron nerve,
and able to withstand the heavy outside
pressure that demanded blood at the ex-
pense of justice. =


- The problem has been solved. The
Committee are worthy of a monument
to their memory. The tumultuous
waves of popular Indignation have beat
en- against them, and firm and immova-
bic have they withstood the shock.4
Keeping their prisoner in a place of safe
ty, and waiting until the storm of popu-
lar fury had abated, they have let him
out from the ark never more we trust to
return.


I The people have already pronounced
their .pprobation of the previous acts
of the Vigilance Committee, and here
after, if not wholly now, will they ad-
mire and appreciate the justice and
moderation which set Terry at liberty





- The Executive Committee have dis
played more moral heroism in this last
act, in Drawing the will of thousands of
their friends, than by the performance
of any previous deeds, however respon-
sible, or good, and beneficial to society
they might be. ,


- 1t could be desired that the friends of
Terry were blessed with a modicum of
that magnanimity and moderation
which has so signally characterized the
Vigilance Committee, in restoring to
freedom the distinguished prisoner OF
the latter, and the valued associate OF
the former. 1t is in exceeding bad
taste to get up a triumphal procession,
like the one at Sacramento, make
speeches, and glOrify the triumph of law
and order. Had the friends of Judge
Terry been sufficiently numerous, or
gifted with oratorv sufficient to revolu-
tionize public opinion, or had they the
courage to take Fort Vigilance by storm
and set their friends at liberty, it might
be appropriate to celebrate their victory
with an ovation. But when they owe
the liberation of friend to the justice,
moderation and magnanimity of foe,
1t IS well to rejoice for the good fortune
of the friend, not to exult over it as a
triumph over enemies. ;


Judge Terry was paraded through
the streets of Sacramento, to the tune
OF "Hail to the Chief" and "See the

During the excitement which has existed

quiet the passions of the people, rather than
to inllame them. In our first article on the
subject, MAY oath we took the position
that whenever the officers charged with the
execution of the law and justice, refuse or
fail from any cause to execute the same, it
was not only the right but the duty of good
citizens to meet out justice to offenders.


We maintained that quiet, orderly associations
formed for the preservation of the public peace
for the purpose of enforcing the laws--or
to rid a community of dangerous and justly
disreputable persons-we maintained that an
association of this kind was not mob, that

so engaged were not outlaws And so we

"The constitution and laws of State are

headline: The Verdict.
article:
The Corouer's Jury, on the bodies OF
Brace and Hetherington, have returned a
verdict to the effect that deceased came TO
their death by the hand of Robert Nixon
and some other person unknown, aided and
employed by the Vigilance Committee" 1t


is also stated that the body of Brace is to
be embalmcd and preserved for some days
with a view of obtaining further evidence
of murder against the committee. On the
evidence adduced before the Coroner's Jury,
it is probable that warrant will issue for
the arrest Of Nixon, and then will commence
a struggle between the committee and the
authorities. Not an armed contest perhaps,
but a system Of management by which Nix
on could evade the plain provisions OF the
law. Would the committee scruple to en-
ploy such means as have heretofore been
successfully employed in San Francisco, viz:
packed Jurys and suborned witnesses Nix
on was but doing the bidding of the COM
mittee, and of course they must clear him
What means will they employ they can
not always maintain the force they now
have at command, to brow beat and over
ride the authorities. They must, then. re-
sert to the means used by the gamblers and
thieves of San Francisco, to screen them
selves from the provisions Of the offended
law. They will be. compelled thus to
evade the law, or suffer the penalty Of their
crimes. Such will be the effect of their
proceedings. so certain is it that one crime
begets another,

headline: ]. Nicely johnson VS.. The People.
article:
The Governor III his letter TO Col. Crockett and
others Committee from the citizens of San Fran
cisco, published elsewhere says: :" By cirtue Of the
Constitution Of the State It is made my duty to enforce
the eaeettion Of the laacs" What laws? Is there
not double dealing in this matter? Does this not
smack of favoritism? Why had the Vigilance
Committee hung Casey and Cora eleven days pr-
to its being made has dutyto enforce the lars,
cording to his Excellency's notion of duty. The
lives Of two men had paid the forfeit of their no.
torious crimes, and those that were charged with
offences of less grade, were confined in the Com
mttee Rooms, ard had been for several days pre-
vous to the dead letter proclamation, and yet the du
ty made apparent by the Constitution Of this State,
and the oath taken by the Governor to make that
duty visible to his india-rubber conscience was
not sufficient to him to q sense of that du-
ty! Why sleep on the justice of that law that was
made your duty to enforce from the very moment
you toek the Constitutional oath in the presence
Of the assembled Legislature Of the State 4? If
you could witness the death of Cora and Casey
the arrest of the % SIX" and the timely death of
Sullivan, without feeling any remorse of con-
science, and believe all the time the people of San
Francisco were violating the laws of the State
your conscience surely had been scared with that
instrument mentioned in the Good Book


The Governors fayorte had not been pursued,
or he was feeling the public pulse His friends
say that Gen. Wool deceived him by promising
that the arms and ammunition of the General Coy
ernment under his control should be placed at the
disposal Of the State authorities, and this promise
on the part of Gen. Wool, caused the Governor to
issue his proclamation. If this statement. made
by the State Journal be true the Executive of this
State is far more reprehensible than we imagined
him to be, although we believe him to be weak.
aud not over scrupulous as 10 his duties as Chief
Magistrate Of the State, yet we were not prepar-
ed for the announcement that he would not do his
duty until he had made every preparation to des-
troy the lives of worthy citizens, that would just
ly entitlc him to be the Cief of assassinators --
What must be the feelings of the Commander-n-
Chief OF a gteat State, when he makes call on
his army to muster to service to see them muster
themselves out Of service. lIumilating indeed.
and annoying as this may be to the Governor of
the state Of California, nevertheless il is true
Nine-tenths of the people are with the Vigilance
Committee, and whole Companies of militia have
disbandcd at the call Of the Governor and ioined
the people. The cup is bitter one but it must
be drank, and that too by j. Neely Johnson. The
proclamation has gone forth, and not been respon-
ded TO by the masses in sufficient numbers to nerve
his heart to the combat. General Sherman has
declined acting any further in this matter for the
reason that the proclamation contains a fasehood.
The General says there is no insurrection in the
city, and hence he declines farther participation
in NeeIy's force Again we say the cup is bit
ter one, for the proclamation must be withdrawn.
or the law and murder party must be defeated-and
God forbid that the folly of an indiscrcet man
should force the people to the latter, but if the
crisis must come the conclusion is foregone and
let the responsibility rest where it properly be-


longs. If blood must be shed to maintain the pu-
rity of the ballot-box and the independence of
the press, then let it be SO, and let it flow until
our fair State is rid of the cause that produced
the result

headline: Resignation of Gen, Sherman.
article:
Maj Gen. VIM. T. Sherman on the 7th
inst at Benicia placed in the hands Of Gov
johnson, his resignation of the Office held by
appointment from his Excellency for the
past few weeks. The Gen. published card
assigning his reasons for resigning the high
est position in the GOVERNORS Army. He
says:


/ think have already said and done
enough to convince all that | am not an ad-
vocate of the Vigilance Committee +; and
whilst would have contributed my assist
ance to expel from our midst all rowdles,
ballot box suffers and shouder-strikers, it
would only be by the application of some
legal mode, which believe does exist, and
not by resorting to the organization of a
Committee which in the enforcement OF its
DEGREES has been compelled to resist the
sworn officers Of the law.


When, however, the Vigilance Committee
had become installed in power and | had
received the orders Of the Governor TO or
ganize the Militia to aid the Sheriff in the
execution of his duty, did my best to inhu-
ence and command all good citizens to en-
roll themselves into companies promising
when a sufficient number were enlisted pro-
vided necessity still continued, to arm,
equip and muster them into the service of
the State. based my promise of armng
/ the enrolled militia on "a verbal assurance
given to Governor johnson by Gen. Wool,
in my presence, to issue from the United
States Arsenal, on aproper requisition, such
arms and munitions of war as the emergency
might call for. 1t is no longer a secret that
when the written requsition was made, Gen.
Wool had changed his mind, and had dis
covered that he had not The legal power to
grant the request.


/ have at all times endeavorcd to calm
the public excitement ; | have counselled
moderation and forbearence, but j was
forced to conclude that these moderate coun-
sells did not concide with the views Of Gov
johnson, and, in justice to him. | felt bound
to afford him the opportunity to select some
representative here whose ideas were more
consOnant with his own.

The people Of Grass Valley are almost
unanimous in their unqualified approval of
the entire action thus far of the Vigilance
Committee of San Francisco. They will
feel greatly disappointed should circumstan-
ces cause that body to disband before it has
fully accomplished the great objects for
which it was opportunely convened. The
action Of the Governor in issuing his proc

We have no military companies here, and

istence, the citizens of Grass Valley view the
clamorS of the bowie knife and pistol advo-

Should any effort be made to enroll men

be met here by counter organization ten
times stronger to support the Vigilance

Col. BAKERS SPEECH.-The high reputation
enjoyed by this gentleman as public speaker
drew together on Saturday night last large
audience who listened to him with respectful at


tenton. The effort of the Col. was by no meaus


equal to those which he was wont to make in
the old whg cause. 1t wanted the spirit and
fire which in former days characterized his elo-
quence. This is perhaps to be attributed to the
fact that the Col has not yet been well broken
into the traces He has been waverng for a
long time and exclaiming ''where am l to go"
and at last has fallen into the embraces of the
Black Republicans. He was toleraby liberal
in his platform, but we think will hardly get the
mass of his allies upon it. He thinks that they
would not if iii power, meddle with the institu-
ton of slavery in the States or the District Of
Columbia, but as he is neophyte, Joshua r.
Giddings, Sumner Garrison & Co. who are older
in the cause than Col. Baker are to be regarded
as better authority-and as for the Coils. infu-
ence in the event of Fremonts election he
would no more be able to restrain the ultra
"higher law" rule than he was to beat back the
vigilantes of San Francisco. We surmise that
the Col. has no very well defined political opin-
ions at this time, save on two questions. His
deadly opposition to the vigilance committee,
and to know-nothingism is well known. Con-
sidering his implacable hostility to these two
parties, it was really painful to see him sur
rounded on the stand by the coterie who have
been well known as the advocates of both. 1t
may be truly said of Col Baker that "misfor-
tune makes us acquainted with strange bed
fellows"


In support of what we say of his want of fixed
political sentiments, we have the authority of
highly respectable gentlemen of this place for
saying that Col. Baker declared in the Stage on
the way up from Sacramento that if the demo-
cratic party had have passed resolutions at the
State Convention condemnatory of the vigilance
he would have taken the stump for the
democracy.

people, for more than a quarter of a century


Those principles are both conservative and

A strict construction of the Constitution.


Equal justice to all men, of whatever State

Strict economy and rigid accountability in

The prompt arraignment and punishment

faithful discharge by the public officers

The support Of the State governments in its

Universal suffrage.


The honest payment of all our just debts

Absolute acquescence in the will of the ma

ernment, and by whose influence, alone, those

ted The Constitution of the United States, as

ism of the people to sanction them. Such is

tegrity. Unfortunately for the character of

would have been settled, without the scandal of

ment as false, and declares that these charges

This gcntlcmans name has been intimately

ters set upon them the seal Of condemnation. We

In an address delivered bV the loV. H. /.
Cutler in the Unitarian Church, San Fran
cisco upou the life and character Of James
King OF Wm., the reverncd spoke as follows

Committee:


There has been Witnessed a general up
rising Of the better portion OF the citizens,
and an extraordinary assumption of power
by the people, to whom all civil power be
longs. 1t was an assumption OF power which
some few Of course, in the community, who

inns Of government, do not approNc-and

cessitics Of the ease are not and cannot be

reply. it does not SO in fact. The ends for

by the assumption Of original power. The

citing What with the Pico grant of thirty

ecutive Committee of fifty that was appoint

time since the meeting A delegation of

meeting in secret session every night 1t is
supposed their object has been to keep
lookout for Pieo's Surveyors, from the fact
that on last "Wednesday morning delega-
ton of the committee were quite active, and
appeared little excited and when they
came back at night it was currently reported
that they had surprised Picos surveyors and
requested them peremptoriy to desist sur
veying any further in the mining region, at
the peril of being deprived of their survey
ing instruments. They replied that their or
ders were to survey lands in certain shapes
and localities, and so long as they retained
their instruments they should continue the
survey. They however, said if the commit
tee wanted the instruments they could take
them rcmarking at the same time that they
thought it was good deal like striking at
the moon. Nevertheless, the committee took
the instruments, and then demanded of the
surveyor his field notes He replied that he
had not got them, and did not know where
they were; but that they had been taken care
of in anticipation that they would be taken
from him. These items l have gathered

others, and / have not the least doubt the
is reliable


Now if Pico thinks he can come up here

mined to defend their homes and their fami-

tive operation some twenty quartz mills

ers, and when he, Pico, is trying to locate

ty and their rights Mr. Pico had better

have been friend of the vgilants and still

| hereas, satisfactory information has been

or of the State of California, by virtue Of the

laws thereof, do hereby declare said County in

and direct all ofthe volunteer companies with
| in the County of San Francisco, also, all per.
sons subject toimilitary duty within said Coun-
| ty to report themselves for duty immediately,
to Major General William T. Sherman, com
manding Second Division California Militia.
TO serve for such term in the performance of
military duty under the command of said Sher-
man, until disbanded from service by his Or
ders. Also, that all volunteer military COM
panies now organized, or which NAV be organ
lied within the Third, Fourth and Fifth mill
ltary Divisions OF this State also, all persons
subject to military duty in said Military Di.
visions to hold themselves in readiness to re-
spond to and obey the orders of the Governor

der and direct that all associations, combina,
tions or organizations whatsoever, existing in
said County Of San Francisco, or elsewhere in
this State, in opposition, or violation of the
laws thereof more particularly the association
/ known as the Vigilance Committee" of San
Francisco, do disband; and each and every in
dividual thereof yield opedieuce to the Consti,
tuition and laws of this State, the writs and
process of the Courts, an all legal orders of
the officers of this State, and the County Of
San Francisco.

B% To an observer, it seems strange

cratic" papers, that for two years past


We abused the American party for ostra-
cising foreigners, now abuse the Vigilance

of men, numbering hundreds of the most

are now denounced with all the epithets
il the vocabulary by the presses that a
few months ago could not find honied

fact a the only sympathy the democratic
sresses have is for such foreigners as Casey

BROKE JAIL.-The town was thrown
into considerable excitement on Wednes-
day night between 8 and 8 o'clock, by
the discharge of pistols and subsequent
report that prisoners had escaped from
the county Jail. The facts, as given us,
are substantially these Two thieves,
named Richard Woods and j. Webster,
were confined in one cell. The former
was committed few days since for
stealing at the Virginia House, the lat
ter was indicted by the Grand Jury and
committed to jail the day ON which he
effected his escape.


The jail being in an unfinished con-
dition, a watchman was employed to
guard it. Sometime after o'clock in
the evening he returned from supper and
approached the outer Jail door, when he
heard stir within. As it was dark he
stepped back few steps nearer the
light to observe what was going on.-
The door was soon thrown open, he was
knocked aside by two persons Fastening
out. Recovering himself he fired twice
at the prisoners as they passed the steps
of the Court House. The prisoners
were pursued but effected their escape.


On an examination of the cells Web
ster and Woods were found missing
They had succeeded in digging hole
through the brick partition wall between
their cell and an empty open one, large
enough to afford egress. An accomplice
probably furnished instruments for the
purpose through crack in the floor
above the hall, in front of the cell in
which the prisoners were confined. A
heavy paddock on the outer door was
also broken, allowing the thieves to
escape from the hall.


A person calling himself Lee Sehell,
is supposed to be the accomplice, or one
of number of confreres. He was hang
ing round the Jail during almost the en-
tire day, talking with the inmates, was
seen running through the streets soon
after the alarm was given, and was not
to be found on Thursday morning.
Webster is somewhat notorious, hav-
ing shot down three men in a quarrel
about claim at Sand Hill, some three
years ago, and in row at Washington
two years since was shot in the mouth,
losing two front teeth. He was also i'm
plicated in robbing sluice at Moore's
Flat, some time since, and was under
bonds for appearance at Court to answer
for the same when committed to jail
1t is quite certain that he was one of
the principal rascals engaged in the
many petty robberies committed of late
in this vicinity.


The escaped are ripe subjects for the
Vigilance Committee, into whose hands,
or some other equally just tribunal,
may they speedily fall.

tof advice


\ The steamer of to-day carries melancholy and
startling intelligence.


On the afternoon of the oath July, Joseph Heth-
erington, a native of England, but who came to
this State in lS49, from st. Louis met DR.. Randall
in the bar-room of the st. Nicholas Hotel and, e.
newing an old difficulty which had it's origin in
some money transactions between the parties, COM
menced an assault upon him by sez:ng hold of his
beard. Randall commenced drawing revolver,
and Hetherington also drew his. Two shots were
fired by Hetherngton and three by Randall The
last shot of Hetherngton's pistol entered the left
temple of Randall and penetrated the brain. Ran
dali Immediately fell, and expired the following
Sunday.


Hetherington was seized by the police of the
Vigilance Committee, conveyed to their rooms and
locked up. On the death of Randall, the commit
tee proceeded at once to the trial of Hetherngton
for murder 1t was clearly proven that Hetherng-
ton had been pursuing Randall for months with
threats that he intended to shoot him. 1t appears
that Randall had borrowed money from Hetherng-
ton, which the latter found it impossible to get
back. This brought on quarrels and bad blood,
which ended by determination on the part Of
Hetherington to take Randall's life. Hethering .on
was therefore convicted of murder by the commit
tee. He had previously been cleared by the courts
of killing another man named Baldwin two years
ago.


The Committee had also been engaged in the
trial of Philander Brace for the murder of Capt.
West. His guilt was clearly shown, and by his
own admission, as well as behavior after arrest, he
must have been one of the most abandoned men
this age of the world has yet produced Both of
these men were sentenced to death, which SEN
tence the committee proceeded to put in execu-
tion on the afternoon of the Goth July. The scaf
fold erected in Davis street, at the intersec-
ton of Sacramento. Long before the hour arriv-
ed every approach to the spot was blocked up by
dense throng of curious spectators, composed of
| men, women and children. Every house top was
covered, and such was the rush that the roofs of
| several buildings gave way under the pressure Of
| the burden upon them.


| At-the appointed time a large force of vigilance
troops, consisting of infantry and cavalry, num-
bcring at least four thousand men, surrounded
| the gallows with fixed bayonets aud drawn sabres
The prisoners were then conveyed to the scaffold
in carriages. Hetherington was perfectly firm and
composed-not a nerve quivered, and, although
his arms were pnoned behind his back, he walked
up the steep steps of the scaffold without assist
ance, and took his position upon the trap, at the
same time loosening his cravat aud barring his
neck for the halter. Brace had to be assisted up
the steps, but when his eyes fell upon the gaping
multitude the hendish spirit OF visence seemed to
take possession of him, and he passed his few re-
naming moments repeating the most blasphemous
and obscene curses.


Hetherington made few remarks, but was much
interrupted by Brace. At length the signal was
sounded upon the large bell of the committee.
The two men were swung into eternity, and the
horrible spectacle upon which twenty thousand
human beings were feasting their eyes was brought
to a close.

and city bonds This banking firm received the
