rible affair. Hour after hour passed by
ers any particulars could be obtained SO
great was the excitement in that city. Tow
ard shutdown, brief dispatch was received,
saying that the affair grew out of an attempt
on the part of police officer of the Vigilance
Committee named Sterling A. Hopkins, to
arrest one J. R. Maloney, we'll known and
obnoxious political trickster. 1t appears,
from accounts then, and since received, that
Hopkins went to the Office of DR.. Ashe, the
Naval Officer of the port, with warranty for
the arrest of Maloney whom be found under
the protection of said Ashe, Judge Terry ana
several other prominent Law and Order men,
who refused to allow the arrest to be made.
The Vigilance Police then returned to the
rooms of the Committee for further aid.
Ashe, Maloney and Terry, Immediately left,
and having armed themselves with rifles, &c,
were on their way to the armOry of the 5. f.
Blues, when they were oVertaken by Hop
kins and his re-enforced party. Maloney was
in advance of the others, and Judge Terry in
rear. Hopkins, who was in advance of his
party, approached Terry and saluted him in
q respectful, though somewhat excited man
ner, and Immediately seized the rife in his
hands as he presented it and made an attempt
ed to wrest it from him. In doing so he gras-
ped Judge Terry by the collar, others of his
party at the same time closing with Ashe and
Maloney. In the struggle Terry let &c his
hold Of the rife and drew. a bowie-knife and
stabbed Mr.. Hopkins in the neck. AT this
time pistol was discharged which produced
a little confusion, and Judge Terry and his
party escaped to the armory. AS soon as the
unfortunate blow was struck by Terry, word
was conveyed to the Committee Rooms, and
the alarm was sounded. Thousands at once
obeyed the summons, and in less than fifteen
minutes the armory of the Blues was sur
rounded by armed men. The streets in every
direction glistened with bayonets, hurrying
foot and horsemen. Judge Terry, as soon as
he saw the overwhelming force brought
against him surrendered, and was taken to
the Committee Rooms, where he is now close
ly confined. The Vigilantes, after securing
Terry and his party, turned their attention
to the other armories of the Law and Order
party, all of which were secured, with their
arms and ammunition together with about

been released.


Two vessels, with arms on board Tor the

From one of the vessels twelve cases OF

commanded one of the parties overhauling
the vessels, has been arrested by the U. S.
Marshal on the charge of piracy. He has not
vet had his examination. 100000 bail has
been offered and refused. The sloop-of-war
John Adams has been anchored off Clay ST..
wharf, in a somewhat threatening position.
No alarm, however, need be felt at this move,
as sme of course will only act in case Of a re-
sistanee to U. S. Officers. No such resistance
will be offered by the Committee. Durkee
will take his trial regularly, and abide the
result. There is very little danger, however,
of q conviction. The whole matter of this ar
rest will end in smoke.


Hopkins was better at last accounts, and
hopes are entertained of his recovery.

article:
Iy- The pen is said to be mightier than
the sword, and if we admit the saying as
true in the main, the quill welded by Cax-
ton has the additional quality of being sharp
er than two edged sword. His cuts and
thrusts always seek the vitals; and generally
when his scimitar flashes it not only dazzes
to blindness of his faults, but cuts to the
bone of his adversary, and from each cash
streams of life blood


In illustration of these comments we quote
from the "True Californian" of the 18th inst.
presenting pitable picture of our Governor,
as he now stands before the world at large:


Governor Johnson.


Our governor seems to be born to misfortune,
as the sparks to fly upwards He never
touches any thing that does not sting him.
The world and its concerns are one mighty
nettle, and he never attempts to play with it
that it does nor prick his fingers. He is sous
ed head and ears in trouble. He seems to be
haunted by the Vigilance Committee like the
hypochondriac was in fable, by the figure
of coffin; wherever he turns his eyes, it is
sure to rise up, gloomy and threatning right
before him.


1t mixes itself up with all his duties, en-
ters into his political relations, and forces
itself into a corner of his fireside. He can
90 nowhere that it does not follow him; he
can listen to no conversation that he does not
hear it mentioned; he can read no newspaper
that does not stare him most terrifcally in the
face If he looks into the Bulletin, the Alta
or True Californian. or the American, or the
Marysville Herald it is sure to catch his eye
before the list of births, marriages and deaths;
or if disgusted with the California Press he
ventures to open the New York Herald, or
Courier and Enquirer, or Tribune, or the
Washington City STAR or the New Orleans
Delta, with hope to escape the annoyance, the
same awful hieroglyphics stare him in the
face and assure him that no spot under Heav-
en- is free from invasion. 1t sits by him at the
dinner table, proceeds him to church on the
Sabbath, and haunts his midnight dreams.
1t has corrupted his political adherents, meta
morphised open eneroies, that snickiring
spies and tawning flatterers, fallen like black
cloud over his aspirations after fame, blasted
all the reputation he ever acquired, destroyed
his future usefulness, and nailed down the lid
of his political coffin. 1t has been peg in
his shoe, a sand grain in his eye, corn on
his toe, a tetter in his head. In short it has
undermined his power as a Governor, and
covered him with ridicule as a man.


Finally, as if to crown all his misfortunes
with perfect climax Of i'll, his own father-in-
law showers upon him flood of bitter invec-
tive and sternly reads him a lecture Of We
racity.


Such are some of the evils that result from
hosting very small men into very high places,
and attempting to manufacture live lion out
of petrifed mummy Such is the lesson
taught to the ambitious, who would aspire to
SUBMITS that make them dizzy when they
reach them, and at the same time demonstrate
their pigmy size to those who gaze upward
from beneath.


Such is the fate of the mere politician whose
vanity hatters him into the belief that he is a
statesman, capable Of graphing with great
question. and controlling popular masses in
commotion.


Such is the figure at present cut by Mr..
John n. Johnson-Gcvernor Of the State, by
virtue Of an accidental nomination at an ac
cidental election.


Let no man in future aspire to be great,
whose shallow brain tried by the actualities
Of life subjects him to pity, and whose falter-
ing soul shrinks responsibilities that it ought
to assume or vanquish. Let such 60 back
into the oblivion in which nature intended
they should mouder and learn to be modest,
after having failed to be wise.

The New York Post learns from parties who
have just arrived from San Francisco that the
Vigilance Committee will be able to maintain
their ground until the next general election,
which is to take place in September, and the
people shall have elected and placed in power
different class Of men to work the govern
ment, and one in harmony with the feelings of
the honest portion of the population. At
present. it is said, San Francisco looks more
like quiet small Connecticut city than busy
metropolis. More than two-thrds Of the stores
are closed.


The Anti-vigilance Committee Side.


The only paper in San Francisco opposed to
the committee isthe DAILY Herald-and in order
to place the version of both parties before our
readers, we copy the comments upon the posture
OF affairs made III that journal on the day of the
departure of the steamer as follows:


ITO the people Of The Eastern States, who,
cognizant OF the growing rebellion in the heart
of this metropolis, will look anxiously to the
news by the outgoing steamer for tidings Of its
suppression, we beg to state that the Governor,
aided by the State officers his advisers, and by
the best citizens ofevery county in the common
wealth. is using all means at his command to
crush out this fostering treason. The ill-advised
refusal of the general commanding the Pacific
department to furnish the State with arms and
ammunition on the requistion of Gov Johnson,
for the purpose of putting speedy end to the
insurrection, has retarded the operations set on
foot for the termination of the rebellion; but
that refusal has but inhamed the zeal of those
loyal and patriotic citizens who have responded
to the call of the Governor for the maintenance
of the law; and their ardor has already over
come almost every difficulty in their path.


"We are in hopes that the immense force now
in process of organization when exhibited, will
be sufficient, without striking blow, to prove to
the misguided men who at present defy the laws
that it will be idle TO attempt to maintain their
position. Arms and ammunition are being con-
centrated at various points, men arc being
drilled and exercised in the use of arms; pre-.
parations the most formidable in extent and
purpose are in progress, so that when a demon
stration is at length made, it will be such a one
as to crush out finally and forever the spirit of
rebellion in California. By all those who sustain
the Governor it is fervently hoped that it may
not be necessary to spill single drop Of blood !;
at the same time that the liberties of the people
and the reputation of the State being at stake,
the whole power Of the government will be used
to extinguish the existing rebellion. The State
will not recede from its position.


General Wool's course has retarded the
extinction of this riotous organization; but it
is nevertheless a mere question Of time; and
even should the President of the United States
follow the lead Of his military representative
on the Pacific. and violate the guarantees of
the Constitution, the result will be the same in
the end. The people of the STATE will assert
their sovereignty over this cabal at all hazards
We have every faith, however, that the Presi-
dent will do his duty"

deputation from San Francisco had waited
upon Governor johnson and requested him to
withdraw his proclamation placing San Fran
cisco under martial law. This interview took
place at Benicia on the 7th June. Governor
Johnson in his reply says:


"By virtue of the constitution of this State
it is made my duty to enforce the execution Of
the laws. This duty | shall performs and if
unhappily collision occurs, and injury to life
or property result, the responsibility must rest
upon those who disregard the authority Of the
State"

AFFAIRS IN SAN FRANCISCO. The San
Francisco Herald learns upon good au-
thority that it is the intention of the Vigi-
lance Committee, to arrest all the officers of
the City and County Government, lock up
the City Hall and take the government into
their own hands.


sit is also stated, with what truth we are
unable to say, in consequence of the myste-
ry which enshrouds the secret tribunal,
which now rules over the destinies Of this
people. that after having taken possession
of the City Hall, the vigilance committee
will proceed to Sacramento, seize the State
officers and the records, form provisional
government, and call upon the people to
yield obedience to it."


Now, it is generally believed that after
the execution of Cora and Casey, and two or
three different shipments of prisoners, the
Governor of the State offered, through
Messrs. Baldwin, Peachy, Bolts and Munson
that if they wou Id disband, and surrender
up the arms belonging to the State which
they had captured; he would recommend to
the authorities of San Francisco county not
to prosecute them--would interpose Execu-
tive clemency if convicted, and would sug-
gest to the next legislature the propriety OF
passing general amnesty. These PROPOSE
tons we're rejected by the Committee, who
still keep on with their secret plotting, oc-
casionally arresting one of the many wharf
rats that infest San Francisco. to keep down
the suspicion of the people. If their object
is not to oYerturn the State Government,
what is it Fellow Citizens, Think, and
think for yourselves

IMPORTANT IF TRUE.-Madame Rumor
has ii that some three or four members of
the Executive portion of the Vigilance Com
mittee, were desirous of leaving on the last


Steamer having pressing business just at
this time, in the Atlantic States We can
not of course vouch for the truth of the ru-
NOR, and should be exceedingly sorry to see
any of them falter at this juncture, as we
candidly think they ought to hang together.

GREAT SMoKE-A great deal Of smoke
and gas has been created, and large guam
tity of ink has been shed, with regard to
misunderstanding between Gov. Johnson,
Col. Zabriskie, and Gen. Allen. 1t appears
from the Governors statement of the facts,
that he authorized the two latter gentlemen
to 90 to San Francisco and ascertain if pos
sible, the objects of the Vigilance Committee


Messrs Allen and Zatriskie claim that they
had full power from the Governor to effect
compromise between the Vigilance Commit
tee and the State authorities. We believe
this is the point of difference between the
parties, and it certainly appears to us that
the Governor has decidedly the advantage
in the reasonableness of his position. and
such, we doubt not, is the opinion Of every
unpreiudiced man in the State. 1t seems
to US impossible that the Governor should
have conferred the power claimed by the
gentlemen composing the committee, upon
them. when it is well known that both Col
Zabriskie and Gen. Allen, sympathized with
and supported the action of the Vigilance
Committee This view of the matter leads
us to believe that the difficulty was OCCASION
ed by an unfortunate misunderstanding be-
tween them rhe official acts of Governor
johnson have been characterized by cam
dor and fair dealing that entities his position
to great weight in community, and all the
ssastonishment" that may be expressed by
the self constituted committee, will not
change the verdict Of an impartial public
The mildest form of that verdict will be
that the Committee misunderstood the power
conferred upon them by the Governor.

Figilanceism aud the Press.


1t has been very generally understood
that the democratic press alone have op-
posed Vigilance-isIl This is correct, in q
measure: but it is nevertheless true that
portion of the Democratic Press of the State,
and given it preference over the republican
institutions of our government. 1t is also
true that the only democratic daily paper in
San Francisco that favored the Vigilance
doctrine, was suffered to die out aud has
been sold under the hammer. 1t was in
bad company, and those who were instru


mental in guiding and controlling Vigi-


lance affairs had ''nary red" of patronage


to bestow upon it. However honest it may


have been in its Vigilance sentiments, there


were other more congenial spirits who
"waxed fat and kicked,' while the demo


cratic Globe was nabbed and sold by the
Sheriff. A lesson, that we trust the demo-
cratic press will always heed, and never
neglect principle, the constitution and laws
of the country to run after strange idols
1t was movement in which the democratic
press were not expected to join, and when
| the Globe favored the movement, and even
made appeals to the democratic press of the
State in its favor, it was, nevertheless, suf-
the State summoned to hold an inquest on
its remains, the verdict would be Served
it right


The democratic press of California are not
alone ia opposition to Vigilance-ism The
two San Jose papers, one Of them K. N, and
the other Republican, oppose the Vigilance
institution. The Shasta Republican, flying
the Fillmore flag, has steadily and perse-
veringly opposed the monster, and its many
stalwart blows have not. fallen harmlessly
upon Committee-ism's one-eyed carcase-
With these few honorable exceptions, the
majority Of the democratic press of the
State have constituted the opposition to the
institution now holding its bloody orgies in
San Francisco.


A portion Of the Ki-Yi and independent
vigilance press, are endeavoring to make
Vigilance or antiVigilance, the issue of the
next election. The press in the employ of
the mob at San Francisco, it would appear,
have no better sense than to insult the in
| telligence of the people, by asking them to
permit the question of Vigilance-ism to
override every other question, and control
their suffrages al the coming election. 1t
matters not with what party men have
heretofore acted, and no matter where the
beck of Vigilance-ism may lead them, they
are expected to abandon their former pro-
fessions and embrace Vigilance ism, the
moment the KiYi and woolly headed press
see proper to make the issue. Was there
ever greater insult offered to an intelligent
people, than to suppose that such question
would induce men to abandon principles
which they had professed all their lives, and
embrace those of their opponents' To
abandon the institutions of their country,
and sustain in their stead, an armed mob
Men who are decidedly in favor of Buchan-
an are to abandon him, and support Fre-
mont or Fillmore, the moment that Ki-Yi-
ism turns into the canvass the one-eyed
monster now reyelling in human gore at the
city of the Bay. Why do they wait before
making the issue' Why do they not trot
out and enter their one-eyed guyastecutus,
and raise over their human flesh loving pet
the KiYi and woolly headed flag of bare
skulls and bloody bones, and see the intelli-
gent freemen of California fail down and
worship the hideous monster, as the heather
worships his wooden god, or as the press in
the employ of the committee, worship the
golden calf of Viglance' If the scheme is
so sure of success, why do they not trot out
their flesh eating Cyclops, and show his
paces' They pretend that they are organ
lied for the punishment of crime, and yet
their organs acknowledge they have viola
ted the laws of the country, by requiring of
the next legislature a general amnesty bill.
They have winked at crime in San Francisco
until it has become familiar to them and they
hope to make its beauties captivate the peo-
pie, and induce them to send men to the
next legislature who will legalize murder
1t is possible that they may do So. We have
serious doubts, however, about the matter.
The Vigilance Committee knew they were
violating the law, and the law should be
permitted to take its course, not as it has
been administered in San Francisco, but
as it has been administered here in Butte,
where offenders can only evade the law by
digging through the bottom of the Jail

ence to telegr aphic despatch from the

We should be pleased to see the Committee

to their duty as citizens, restore peace to a

We are not among those who wish to insin-
uate that the Committee have been induced

What means will they employ? They can

ride the authorities. They must, then, re-

selves from the provisions Of the offended
law. They will be. compelled thus to

article:
and Order men and Vigilantes alike, the
earnest and anxious inquiry is propound-
ed thousand times day. "What is to
become of the affair at San francisco %
Were we nearer the national seat of gov
ernment, a ready reply might be furnish
ed. The Vigilance Committee would
soon lay down their arms, or a bloody
contest must ensue.


Upon the requisition of the Governor
of a State, the President is bound to bring
the force of the nation to suppress re-
volt against the legal State authorities
Living, as we do, far removed from the
power of the Union, it cannot be directed
against us, till the people have quite thor
oughly purged themselves of the un-
wholesome causes of complaint, and re-
stored health for the present and some
time in the future.


By proclamation state of civil war ac-
tually exists. The people are opposed by
authorities they have once delegated with
power for certain length of time which
has not yet expired But the Governor
and his adherents can claim nothing but
the shadow of force. The Constitution
may be appealed to, but it furnishes them
with neither men, arms or money. The
records of the last gubernatorial canvass
may be shown, the commission of the
Executive, his inaugural, and the recorded
history of his many vetoes, proofs conclu-
sivc of the highest authority, but they
avail nothing against the sovereign will Of
the people at this moment. The delega-
ted voice of the State, so far as San Fran
cisco is concerned, has been revoked for
time. A large proportion of the available
arms in the country, except those belong
ing to the general government, are in the
hands of the people. In point of num-
bers, and munitions Of war, the Govern
or is powerless, compared with the Wig
ilance Committee and their supporters
He cannot do much damage if he would.


Under such circumstances, knowing that
the sole design ofthe people of San Fran
cisco is to obtain their rights as citizens,
and secure them for the future, without a
desire to subvert the civil authority of the
State, only so far as necessary for imme-
diate self protection, it is not difficult to
see what the result of the affair at San
Francisco will finally be. The President
can move no number of men or arms, suf.
ficient to put down the people of this State
in shorter period than three months, and
long ere that time will have expired, peace
and quietness will once more reign among
us. The rascais who have so long con-
taminated the fountain of justice, will have
been extirpated, and nothing will be left
deserving the sword and bayonet, when
the United States troops arrive, should
they arrive at all, which is extremely
problematical.


With the restoration of civil authority,
new era in the history of our State,
young in years, but old in vice, may be
reckoned to commence. That standard of
virtue known in older communities, we
hope will be emulated hereafter among
our people. The rufianism which has
characterized the State, giving it the rep
utation of being the hell of the world, will,
we trust, be known no longer Give Cal
! ifornia but fair and spotless name, to
which thebest efforts of San Franciscans
are fearlessly devoted, and with her mild
climate, unbounded and undeveloped
wealth, and her ample fields for the dis
play of energy and enterprise, immigrants
will pour in upon the coast, making the
western arm of the Republic powerful
and its people prosperous and happy


We trust that the effect Of the Vigilance
Committee will end in so great and desira-
bic blessing.

STEPHEN "A. DOUGLASS ON VIGILANCE
COMMITTEE PRINCIPLEs.--In late speech
of Senator Douglassswe find the following
passage. The application is easily made:


"The principles of the Black Republicans
is to obey such laws as they like, and repu-
date those they do not like, They claim
protection under the Constitution, and refuse
to yield obedience to it. The difference be
tween them and the Democracy is, that the
Democracy support the Constitution in all
its parts, with equal fidelity, without refer-
ence to whether they like it or dislike it.
1t is no excuse for man 10 say that he does
not like law, and therefore will not obey it,.
Did they ever know criminal who liked the
law? Law breakers never like the punish
ment that follows the act. Law abiding
men have no fear Of the supremacy Of the
laws and the question to be decided in this
contest is, whether law made in pursuance
Of the Constitution and as expounded by the
Courts, shall prevail, or whether such law
is naught, and cowardly leaders shoot down
the officers with impunity."

Sheriff having nine prisoners on hand at

Governor johnson on the Sd inst, issued
his Proclamation to the volunteer militia of
the third, fourth and fifth military divisions
of this State, calling on them to aid in the
suppression of what His EXcellency is
pleased to term an insurrection in the county
of San Francisco on the part Of the Vigi-
lance Committee, in the execution of con
victs and assassins that have been commit
ting theiR diabolical acts in that county un-
til patience has ceased to be a virtue This
the Committee have done, and they have
done more. They have arrested other no
torious characters in crime and accompliceS
of Casey, and are determined to rid the
city of their presence.


James King of VIM. was assassinated on
the 10Th day of May, and on the 18th day
Of that month the Committee took Casey and
Cora into their custody. His EXcellency
was in San Francisco prior to the delivering
up of Cora and Casey to the Committee by
Sheriff Scanned and was consulted in regard
to the propriety of the step by the Commit
tee as well as by the Sheriff, and not one
word was heard about calling out the militia
to aid the So-callcd officers Of the law, and
the fair inference is that he approved the ac-
tion on the part of the people. On the 22d
the two culprits were executed by the peo-
pie, of all of which the Governor was duly
advised Here the matter rests quietly so
far as lie is concerned until the Sd of the
present month, and for the first time it oc-
ours to him that it is his duty as Comman-
der-in-Chief of the State of California to
call on the strong arm of the law to suppress
an insurrcction that has been in full opera
ton for the last IS days and its work almost
completed. Wise and sagacious statesman,
If the Committee are wrong now, they were
doubly so at the time j. Nicely Johnson
countcnanced, if not advised, its course
Wise physicians tell us that it is far better
to administer a preventive than await the
action of disease so that a cure may be ef-
'ected, Had the Governor acted indepen- |
lcntly in the first place and not waited the
restoration of the fear stricken kindred |
spirits of the culprits to be melted into ac-
tion in support of his proclamation, he might
have been credited by the honest portion of
the State with sincerity, but as it is, he will
held in utter contempt by all classes.

The Address Of the Vigilance Committee of San

In consequence of our issue being only


weekly, we have not before had an opportu-

the action Of the sovereign people in the pre-


misses. We are thus necessarily behind


many Of our contemporaries, but feeling that


it is a solemn duty incumbent upon every
public journalist in the State to meet the i'm
portant moral issue that is presented we
must ask the indulgence of the reader while
we briefly present our views.


Municipal law is a rule of civil conduct,
commanding what is right and prohibiting


what is wrong The constitution and laws OF
a State are laid down as the bulwark of So


cial and political rights and privileges


Without law there is no such thing as ber-


erty. 1t is therefore the duty of every true


citizen to cherish, sustain, and support the


laws, not only by his acts, but also by the in


fluence of his voice, his pen, and if necessary


by the strength of his good right arm, even
should his life be endangered Blood thus
spilled is an honorable legacy to his children's
children.


No one deprecates mob violence more than
we. The wrong-doing Of an excited and en-
furiated populace, whereby justice is dethron-
ed and the law trampled under foot, will al
ways receive prompt and decided condemna-
ton at our hands. In cases like this, no mo-
tive Of personal policy should influence
newspaper the breadth of single hair
This much have we said, in order that our
position respecting mob law may not be mis-
construed.


Now for the action of the Vigilance Com
mittee of San Francisco A portion of the
press have stigmatized the Committee as a
mob This is an ungenerous misnomer. Its
organization has been pronounced popular
outbreak This is Misrepresentation One
journal has gone so far as to say that three
thousand ouilaws are nnder arms in San
Francisco" This ismonstrous. None of the
elements that are necessary to constitute a
mob have entered into the organization of
the Committee; there has been no evidence
of that which is usually understood by the
term outbreak; and to pronounce the three
citizens under arms outlaws, almost
amounts to denial Of the sovereignty Of
the people themselves There is a vast diff
ference between mob, or a popular out
break, and general uprising of the people
in behalf of justice and social liberty. Those
who are so tender-footed as are some of our
should remember that the
people are the source of all power; and we
hold it as a principle beyond controverSion
that the superior power has the right to exc
cute its DEGREES, when its appointed agents
rom any cause fail or refuse to perform the
luty assigned them If this is not sound
doctrine, then there is no such thing as law; {
or those who are entrusted with its execu- {
ion would have the means within themselves j
If setting it at naught. {


We hold that the citizens of San Fran
,isco have maintained the laws--not violated
hem. We make no assault upon the legal
authorities there. Perhaps they have done
he best they could But San Francisco has |
ong been the charne house of corruption, ,
perjury, and bribery. Murder, rapine, vio- ,
ence and theft have stalked abroad, and de-
led punishment. Cut-throats, robbers and
gamblers have reigned supreme. This out '
,reak,D as it has been styled, is not simply |
because Jim Casey killed Mr. King 1t is
that within six or seven years,
everal hundred murders have been committed
n that city, and yet only two of the crimi-
lals have received the punishment prescribed
~ statute at the hands of the law. We
would repeat that we make no charges against
he authorities; the District Courts Of the
Fourth and Twelfth Districts are presided
over by as good men as can be found in the
State; yet history proves that they have
been powerless for good. The gambling,
Misunderstanding, pistolshooting and Bowie
Snife influence has thwarted the ends Of JUS
lice and controlled the government of the
,ity. Juries are doubtless more in fault than
Courts, sheriifs, or policemen; still the one

headline: Taxing Mining Capital.
article:
Taxing Mining Capital


We find floating about the following note which
was recently received by the Assessor of Nevada
county, in reply to query on the subject, addressed
to the Attorney General:


ATTORNEY GENERALS OFFICE,


June 18TH 1856


SIR: / am of the opinion that capital invested in
Mining Claims is proper subject of taxation under
the Revenue Law of this State.


Very respectfully, Yours.


WIN. T. WALLACE. Atty Gen'.
Mr. John Mccoy, Assessessor Nevada Co.


Are that law" The Revenue Law of "a sets
mining claims aside as exempt from taxation. In
the list of taxable property occurs the item ina
chinery for mining" Is money paid for gum boots,
Spanish beef and sharpening picks, machinery for
minng?" IF the sinews of war" tanned down into
provision expenses of halfdozen hardfsted miners,
while running tunnel into one of the rock-crested
treasure banks of the mountains, to be taxed
capital invested then are fallen on uckess times.
Suppose twelve men, six miners and six mechanics,
form themselves into mining company, for the pur-
pose of driving tunnel into the side of one of the
thousand gold hills in the State. 1t is arranged that
the six miners Immediately commence the tunnel, and
that the mechanics proceed with their several pur-
suits, and turn their surplus earnings into fund out
of which to deray the expenses of running the tun-
mel. The work goes on for six months, $4,000 has
been paid for the various items of picks, drills, flour,
powder &c The Assessor drops in, and wishes to
know the amount of capital invested in the tunnel.
The cars and track are given in to him as-"ma-
chinery for mining, $1,000 But that is not a
moiety of the "captal invested in mining claims" ="
and the Assessor proceeds to investigate the matter
in another course. He finds that the company has
paid $4,000 at store by, for the various arti
cles of food and clothing, and for lumber, shoves,
and the like. He thereupon sets the company down
for $4,000 additiona!-"capital invested in mining
claims"


Our company keeps along several months-the me-
chanics paying the cash expenses and the miners
digging and blasting. Times grow dull, and the
mechanics compound with their partners, and with
draw from the company after having paid in cash to
the amount of $4,000 They lose what they have
paid and their recent partners get credit at the store
for six months provisions. The Assessor comes
round once more, and finds the account to run thus
"June goth, 1855, capital invested, $4,000 Dec
20, 1855, account paid Jones & Co. for provisions
$4,000" The latter item being an exact fellow to
the original statement of the company's capital SIX
months earlier, he takes down. and figures up cap-
tai invested in mining claims, $4,000" But, recol
lecting that our company has subssted sp to this
time, he sets about ascertaning the amount expend
ed during the past six months. He finds an unsettled
account of $4,000, for provisions to date. Concludes
that the latter item can not be called capital invested
until it is paid. The company breaks up, and the
men commence in other projects, after arranging with
Jones Co. to pay their indebtedness in monthly in
stalments of $500 Suppose they promptly meet
their engagements what will their capital invested
in mining claims amount to on the Goth April, 81?
Then suppose another company Jumps the aban-
doned tunnel, and after outlay Of $500 strikes
good pay, and you have the picture complete


Taxing capital invested in mining claims" will
never be submitted to by the miners. To enforce
the collection of such a tax would be an mposslbility.
If it could be enforced it would be suicidal policy
to place such an incubus upon the first and dearest
interest of the State. 1t would cut off the expendi
ture now amounting to thousands, and reduce it to
nothing Men would send their money to the East
to be loaned at 10 per cent. per annum rather than
be taxed on investments in projects the most preca
rous of any in the State.


But the tax can not and should not be enforced.
Newspapers say it should be collected and that per-
sons interested should not oppose itthat the miners
receive the protection of the government, and it is
only proper that they should pay such tax, for the
support of the State Government! Bah! talk to
the winds, of State Government Well have Vigi

headline: GRAND PARADE OF THE VIGILANCE
article:
GRAND PARADE OF THE VIGILANCE
CoMMITTEE.--The Vigilance Committee
turned out in grand parade to the num-
Der of 5000, or according to some ac-
counts, 5000 men, on Monday last. 1t
is understood that this exhibition of
themselves and their strength is prepa-
ratory to disbanding or adjourning till
the necessity of convening, shall again
bring the Committee together. 1t is to
be hoped that a sufficient publication
has taken place in San Francisco, that
the people may be able to 1--we and die
according to law hereafter, without the
necessity of an anomalous assemblage,
like the one we are told, that is about
to suspend its armed organization for
the present, and we trust, forever.


Let the people attend to their duties
as good citizens, and we need not be
shocked with the recital of deeds that
blot the fair fame of the State. A large
number of the pests of good society have
been driven out of the country. and a
wholesome terror struck to the hearts of
the rest. Society can now organize un-
der favorable auspices again, and by a
proper attendance upon those important
duties which every good citizen owes
the community in which he lives, there
need not be a recurrence of the scenes
recently enacted.


The most reliable prints at the Bay,
state that the Committee are still strong
in the affections of the people, and may
be said to be about to lay down their
arms in the full zenith of popularity and
power.


We hope to hear soon that law is
once again restored to its wonted chan
nels in San Francisco, and order reigns
in accordance with it.

fore peoples party must be entered for the

This movement for "People's Party" is
the illegitimate offspring of the Vigilance
Committee That body is fast being crushed
out of existence by the overwhelming force
of correct public opinion, and they find it
hard to surrender the power they have
usurped, or the fat Offices they have had in

looks to the qualification Of their ambitious

extend beyond the limits Of San Francisco,

intention of those who are urging its forma-

their character; but the ambition of its

boundaries of the Republic. "No pcnt up

Our streets have assumed a more quiet

article:
We give below an article from the Ohio States
man, of July 18th, in reference to the Vigilance

News FROM CALIFORNIA.--There is bad state
of things in California; most dangerous exam
pie for the country. While we have no sympa-
thy for the murderers and ballot box suffers,
and do not think that any punishment can be
too great for such outlaws, yet it is a bad state
of affairs when q self-constituted Committee un-
dertake, in the face of the constituted authori-
ties, to administer punshment-esp especially un-
der the heated state of excitement that seems to
exist there--that must exist TO pFolong the Com
mittee's power to act.


In country like ours where the people have
adopted a rule of law, it is better to await the
return of reason and justice in community, than
to take the law into our own hands,


What we oppose in the attempted revolution
in Kansas, we should oppose any where Any
other view of the subject will lead to civil revo-
luton everywhere, instead Of peaceable elec-
tions, the only test known to our system of
government.


We have in our time, witnessed acts of legis-
lation in our own State that seemed enough to
excite any people to a great rebellion, but was
it not better to submit peaceably for the time
being, and trust TO the future enlightenment OF
the public mind +?


We see that already move has been made in
California to call State Convention by the
party that sustains the Vigilance Committee,
form a new Government without the regular
process of law-or to use the language of Cal
iiornia paper, proclaim new Independence"
This independence is understood to be a Gov
ernment, not only Independent Of the present
State government of California, but independ-
ent of any other government-wthdraw from
the Union and set up for themselves. 1t is thus
the public m,nd is led on from one error to an
other until dissolution stares us in the face and
all government is at an end. These fearful
fOrebodings are everywhere developing them
selves, and it is high time that the good and pa
trotic were banding themselves together every
where to check the fearful evil.


We are happy to see, however, that this revo-
utiOuaPy proposition does not meet with favor
in California, even in quarters where it might
have been expected. The clergy there, as here.
have taken the side of disorder, and we are glad
to see the papers doing them full justice aud
demanding that they return to their calling, and
preach peace aud not evolution--prcach order
and not disorder. We have read one of these
sermons published in San Francisco paper,
and it out-Beccher's Beecher for blood and car
mage, though Slavery had nothing to do with
the subject and was not alluded to. Thus show
ing that this unclerical conduct rife over the
land is disease, and any d sturbance is seized
upon, as preteXt for mixing in the eXcitements
Of the hour

JAMES CUsICK. who was ordered to leave
the State by the Vigilance Committee, but
who did not go and whom the Committee
have not yet hung, recently visited the sen


Tor editor editor of the California .Ameri-
can. Mr.. Cusick "looked straight in the
face of the senior, with o " bold Irish eye,"
and from his apparant honesty and fear
lessness," the senior is of the opinion, that
" he has been made the subject of injustice
and persecution The senior Of the finer
ican; in making this admission lays himself
liable to expulsion from the Committee, and
may possibly receive a note from "93
Secretary" ordering him to leave the State,
or suffer the :" usual penalty" Seriously,
however, we are pleased to see this frank
and honorable admission on the part Of the
american. 1t is an evidence of returning
reason, which would hardly have been con


sidered orthodox previous to the election.

headline: The VIGILANCE Committee.
article:
The existence of this body is an anomoly
in the history of people, without authority
of law, and ought not to be continued one
moment beyond actual patent necessity.


The extraordinary armament which they
seem to be gathering about them in San
Francisco will be regarded with jealousy BY
the people of the State. Theil power should
not rest so much upon the force of powder
and ball, as in the moral business Of their
acts. Violence breeds violence, is an apllor
ism long since too often verified.


The Executive Committee may exercise a
commanding influence At this time, but how
long may this continue?-unti difference
Of opinion produces a split, and denagogues
will bring this about.


Some act will disgust the better members,
ana they will drop out-oue by one-leaving
the controlling power in the hands Of the
rash and less scrupu'ous-and then, remcm-
Der they are provided with two thousand
muskets, and two or three pieces of artillery.


We have great faith in the intelligence
and the Inherent love of law Of the Ameri-
can pcopIe-give them time to think. The

as to forbid our forming an accurate iudg-

1@ The recent excitable times created
by the assassination of James King of
William, and the summary punishment of
murderers, has produced for the time be-
ing, an almost total stagnation in politics.
Little has been said by papers of either
side, except a paragraph now and then,
just to show they "were on it." All
seemed to eschew political issues to es-
pouse one side or the other, in the tragi-
cal scenes which were being enacted
And now, that the first great act in the
drama is over, the criticisms of the
press are forthcoming, either laudatory or
otherwise.


Generally, the American press of the
State has taken part with the people, and
sustained the action of the Vigilance Com.
mittee.


The Democratic press has, in a major
ity of cases, devoted itself to the vindica
ton of violated and imperative "law and
order.' The San Francisco Globe, Shasta
Courier, and l or 2 others, do not follow
in the wake of the party press in general
but range themselves on the side of jus
tice and right.


1t is not strange that the State Journal
and other papers of the same kidney.
should be found where they are. The
strangulation of such men as Casey, is an
irreparable loss to the Democratic party
By the services and influence of such men
a Democratic Governor has been twice
stuffed upon the people. Millions of dol.
lars have been wrenched from the honest

Under the dictation of Palmer, Cook. &

doned Of the race. The recent rising o.
the people, is an indication that such pro
ceedings are at an end. The Democratic

is fitting that other papers of like stripe
should cotton to the side of the murderer
"Ephraim is joined to his idols, let him

full and of vast Aesponsibility, by an au-
thority amenable to none but the silent
monitor and the Ole to whom ultimately

long and we'll.


That the dreadful necessity existed Of
suspcnding for time he legal code es-
tablished by properly constituted author
tiles, to check by the strong arm of society
in its original form and purity, the abuses
which had found shield under the cor
rupt workings of well designed but in

do not doubt. Indeed the most attrocious
acts of consummate villainy for which San
Francisco was long since proverbial, the
character of the men who have perpetra-
ted the deeds, and the character of an
opposite nature which the populace that
took the law and the execution of Justice
into their own hands, leave little room to
cavil that one Of those rare and awful
crisiscs had been brought to the option..o
the citizens Of San Francisco, either to
surrender all hope of justice forever or
rise to assert an Unborn social right, and
vindicate the majesty of a ler non scripta
from which there can be no escape, no
appeal.


The calmncss and deliberation of the
Vigilance Committee in the discharge of
the grave duties they had assumed, is an
index Of the moral responsibility they felt
resting upon them in the extraordinary
emergency they were called upon to meet.
GA mob is monster with many heads
and no brains" But there was nothing
on the exterior of the moving of the
masses in the late tragedy which indicated
the workings of a mobocratic spirit On
the contrary the solemnity which charac-
terized the whole proceedings has rarely
been exceeded in any court of Justice
There can be no question that the master
spirits in the late reign Of pure democracy
in San Francisco, were actuated By pa
triotic and rational motives. In the
community for which they heroically acted
their deeds will be salutary in the highest
degree. A score of others not less guilty
than Cora or Casey ought to feel the rod
of offended justice, and San Francisco
might possibly indulge the hope that it
would not be worse for her than Sodom,
in the day of reckoning.


But just as the action of the people at
San Francisco many have been, and was,
we very much fear, the example will be
deleterious upon the State at large.-
There is in every community class who
cannot discriminate between a case of
absolute necessity for the assumption of
original right, and one where the grievance
is slight and better to be punished not at
all than not by law. These, on occasions
when the passions of men are overheated,
may he disposed to initiate the example
which has been set. There is love of
notoriety, no matter how to be acquired,
in the bosoms Of hundreds of our popula-
tion, which seeks to be gratifed at what
ever expense.

lives of their fellows if in SO doing thew

dismal tales of blood being discovered
under suspicious circumstances of shrieks
and groans being family heard in a certain
locality; of jew pedler being seen and
then missing, &c. These in times of ex-
citement help to fasten suspicion upon
persons more innocent than themselves.
and passions once let loose without the
restraints of law, a case of righteous ret
ribution is cited as precedent, and sonc-
body is sacrificed to appease the morbid
state of public feeling.


The San Francisco tragedy was well,
and if the well-disposed citizens of other
communities are not too eager to initiate
the example which has been set, no harm
will result to the balance of the State

the organization of Vigilance Committees

From the Albany Statesman.


The article quoted below from the United States
Economist, journal of high standing, especially in
the business and commercial community, makes
disclosures of transactions with which John c. Ere.
mont is connected of the most startling character
In view Of what is here said the intelligence from
California will be awaited with interest. Fremonts
coming to New York and taking up his residence
there, has long been known to have some connex-
Ion with the schemes Of Palmer, Cook, & Co.
schemes which in some respects had already come
to be of so questionable character as to cause
honest men to stand aloof As silent partner in
the concern, Fremont could facilitate their opera
tions by residing in New York, and this we are all
well assured is the whole secret of bis change of
residence.


We are greatly mistaken If the public mind is
not to receive disclosures that will more fully than
anything yet illustrate the folly Of "new men, ex-
periments in conneIion with the Presidency.


"When the news arrived of the late revolution
in California, the vigorous and righteous action OF
| the Vigilance Committee met with one response
The necessity for the defensive action of the peo-
pie through vigilance committee and against the
| corruption and iniquity with which they had been
overrun and oppressed, was acknowledged with
one accord. Gradually, however, facts seem to
point to the source of the great evils that have
been experienced in that country. The food Of
COTIuphou WHICH secueu uniNefsAl IN Lne StAt6
has apparently been traced, and proves unmis-
takably in narrowing the circle around the house
Of Palmer, Cook, & Co., the defauting agents OF
the State. The house is alleged to have placed its
own creatures in every Office Municipal officers,
judges, members Of the Legislature are all said to
have depended upon this firm.


Having the State authorities in its till, IL sent
one of its members to Congress, and another to
the United States Senate. Two years ago il failed,
In scandalous manner, to pay the State interest
This Legislature, alleged to be its own creatures,
white washed the affair. II has now failed again
with the State money in its possession. The news
Of the fact has now returned to California, where
the committee rule. The committee with it's re-
sistless power and accumulated acts will not fail
to investigate the matter, and the whole connex-
ion Of Colonel Fremont with that house, from the
requirement Of his claim 10 lands in California all
through the prosecution Of that claim his election
TO the United States Senate and the efforts lately
TO sell his own notes In Wall street to cover the
defalcstion Of the firm for the State interest Ii in
danger of being laid before the world, hence the
anxiety with which the Fremont papers, led of
by the Courier and Herald, are taking ground
against the San Francisco vigilance committee.
One member Of the firm is now in Washing
ton attending to . bin before Congress in relation
TO the Bolton 4 Barron grant Of land. On the
passage o. the bin the patent for the snds is TO
issue, and then, IL has been stated Palmer, Cook,
Co, viii be required to make large payment 70
fulhl contrscts To make this payment IL has
been alleged, the State interest money and other

funds that came into their hands were retained
The delay in Congress 10 pass the bill has caused
the continued retention Of the money. In the
meantime the honor Of the State is under cload,
and 1t remains to be seen what action the Vigilance
Committee will see proper to take in the matter.
The next news will be of interest"

headline: PRESIDENT COMONFoRT.
article:
dant evidence OF the accommodating exIGen
cies that surround President Comoniort il
the rule of Mexico. From all appearance.
he will, In the next four months, be sub
iected to tests such as no common man cal
successfully meet He has dared to d,
what no other ruler of that country ha:
dared, unless we except the futile effort o
Gomez i'arias, who, when Vice Presiden
to Santa Anna, some years since, made al
attempt upon the possessions of the church
In that attempt-which was an experiment
of S nta Anna's, but performed by proxy
the result was such that the brave Die
t,tor drew back in alarm, and disclaimed
aud revoked all the acts OF the Vice Pres
ident, whom he had purposely left in charge
for short season. Bolder than Santa
Anna, Gen. Cononfort has had the cour-
age to propose to Congress the passage, aud
then to execute the law when passed, ex-
propriating to the State the vast posses
sons of the Mexican church.


That this was a necessary measure, eve
ry student of the affairs of that country
will allow. The vast accumulation of real
estate and landed property by the clergy
was pressing like an incubus upon the ma
terial welfare of the people. Its aggrega-
tion continually threatened to swallow up
the land, and convert the population into
servile retainers of the priests, or else to
drive it to the obtainance of miserable
subsistence from the thin and more sterile
soils. A theoeracy with subsidized Die
tator as its nominal head, or a revolution
that should overthrow the existing organi-
zation of the church, and make it spiri-
tual, and not a temporal corporation, were
the only alternatives for the country


Gen. Comonfort has recognized the true
difficulty, and has adopted a solution that
many deem the only possible one He has
struck at the root of the evil, and is carry
ing out his work apparently in manner
calculated to give him a widespread pop
ular support, and to confer upon his coun-
try great benefits. While the sales of the
possessions of the church are bringing in
abundant resources to the national treasury;
The possession of which will give him grea-
ter power to resist the Vaccinations of the
enemies of the law; the adoption of tho
principle of preference in the sales in favor
of those who hold possession, leases, or
claims for Improvement of urban and IAN
ded estates, has an air of popular Justice
that is emlnently beneficial to the cause he
represents. This course is creating LARGE
class among the people directly interested
in the support of the new policy. and in
any other country would be looked upon as
one OF the guarantees Of its permancnce.
" hat the result may be among the anon
alous race that peoples Spain and its for
sner colonies, no one can judge.


The opposition of the clergy to tie law
of appropriation, is taking violent and
active form in all parts of the Republic
and in our view the greatest danger to Gen.
Comonfort in resisting and suppressing it.
is to be found in the known want OF preb
ity among the Mexican leaders and public
men. There are few there, in the army
or in civil service, that have not been ia
nus-taced and Protcan-sided in the course
of the last fifteen years. In addition to the
clergy, in their opposition to the Govern
ment, there is large portion OF the old
officers OF the army, which Gen. Comon-
fort has in part endeavored to break up, as
being inimical to popular freedom. These
men, who have passed large portion OF
their lives in the camp or in the barrack,
are untitled to return to the walks of civil
life, and finding their only means ofliveli-
hood in military employment, and a chance
to pillage, are ready topronounce, in tayol
OF anything. or anybody.


In the measures adopted to support the
new policy of the Government, Gen. Com
nonfort has adopted course somewhat
/ fi,-,%.
The press is not relied upon to defend him
from unjust accusation, but is kept under
strict censorship, that it may not contri-
butte to popular excitement, while his own
partisans are busily employed in vitupera-
ting all the Opposers of the Government as
thieves and robbers. Public banquets, too
are given to the lower orders, at which the
President makes grandiloquent speeches,
and distributes aims, and branches of flo
raj ornaments hung with gold coin. The
cry of anarchy and spoliation of the mid
die classes, is family echoed as being the
aim of the enemies of the Government,
and an. effort is evidently made to get up a
popular scare. 0 Fr....a .'-..-
| All of these things are producing their
natural effects in Mexico, and in some pla-
ees the movement against the Government
seem founded in logical reasons, as, for in
stance, some of those alleged by Gen. Vi
daurri in New Leon. His cry is almost
an echo of that of the old Mexican State
of Texas against the despotism of Santa
Anna. Vidaurri says he resists the cen
tralist policy of Gen. Comonfort- We are
only told by the press of Mexico that the
cry of the Insurgents throughout the inte
rior is ''Relijion y Fueros" (Religion and
the rights of the people.) Whether Gen
Comonfort is capable of resisting all the ad
verse movements now on foot we shall soor
see. To do SO successfully will require
we believe, genius and practicability of ;
high order--N. o. Picayune.

MESsRs. EDITORS The object of thi:

she people OF the county for their consid-

tee found in their possession u number OF

Last Saturday, the 9th instant, was the

damning designs. At late hour at night

peratc effort, with from two to ten appor-
toned to nearly every house in the coun-
ty, kill all the whites save the above excep-
ton, plunder their homes, take their hor-

State, (Mexieo.)


Notwithstanding the intense excitement
which moved every member OF the com
muni5y, and the desperate measures to
which men are liable to be led on by such
impending danger to which we had been
exposed by our indulgence aud lenity to
our slaves, we must say the people acted
with more caution and deliberation than
ever before characterized the action OF
any people under similar circumstances
| 3Iore than two hundred negroes had vi
dated the law, the penalty of which is
death. But by unanimous consent the
law was withheld and their lives spared,
with the exception of three of the ring
leaders, who were on last Friday, the 9th

arrested and ordered to leave the county

is proven to be one of the prime movers

demands.


We are satisfied that the lower class of

for the benefit of the Mexican population,

passed by the unanimous voice of the coun-

tiers, we are persu ,ded that there will nev.
er again occur the necessity of commu
nication of the character of this.


Yours, respectfully,


JOHN a. ROBSON,
H. A. TATUM,

article:
We are heartily tired of the San Francisco
Vigilance Committee-of their extra judi
cial actions-and the feeling which their e1
istence has created and is now fostering in
community No subject that has ever agi-
tated the public mind, has been fraught
with SO much evil. or given rise to such acri-
monious feelings, or excited the public mind
to such pitch. Neighbors regard each
other with perfect astonishment, and dis
trust and foul suspicion is engendered among
those whose intercourse has formerly evi-
denced the most honorable feelings and
| friendly relations.


The press, too, has felt the influence of the
mob at the Bay. and forget that their ap-
peals should be to the judgment of the peo-
pie, instead of their passions, and indulge
| in the most bitter and acrimonious feelings.
1t is almost impossible to open a paper from
below, without reading the disgusting de-
tails o. lynch law execution, or the specu-
lations of mob editors upon the next victim
of the tyrants who now rule San Francisco
with the secret conclave and the bayonet, to
everlasting disgrace of our republican insti-
| tutions. As if to add fresh fuel to the feel
ings already agitatiDg the State, the Allan
tic papers are now favoring the California
public with republication of their pro-
ceedings, and Casey and Cora have just been
re-hung by the arrival of the last Steamer
Editors, who have remained tranquil during
the widest political excitements through
which the country has passed, have yielded
to the deleterious influence arising in Sar
Francisco, and given vent to their pent-uI
feelings, in bitterness of language in strong
mosphere is impregnated with lawlessness-
the times are demoralized-and the public
sense vitiated and perverted into unhealthy
channels. In proof of this, is the chroniclet
| fact that hundreds rushed to San francisco
to witness the execution of the first Ylgi
lance victims. On the circulation of a ru
NOR that some unfortunate individual is tt
be hanged at a certain hour by the Vigi
lance Committee, and men, women and chill
dren--old and young-hurry to the Vigi
lance Bastile for the puopose of witnessing
the expected execution. The depraveC
taste which seeks for its qualification the dy
ing agonies-the throes and commissions o
fellow being hurried into eternity, is
disgrace to humanity. When we find wo
men bringing their young children to feas
their eyes on the horrid spectacle-ladies il
their carriages with their lorgnettes ready
to be used to bring the object nearer-mor
ais, refinement and sensibility-in a word
all the finer feelings of our pature must b.
at low ebb indeed.


The evil influences which this VigilaDc,
movement has scattered abroad, arising
from familiarity with blood, from the sigh
of thousands of armed men taking the Law
into their own hands, or. rather, trampline
upon all law, and in the language of Jeho
vah, saying Vengeance is mine," will no
be erased till another generation shall have
passed away, and principles of right, rever
ence for the law, and respect for the com
mands of God, shall have rooted out tn,
memory of the lawless of the San Francisco
mob. The safeguards of the people in theil
persons, property liberty and lives, are tn,
constitution and laws of the land "Thest
are cast down from their high places in thu
affection and regard Of our citizens, an(
trampled in the dust, and in their stead, WI
have the uncontrolled will of a committee o
twenty nine, enforced by three Thousand
cleaning bayon ets." The committee have
fearful responsibility resting upon them
"Not mere physical responsibility and ac-
countability, but a responsibility which, il
their calmer hours, when excitement, and
passion shall have passed away-when il
after life they shall sit down to reflect or
their past lives-when age. creeping or
apace, shall silver DER their locks, and tht
messenger of death shall claim them for hi
own-then, when their own souls shall ST
in judgment on their acts, will they feel tn,
weight of that moral responsibility. which
will weigh th,m down with a repentance
which we trust may atone for ALL

article:
nature have thickened upon us in manner
to CRAFTY the most morbid taste. We were
consoine ourselves with the idea that the
ugly business at San Francisco was about to
die an easy death, without further agitation
when the telegraph Of Sunday evening threw
the entire public into an excitement, by the
report of the stabJing Of Hopkins and the
capturing of Terry, and subsequently the
arrest of Durkee upon the charge of piracy

If facts were wanting to prove the neces-
sity Of a thorough moral and political reyolu
ton in this State, we think the transactions
of the last seven days, have furnished them
beyond doubt.


We have before had occasion to allude to
the officious intermeddng Of Judge Terry in
this business, and we have now only to re-
mark that we regard his present position, as
the legitimate result of his violent dictatoria
rashness To say that his mission to San
Francisco, as some assert, was a pacific one
will not 60 down with those who are ac-
quainted with Judge Terry. The olive branch
never had much popularity with him, his
favorite arguments being the doube-barrelled
shotgun and bowie knife. His respect for
law and order has never prevented him in
the use of this very peculiar species Of elo-
quence-eyen in the presence Of Court.
Such conduct may be considered chivalrous
by some, but the moro sober and common
place characterize it by different term
Neither can we regard the meeting together
at the rooms of his particular friend, DR..
Ashe Of so many of his faithful clansmen,
as mere matter Of chance. One or two Of
those men we should consider very poor
society for a Judge Of the Supreme Bench;
and taken as a council would look for any
thing but pacific measures from them. There
was concert Of action, and an arsenal Of arms
ready at hand These facts do not indicate
a mission of peace, but preparations for an
offensive move.


However, let justice be done. He has
drawn the ermine into the ditch and befoul-
ed it with violence. For this he stands con
demned before the people Of California, for
upon this point they are the Judges. II,
stabbing OF Hopkins, upon calm and delibe-
rate examination Of the facts, he be found to
have acted in selt-defence, as his friends in
sist that he did, then touch not a hair Of his
head. Let no outside pressure induce diff
ferent action on the part Of the Vigilance
Committee should they bring him to trial,
Let him be treated as a man, without regard
to his position; give him the benefit Of rea-
sonable doubt, for no public will support you
in q different course no matter what present
appearances may indicate, Meet folly and
violence with prudence and wisdom.


The arrest of Durkec upon the charge Of
piracy, is marked indication of the respect
these men have for law. Durkee by direc-
ton of the Vigilance Committee, and for no
private gain Of his own, selzes quantity
of arms which the law and order men pro-
pose to use in subdung the Vigilance Com
mittee, and turns the same over to the Com
mittee, safe and unnjured. He does not
propose to sell, use, or destroy this property,
it is a precautionary measure Of the men
under whom he is acting. Where is the
felonious intent2 the wicked design that
makes it robberyl Bah. There is not an
unbiased mind in the State, but sees in this
move Of those great apostles of law, a vicious
trick-a using Of the law in violation OF lis
spirit, for the qualification Of their small re-
venge


If Durlee suffers let them ndict the two
or three thousand men who assisted in taking
the muskets from the armores on Saturday
night. If Durkee has committed piracy or
the high seas, they have committed robbery
on shore, the offences are identical, the only
difference being in the place of the act,
These men use the law as boys do a football
now tossing it from their path, and anon
pushing it full ia your face. Whether Gov,
johnson has had any hand in authorizing the
movements of the past week, does not ap
s,ear, but if not, we may reasonably look for
something of a pacific nature e1uinating ifon
his Office The people demand it under the
state of affairs, and it is his duty to con
.cede il,


In these distracted times it becomes

Suicide of Yankee Sullivan.


This morning the notorious Yankee Sulli-
van committed suicide, by cutting into his
left arm. and bleeding to death. The pub
lie are well aware that Sullivan has been in
the hands of the Vigilance Committee during
the last few days. He dad confessed to
them his evil deeds, and made important
revelations as to the oallot-boX stuiing OPP
eratons in which so many high and low
scoundrels of this city have been engaged
for years past. Until it was decided what
course should be taken with Sullivan, he
was kept in close confinement He was,
however, allowed every indulgence in the
supply of food and other necessary refresh
mentS that the Committee could give His
nervous system appears to have been great
ly affected and broken down by the tragic
events of the last few weeks. He witnessed
the execution of Casey and Cora, and since
then has showed much anxiety and appre-
henson on his own account. He appeared
to have lost his appetite, and usually ate
very Sparngly.


/ This morning, about six O'clock, Sullivan
called the guard and asked drink of wa
+ ter. He told the latter that he had just
had horid dream. He dreamed that he
had been condemned to die he saw the
guards approach-they seized him and pin
oned his arms-they lead him to the fatal
window-the rope was placed round his
neck-he stepped on the platform, he saw
the deridng crowd, his sins crowded upon
him-the platform fell, he struggled-and
awoke, in the most frightful state of mind
g. !, i'll
cheer him. He said that the Committee
did not mean to hang him, but only to send
him out Of the country Sullivan, however,
was too much frightened to accept at first
the friendly consolation. He received the
drink of water he had asked for, and after q
time appeared to be more cheerful. The
guard then left him. A bout two hours later,
when Sullivans's breakfast was being carried
into his room, the prisoner was found on his
bed dead. He was dressed in his panta-
looms and shirt, and lay extended on his back.
He had cut his left arm at the elbow Joint,
ON the inside, to the bone. The main artery
was completely severed, and he must have
died in few minutes afterwards He in
Aicted the wound with the knife which he
used to cut his food with.


The body was cold at this time, SO that it
is probable Sullivan committed the rash act
Immediately after the guard had left him at
six o'clock. Remorse and terror produced
by his dream, had no doubt prompted the
suicide. Two medical gentlemen were i'm
mediately called in, who declared that Sui
liyan had been dead for some time and that
he could have suffered no pain lie had
/ allen, as it were, into a faint, and in that
condition expired. The counteuance of the
deceased showed no marks of pain.


Sullivan has made important disclosures
to the Committee, the result of which will
be knowa before long. lie confessed that
he had been convicted IN England for steal
ing, and had been sentenced to tranSporta-
ton to New South Wales for fourteen years
When there his bad conduct was such that
he had been placed by the Government un-
der regimen of the seyerest kind, different
from those other convictS who underwent
the ordinary penal sentence. lie escaped,
however, from New South Wales. 1t was
one of his greatest fears that he should be
sent back there again. He had Solemnly
promised the Committee to fight no more,
prize battles to drink and quarrel no more,
and had vowed that hencetorth he would
live an honest and peaceful life lie was
desirous to be sent out of the country, and
promised that, if he were sent TO the \ tlan-
tic States, he would avoid the large towns
and keep himself retired from the public
gaze. \ guilty conscience would not allow
him to wait the course of events in sud-
den fit Of remorso and horror he ended his
vile reer.- Ereatag Bulletin Isl uH.

ticket. The Convention was styled Fill

bers announce that they are not supporting

mined to do anything that will defeat the

objects and intentions Then if the people
desire their success, it is all right. Ii they
are supporting Mr.. Fillmore without the

object, if it be not to secure the election of

The Foote Convention nominated for Mem

first stretch. He has been on ranch for

| ly expected that he will notrun over two

didate, upon that question alone. The in
fuence of Spanish Grant holders was to
carry him through. But it didn't quite do
it. How does the gentleman stand now !:

settled upon Spanish Grants in good faith,
from their claims without the value of their
improvements? Is he willing to turn the
Quartz Mills and the rich mining claims on
the Larkin tract over to the grant holder,

handed, after having spent thousands of
dollars in improvements? How does the
little Spanish nag stand upon this issue af-
ter having been ranched for two years.


The other nominee of the Foote party has

some two or three years-about the same
length of lime that Gov. Foote has Durin =
this brief period ne has been in various por-

headline: Suicide Of Yankee Sullivan.
article:
lnlS morning the notorious anEee sullivan
committed suicide, by cutting into his left
arm, and bleeding to death The public are
well aware that Sullivan has been in the
hands of the Vigilance Committee during the
last few days. lie had confessed to Them
his evil deeds, and made important reyela-
tions as to the ballot box stutfing operations

until it was decided what course should be

tinement. He was however allowed every
indulgence in the supply Of food and other
necessary retreshment that the Committee
could give. His nervous system appears to
have been greatly effected and broken down
by the tragic events of the last few weeks,
He witnessed the execution of Casey and
Cora, and since then he exhibited much ankle
ty and Apprehension on his own account. He
appeared to have lost his appetite, and usual
ly ate very sparingly.


This morning, about six o'clock, Sullivan
called the guard and asked for drink of wa
ter. lie told the latter, that he lad a most
horid dream. He dreamed that he had been
condemned to die; he saw the guards approach
they seized him and pinoned his arm-thev
led him to the fatal window-the rope was
placed around his neck-he stepped on
the platform fell, he struggled-and awoke
in the most frightful state of mind Tho
guard reasoned with him, and tried to cheer
him. He said that the Committee did not
mean to hang him, but only to send him out
of the country. Sullivan however was too
much frightened to accept at first the friend
y consolation He received the drink of
water he had asked for, and after time APP
peared to be more cheerful. The guard then
left him. About two hours later, when Snl-
Nan's breakfast was being carried into his
room, the prisoner was found on his bed
dead. He was dressed III his pantaloons and
shirt, and lay extended on his back. He
had cut his left arm at the elbow Joint, on
the inside to the bone. The main artery was
completely severed, and he must have died
in few minutes afterwards. He inflicted
the wound with the knife which he used to
cut his food WITH


The body WAS cold at this time, so that it
is probable Sullivan committed the rash act
Immediately after the guard had left him at
six o'clock. Remorse and terror, produced
by his dream had no doubt promted the sui
eide. Two medical gantIemen were imme-
diately called in, who declared that Sullivan
had been dead for some time, and that he
could have suffered no pain. lie had fallen,
as it were, into a faint, and in that condition
expired The countenance of the deceaed
showed no marks Of pain


Sullivan has made important disclosures

be known before long. He confessed that
he had been convicted in England for steal
inc and had been sentenced to transportation
TO New South Wales for fourteen years.
When there his bad conduct was such that he
had been placed by the Government under Il
regimen of the severest kind, different from
those other convlcts who underwent penal
sentence. He escaped however, from New
South Wales. 1t was one of his greatest fears
that he should be sent back there again.
He had solemnly promised the Committee
to fight no more prize battles, to drink and
quarrel no more, and had vowed that hence
forth he would live an honest and peaceful
life. lie was dcsirous to be sent out OF the
country, and promised that if he were sena
to the States, he would avoid the large
towns and keep himself retired from the pub
lie gaze. guilty conscience would not al
low him to wait the course of events; III II
sudden fit of rcmorse and horror he ended
his vile career.


1t was generally understood at the Com
mittee Rooms that Sullivan would soon
have been liberated, or sent out of the coun-
try. 1t seems also to have been understood
by some persons that he personally was un-
der the impression he might meet with some
other fate as Charles T. Duane was heard to
remark this morning that Sullivan had said
that sooner than be branded and sent from
the country he would kill himself Sullivan
was not the real name of the deceased.


Coroner Kent was duly notified Of the
death, and the body was taken i'll charge 10y
him. An inquest will be held tomorrow
morning.

article:
Ostracism Prescribed.


The persons who have hitherto been most active
in their opposition to the Vigilance Committee,
endeavored to make the Committee odious by
charging upon its leading members a covert in
tention of turning its power into the politics of
the day. The imputatiou has been as often and
Indignantly denied by the members and friends
of that body, and the people have credited the
latter authority. The charge grave one
and the authorities upon which it was made have
been carefully scrutinized before the people, and
we feel assured that had they discovered grounds
for the assertion that the powerful moral force
which sustained that body, would have been with
drawn from it at once. No one believed there ex-
listed any such intention on the part of the ruling
influential men of the Committee. and the matter
passed off without elcitng apparently any notice
outside of the large towns of the State.


With the Inconsistency which attends the acts
Of men who persist in false step, these very same
men who thus attempted to make the Committee
odous by fastening upon its members the false
charge. are now, themselves moving heaven and
earth to introduce this temporary and local mat
ter into politics, and make it vital issue, in the
great national contest now going on before the
people. Repudiated men, crippled in business
arising from the withdrawal of the confidence of
the business men about them, blasted in political
hopes, athirst for revenge and impotent in them
selves to effect it--would restore themselves to
public favor, and recuperate their finances by
foisting their cause upon the Democratic party,
and making adhesion TO their ruined fortunes
sine qua non of sound political character.



acknowledging adhesion to no particular party.
and which by its position upon the Vigilance
question. lost the greater part of its paying pa
tronage, hoists the Democratic national ticket at
its head-joins in this clamor ostracising those of
its neighbors who will not follow its crazy head,
and carry the EDITORS quarrel into the arena of
party. Mr. Nugent, writer of ability, and the
presiding genius Of the Hoald, is the President
and we presume the ruling spirit of the Young
Mems Democratic Club of the city of San Fran
asco, which body recently passed certain resolu-
tions one of which is as follows:


"Resolved therefore, That the Young Mems De-
mocratic Club, believing it to be the sense of the
great National Democratic party of the Union
and because of their detestation of all combina-
tions opposed to the Constitutions and laws of the
lard; and for the sake OF preserving perfect har-
mony in their association, do expressly declare
that no member Of the organisation StV1ed fhe
Tig1ance COMMITTEE shall be eligible to n,eta5e,-
ship in their Club"


Here is language sufficiently plain. These youth
full Democrats would set up new test of party
fath--one must not only be Democrat. but he
must coincide with them upon the Vigilance oues-
ton. AS further demonstration of their feel
ing upon the point, they elected Judge Terry an



honorary member of their order. and sent a com
mittee in Haunting regalia. to escort him, on his
release. TO Sacramento. As citizens these men
had perfect right to condemn the Vigilance
Committee and its members, and express their
JOY over the release OF Judge Terry-they have
light to incorporate their bitter hatred Of per-
sons as the creed OF such Club and in sacrlege
of a name, mighty with the people, invoke the
aid of all Democrats to avenge the private griets
OF themselves or Judge Terry 1t is not now a
question whether Vigilance or anti-Vigilance, but
whether we will permit the usefulness of the
democratic organization in this State to become
at this time burthened with the quarrel of these
men. For one We repudate the leadership of
such advisers; we suspect their motives and doubt
their Democracy


We do not speak as partizan either for or
against the Iga9e,s, mmdton e came 6a from Is
friends, our position would be the same. We
gave expression to our views when the Nevada
resolutions came out, and we believe the reasons
then urged by were considered good by the
democracy of the mountains generally.


The "Oroville Butte Record" an enthusiastic
igiance paper, in the issue of the 7th inst,
makes the following remarks evidently under the
impression that the Vigilance men were trying to
make the question political;


"a portion of the KYi and independent vig-
lance press, are endeavoring to make Vigilance
or anti-Nigilance, the issue of the next election.
The press in the employ Of the mob at San Fran
cisco, it would appear have no better sense than
to insult the intelligence of the people, by asking
them TO permit the question OF Vgilance-ism TO
override every other question. and control their
sutrages at the coming election"


We have said our say upon this question. And
for our part we are determined to condemn this
political question; and those who shall attempt
to force this unheard Of test of democracy upon
the party. The test is: Are you Democrat"
and it is the only one that can be applied.


Present appearances indicate desire, on the

to saddle the vigilance question upon the party,
