The Execution of Hetherington and Brace


by the Vigilance Committee.
article:
Az CLOCK To-Day, tne Military cOmpa-
nies of the Vigilance Committee com
menced issuing from the Committee Rooms,
and marched and countermarched all around
neighboring blocks. At o'clock there were
five companies stationed opposite the Com
mittee Rooms, three at the corner Of Sacra-
mento and Davis Streets and the cross streets
leading to the locality were occupied by com
panies Of dragons. 1t was the general expec-
tation Of the public that 5 o'clock was the
hour of execution. Every house top having
a view of Sacramento and Davis streets was
covered, and also every spot commanding a
view. Fifteen thousand people witnessed the
tragedy. At this time, the roofs of the
houses in the vicinity fell precipitating all of
them into the houses; five persons were in
iured.


The scaffold was erected on Davis street,
between Sacramento and Commercial streets
The dimensions were ten feet square, with an
upright beam seven feet above the scaffold.


At 5:35, two carriages proceeded to the
building, and Brace and Hetherington were
placed in them, and conveyed to the place of
execution, Brace, assisted by two persons
assembled to the fatal platform. Next came
Hetherington; he refused all assistance, and
though his arms were pinioned, he walked up
the narrow stairway firmly, and with unquiv-
ering nerve.


The prisoners then took their places on
the trap-door Hetherington next to Com
mercial street. They both faced the west
When they reached the drop each had on a
light straw hat, but Braces blew of, and his
head was left exposed to the wind. The ropes
were then adjusted. An attendant united
the neckcloth Of Brace, but Hetherington
performed that office for himself


The appearance of the prisoners on the
scaffold was characteristic of each. Brace
acted like drunken man, and declared that
he was drunk. He appeared so. Hethering-
ton to the last, stood firm and spoke firmly.
What he said was to this effect.


"You may, and probably do think me a
hardened criminal but am not. | have
never lived day at the end of which was
not willing to meet my Maker, as I am now
about to do, in few moments. have not
had fair trial by the Vigilance Committee.
In shooting Baldwin, acted in sef-defense
was acquitted, yet find that that act bears
on me in my present position"


Ilclo anu dC various CiIIleS, Ho WIS lHIci- =
rupted by Brace, who spoke in an incoherent
manner, and wanted him to get done and
through with it.


"In the difficulty with DR.. Randall" said
Hetherington, 81 only drew to defend myself.
l only wanted to settle difficulty with him
and so told Mr.. McCorkle. He drew his pis-
tol, and was obliged to draw mine in self
defense. | know | am about to be launched
into eternity. I have had a long conversa-
ton with Bishop Kip, to-day, on religious
subjects. am not afraid of eternity"


Hetherington was frequently interrupted
by Brace, and it was impossible to follow
him fully.


81 forgive all my enemies. God have mer-
cy on all; and forgive you as hope to be
forgiven"


These were his last words. When Hether-
ington had got nearly through speaking,
Brace said, turning to his companion:


"Dry up, old fellow; you have talked
enough, don't keep me here any longer.
Damn it, dry up"


He died with an oath on his tongue


The bell of the Committee rooms toled
when Brace and Hetherington were launched
into eternity. Neither suffered much. Brace
scarcely moved. Hetherington moved but
once.


The bodies hung thirty-fve minutes, and
we're taken down by Coroner Kent.

uENTLEMEN-Since the organlzation of the vigilance Committee, the tyranny under which we are now living, something has transpred to prevent my writing to you, either absence from the cisy, or TOT other reasons equally good But do not thlnk, in justice to the cause of which am put humble advocate that I should de-

 lay longer Tn laying before you full state-

 neht or facts which have led to tie present de- PioraDe state of affairs in San Francisco. All .ne demons of the internal regions appear to nave been let loose upon this city of hills. and all the evil passions which can possibly animate the bosom of man, are at work for its destruc ton. Reason is lost sight of, and he who an. PealS to 1t Is regarded as fool or a madman The only law known to them is the bavonet and he who is in favor of 1aw and order, is the greatest criminal in their eyes. will not at- tempt to relate minutely all the circumstances leading to the formation of the Vigilance Com. mlttee, for 1t would be too tedious and too long but will content myself by giving you gene ral view. About SIX months since paper was started in this city called the "Evening Bulle- tln," edited by James King of William, (son of Wm klng) In the flush times of California, Ming was wealthy banker, and entered large iy into specuations, but, like many others, could not withstand the pressure of hard times which soon followed. He "wound up, his business as best he could, and immediately af rewards received the appointment of confiden- tlal clerk in the banking house of Adams & Co.,, on condition of transferring his depositors to that house; knowing as he must, upon the ex- animation of their books, that Adams & Co.,. were lnsovent, and as he afterwards admitted to be the case Upon the failure of Adams & Co., he was again thrown out of employment and made several intellectual attempts to estab. llsh himself ill business As last resort he became editor and proprietor of the "Evenng Bulletin" From the high position of an hon. est, wealthy banker, he had fallen, and had lost the confidence of those, by his connection with Adams & Co.,, who had previously enter talned the highest regard for him. Naturally he felt chagrined when he compared his pre- sent position with the one he formally occupied, and secretly entertained hostility to his former friends. His first efforts were directed against certain rotten firms in this city, all of which every one knew to be true, and applauded him for his boldness. Then series of attacks, of general nature, upon the characters of men above reproach folowed-such men as Judges Thompson and Peachy were included His sheet was so low, and his attacks so general, that no one would notice him; for he made no dlscrlmlhatlon between gentleman and blackguard At last the courts began to inves- tigate the affairs of Adams & Co.,, and the most enormous frauds were exposed. The poor peo- pie lost their all by this firm. King threw of the secrecy which hung around him as conf- dential clerk, and seized this opportunity to ingratiate himself in the affections of the people at the expense of the reputation of those of the firm who had saved him from starvation. and who had taken him into their confidence. This succeeded, and James King of William sud

 denly became an important man in the com munlty. Here was chance for him to wreak his vengeance upon those whom he secretly hated and envied, and who had always been his best friends. He attacked the characters of such men as Thompson, Volney E. Howard, $. w. Leigh, son of the distinguished Virgin ian, and others of reputations equally pure, without regard to the truth. He did not and would not hold himself personally responsible to them, and there were many reasons why they would not make a street fight with him, and which were regarded as sufficient by their friends, and which the sequel proved to be well founded. Indeed, he was much severer upon gentlemen than upon tho black guards It was well understood that he had forfeited his life, and that he would have been shot long before in any other country. It was a fixed fact, and Wa; only a question of time, and his tune had come when he preferred charges against Casey, (though what he said about hm was true.) Casey had warned him against using his name in his paper, and King felt se- cure in any thing he might do. But whatever might have been the aggravating circumstances in the shooting of King by Casey, it did not warrant body of citizens in forming them selves into Vigilance Committee, employing about two thousand foreigners, with about four thousand natives armng themselves with mus kets, and marching on a Sunday to the jal, forcing its surrender, and overpower;ng the officers of the law. Not only did they take Casey but they took Cora, who shot Richard son, and who had been tried by jury of twelve men chosen from among themselves, and who could not agree upon verdict. These men were hanged without any trial, and without any defence being allowed them. It was supposed that they would stop here; but, alas for human hopes. Men who thus acquire power are not so willing to yield it up; and they have gone on from step to step, until they now have Judge of the Supreme Court incarcerated in their dungeons, whose fate will either be death or punishment. Men have been sent away from the country in irons without any cause shown, and still there is no sign of their disbalding.

 The Governor, who Is poor, weak man, at first thought 1t best to treat with them, and yield to their mad excitement. Finally he was aroused to the alarming state of affairs, but too late, as the result showed. He called upon them to dsband, and upon their refusal issued his proclamation, declaring this county in a state of instruction, and called upon the mili- tia to enroll themselves. General Wool prom iSed him arms, and the work of enrolment went on bravely. But the hopes of those who were in favor of maintaining the laws and the constitution of the State, at the point of the bayonct, were doomed to disappointment by General Wool discovering at this period he had no authority to furnish the State with arms, perhaps because he General Mough tue laao party was in tue minority. Though the Governor was here checked, he still hoped, with the means the State had at its disposal, to check the progress of this inqusition. In attempting to concentrate the arms of the State at this point, they were seized by the Vigilance Con- mittee while in transit on the bay of San Fran cisco. The man in charge of them escaped and hastened to San Francisco to make re- port of what had happened to the proper au- thorities, and in the presence of Judge Terry who was here at the time. While giving an account of himself, the Vigilance Committee sent party of men to arrest him, which they attempted to do in his Che Judge's) presence and the presence of the other authorities. The Judge remonstrated as peace officer and suc- ceeded at the time in preventing them. While repairing to place of greater safety with the man, whose arrest was contemplated by the Committee of Vigilance, they were again ac- costed by the same party of men greatly rein forced. After repeated remonstrances, and find ing his own life in great danger, (for several pistols were drawn upon him. he stabbed man by the name of Hopkins, the leader, in the neck, and by the greatest exertions succeeded in reaching one of the State armories Imme- diately the Vigilance Committee sounded the alarm, and in a short time surrounded the building with seven thousand bayonets and several pieces of artillery. Terry had only fifteen men with him, and consequently had to surrender to the executive committee of the Committee of Vigilance. Had Hopkins died Terry would have been hanged beyond ques- tion, but as he is now out of danger there is no telling what disposition they will make of the r. ,,th ci, q o4x,

NORTH SAN JUAN. Sent. 17th
article:
II. d.


A a. Sargent and T. B. Mcfarland.


North SAN JUAN, Sept. 18th.


EDITOR JOURNAL The largest and
most enthusiastic meeting ever before
convened in this county hasjust adjourn
ed. Over one thousand of the "bone
and sinew" of the country were in at
tendance. Speeches were delivered by
Gov. Foote, A. B. Dibble, Esq, A. A.
Sargent and I. B. Mcfarland.


For two hours and a half G ov. Foote
occupied the stand in defense of our
glorious standard bearer, Millard Fill
more. He handled the administration
of Franklin Pierce without gloves, and
exposed in an eloquent and mastery
mannerits short comings and corruptions,
its violated pledges, broken promises and
anti Republican tendencies. With with
ering sarcasm and cutting irony he por-
trayed the present position of poor "ten
cent Jimmy Buchanan" and the party
who now support him rthe Presidency.
Never since our country has had page
in history did any man receive such a
castigation from a stump orator as did
poor "Dimocratic Jecms Buchanan" at
the hands of Gov. Foote, and never, in
all my life, did l witness such enthu-
siasm at public meeting as was mani
tested during the speech of Gov. Foote


1t is impossible at this late hour of the
night to give you anything like an ade-
quate account of the meeting or asynop-
sis of the speech delivered by Gov.
Foote. Suffice it to say, it was one of
his most happy efforts, in which he did
good service to the cause in which he is
engaged.


Gov. Foote, on retiring from the stand,
was greeted with six loud, long and
hearty cheers by the immense multitude
that surrounded him. So enthusiastic
were some of our good Fillmore men,
and SO we'll satisfied were they with the
Governors speech, that when he step
ped back to leave the stand, they caught
him up in their arms and carried him to
his apartment, amidst the cheers of the
vast crowd who had listened to his elo-
quent remarks.


A. B. Dibble, Esq, our eloquent can
didate for Congress, being called for,
came forward, and for nearly an hour
discoursed eloquently upon the affairs
of State; he gave lucid history of the
present state of our country; spoke Of
the Kansas-Nebraska agitation, its
causes, and results if either Buchanan
or Frement are elected to the Presiden-
tial chair. Announced himself as a
warm advocate of the Pacific Railroad,
and in favor of putting an end at once
and forever to that great question which
now agitates and divides our common
country, slavery. His speech was an
eloquent one, and was listened to by his
large audience with great attention and
enthusiasm.


Mr.. Dibble was followed by Mr.. A. A.
Sargent, our very popular candidate for
State Senator He diseoursed entirely
on the affairs of State, and most nobly
did he acquit himself. He spoke of the
Vigilance Committee of San Francisco,
and of the effort of the Buchanan party
to force that subject into the canvass ;
of the failure of his Democratic opponent
to make known his views upon that
question; proclaimed himself warm
and ardent supporter Of the Vigilance
Committee and their cause spoke Of

Vigilance Commi ttee.


The Executive portion of Vigilance CON-
mittee have issued an address to the gen.
eral Committee on the occasion of their
suspension of business. 1t is 'a
diarrhea of words and q constipation of
IDEAS" chiefly devoted to the laudation of
the Committee, extolling the purity and dis
interestness of their acts, and assuring the
public of what the Committee might have
done had they been disposed. We have not
the least doubt but that the public duly ap-
preciate the position of the Committee, and
have a very general understanding of their
acts, if not of the motives which prompted
them thereto. We doubt not the public
duly appreciate the cowardly prudence
which which prompts the Committee to re-
tain the arms which belong to the State,
while our citizens are being murdered by
savages and plundered by organized bands
of robbers. We doubt not the public duly
appreciate the act of the Committee in plum
deriny the State of arms furnished by the
General Government, and selling them to
their hirling soldiery at "a apiece. Why
should the Committee attempt to deny their
interference in political matters,w when their
prominent member. figured at the different
resignation meetings held in San Fran
cisco. and when their minors marched off
to the Vigilance rooms, as prisoners those
who yentured to vote against requesting the
officers to resign Why talk about the
generosity and .manliness of the Committee,
when they manacled and marched through
the streets of San Francisco men whose only
offence was that of obeying the call OF the
authorities, and volunteering to sustain the
laws and constitution of their country /?
Why talk about the purity of the ballot box
armed and self constituted body of men !:
Let the Committee retain the arms belong
ing to the State for the protection of their
own worthless carcasses, and thus aid the
organized bands of Williams to plunder the
miners in the mountains, and the Sayages
to murder defencless families, and then in
suit their victims by publishing to the world
that NO one opposes them but politicians,
and men who have no permanent interest
in the country.


The Committee having adjourned will

ment of the Executive Committee, occasion

ent that the laws, are insufficient for the
protection of the citizen or punishment OF

ty of the ballot box or the sanctity Of the
elective franchise.


Let this committee continue their organi-
zation, if they think there is no limit to hu-

iniquities much longer than the Committee

shelter amongst the beasts of the field.

article:
DrsBANDrSG OF THE VIGILANCE COMMITTEE
This body was to have had grand parade on
Monday last, and some of their organs have
announced that they will disband to-day. The
Alta, however, denies the report that they are
to disband, and says they are only going togive
up some of their rooms, and dismiss the most OF
their guards; that rooms only will be retained
for the executive committee to hold their ses-
sions, and that the general committee will be
called together whenever occasion may require.
The probability is, that those who have been
furnishing funds to keep up this organization
are finding it rather expensive, and by giving
up the most of their rooms and dsmissing their
guards they are in hopes of getting clear OF
the heavy outlays to which they have heretofore
been subjected. 1t is the wish of great por-
tion of the Vigilance Committee to keep up the
organization until after the November election,
in order to affect the result and as much as pos
sible get their sympathzers elected to Office
Others, however, are now, and for long time
have been, in favor of disbanding Which par
ty among them will carry the day remains to
be seen. One thing is certain, that no reliance
can be placed in the report that they intend to
disband to-day.


The vigilance organs are publishing pretend
ed letters from Washington, to the effect that
the President has no authority for putting
down the insurrection, unless he is requested so
to do by the Legislature of the State There
appears to be no authority for these statements.
The requsition of the Governor had been re-
ceived by the President only day or two be-
fore the sailing Of the steamer and the agents
sent to Washington by him had not even arrived
there The statement which has also been put
forth, that Secretary Marcy had written to the
Governor, to the effect that the general govern
ment cannot interfere to quell this insurrecton
appears to be equally without foundation
There is every reason to believe, if the vigilance
committee does not voluntarily disband before
the arrival of the next steamer, that the govern
ment officers here will have orders to put them
down.

THE SAN FRANCISCO REVOLUTION
article:
COMMITTEE TRIUMPHANT.


The cause of the excitement and move
ments which will be found detailed below.
was an attempted assassination of Mr.. Ster-
ling A. Hopkins, a member of the Police
Department of the Vigilance Committee, by
ID. 5 Terry one Of the Judges of the Su-
preme Court.


The particulars of the assault, which we
gather from an eyewitness and are conse-
quently reliable, are as follows


An order was issued yesterday for the
arrest of one James II. Maloncy, better
known as Rube Maloney, and we'll known
as notorious political trickster which was
placed in the hands of Mr. Hopkins, with
instructions to take him into custody.


About three o'clock in the afternoon Mr.
Hopkins went into the naval Office of DIR.
Ashe, where were the Dr., Maloney, IL.
Bowie and several others Mr. Hopkins
said he desired to see Alaloney DR.. Ashe
told him that that was the naval Office, and
he had no business there at the same time
Terry drew a knife and would have used it
upon Hopkins had not DR. Ashe interiered.
Hopkins then left and joined his companions.
and the other parties at once armed them
selves with double-barrclled guns and went
into the street to defend Maloney. Tho
two parties, consisting Of DR. Ashe, IL.
Bowe, j. r. Maloncy, ID. s. Terry and
Martin Reese on one side, and S. A. Hop
kinS, j. S. Bovco and three Others of the
Committee on the other side, again met in
Jackson str't between Dupont and kearny.
Mr. Hopkins approached Terry and sainted
him in q gentlemanly manner, when he
turned upon him with his muSkct, which
Hopkins seized to prevent him from using,
and succeeded in wrestling it from him.
Terry then drew his knife and stabbed
Hopkins in the neck At the same time
Dr. Ashe also placed the muzzlc of his mus
ket to me breast Of Mr. Bovce, but before
firing asked him if he was friend to which
Bovee replied that he was, but at the same
instant forcing the weapon from him, and
drawing his pistol he placed the muzze at
the head of the DIR. and commanded him to
surrender his arms, which he did instantly.
During the melee one or two shots were
fired accidentally or otherwise, neither of
which took effect.


As soon as the fatal blow was struck the
five law and order men fled to their armory,
at the corner of jackson and Dupont streets,
and were attended by several of the law
and order party, who rushed in to protect
them. Several of the Vigilant boys were
in tho vicinity, and they at once locked
the iron doors of the entrance to the build
ing, thus preventing any Of the opposition
from entering the building, and tho entire
block upon which it stands was ut once sur
rounded by the Committee to prevent his
escape.


No sooner was the dastardly blow struck
than swift courier conveyed the inteli-
gence to the Committee rooms, and The
alarm bell was sounded for the first timo.--
Thousands at once obcycd the summons, and
enthusiasm prevailed throughout the city
People were hurrying in every direction aud
many were not aware of the cause of tho
alarm and besought the swift pOsscrs-by for
an explanation. The announcement in bro
ken sentences that Terry had stabbed Com
mittee man, was all that could be gathered
before they were beyond hearing The real
facts were soon obtained, and crowds began
to gather in the vicinity of the Committee
rooms and the armory where Terry was Sc
creted


In less than fifteen minutes after the first
stroke of the bell, the Committee had de-
tailed armed mon and completely surrounded
the four buildings where The law and order
party were supposed to have arms deposited.
This sudden and wel-timed movement took
the opposition by surprise and prevented
them from getting into their armory, except
o few squads who entered or we're in before
the guards arrived Every Committee man
seemed to be on duty, and each wore q white
ribbon in the left lapel of his coat which we
suppose was done to designate the members


Several draymen on Front street were
loading up goods to be shipped by the up
river boats, and on the alarm being given
they stripped off their harness, leaving their
drays half loaded, mounted their places in
the ranks of the cavalry. The streets in
every direction glistencd with bright bayo-
nets or flying horsemen, who were hurrying
to the scene of action The streets and
buildings in the vicinity Of the armorics and
the Plaza were literally alive with human
beings such was the feeling that peryaded
all classes.


The Committee having taken the precau-
ton to guard all the armories, the Law and
Order men were rendered powerless. There
was not enough of them inside to force their
way out and contend with their capturcrs.
Meanwhile active preparations were going
on for the rescue of the men Terry and Ma
loney. A large proportion of the forces
were concentrated at thc principal armory,
at the corner Of Jackson and Dupont streets,

is on the second floor In about thirty
minutes after the alarm the military had
possession and control of the entire grounds
about that corner, and armed men were
stationed upon the roof of the Building, and
every approach was securely guarded so as
to prevent any possibility of escape Scarce

article:
of the late Sheriff, the all-absorbing
Iquestion seemed for time to lie, y he
shall be Sheriff? Mr.. John Grimes
claimed the Office as Coroner of the
county. The Board of Supervisors met
on Monday, and in accordance with
their duties, appointed Wm. Butterfeld,
Esq, to serve the remainder of the term
of w. w. Wright, as Sheriff of the
county. In the evening of the same
day on which tue appointment was
made, Grimes, in company with Frank
Dunn, Marshal Plumer, Ben Conyers,
and Mulcaha, entered the room occupied
by the deputies of the late Sheriff and
the District Attorney, and took by force
therefrom property belonging to the
county. They were resisted by G. F.
Wood, Under Sheriff. and Sargent, Dis
trict Attorney. but without success
We understand the property has since
been surrendered into the hands of the
appointee of the Supervisors, and that
no farther interruption in the affairs of
the Office will be attempted.


The Democrat, with barefacedness
worthy of it, says the appointment of
Mr.. Butterfeld "has given much dissat-
isfaction, as it was thought the condi-
ton in which the office has been left, re-
quired such change in the control of it
as to secure the interests of the county
as well as litigants having monies in the
hands of the Sheriff"


To secure the interests of the county
and of private individuals, it became
necessary that John Grimes should take
forcible possession of the Sheriff's desk,
&c! Now, John Grimes is personally
interested, perhaps, in the security of
the interests of the county, like any
other good citizen, and no further. He
is invested with the same right to guard
public and private interests as we are,
but has no real or legal right beyond us.
He is under not even the trihing bonds
required by law to be given by the
Coroner, much less the forty-fve thou
sand dollar bond the Sheriff He had
not taken an oath to discharge the du-
ties of the Office of Sheriff at the time
the forcible entry was made; and had
he been duly qualified in every respect,
still an order from the County Judge or
Board of Supervisors was requisite to
obtain the Sheriff's papers from the
deputies having them in charge and
sworn to perform duties, which the
Coroner elect was under no obligation
pecuniarily or otherwise to discharge
1t seems the Coronor's posse were self
constituted Vigilance Committee, to
guard public and private interests, which
were in the most imminent danger, not
withstanding the heavy securities of the
late Sheriff and the oaths of deputies
who have heretofore been intrusted with
the affairs of the office, and against
whose integrity nothing has been
breathed. The Coronor's posse doubt
less consider themselves more honest
and responsible without bonds or obli-
cations than other men. Each is a
watchful Cerberus. standing self-respon-
sible, to guard the interests of individuals
and the public. This is an assumption
of superior virtue which, it is to be
hoped, their future conduct will warrant.

at is also stated, with what truth we are

mittee, were desirous of leaving on the last

not of course vouch for the truth of the ru-

A GREAT SMoKE.-A great deal of smoke
and gas has been created, and large guam
tity of ink has been shed, with regard to
misunderstanding between Gov. johnson,
Col. Zabriskie, and Gen. Allen. 1t appears
from the Governors statement of the facts,
that he authorized the two latter gentlemen
to 20 to San Francisco and ascertain if pos
sible, the objects of the Vigilance Committee.
Messrs Allen and Zatriskie claim that they
had full power from the Governor to effect
compromise between the Vigilance Commit
tee and the State authorities. We believe
this is the point of difference between the
parties, and it certainly appears to us that
the Governor has decidedly the advantage
in the reasonableness of his position, and
such. we doubt not, is the opinion of every
unpreiudiced man in the State. 1t seems
to US impossible that the Governor should
have conferred the power claimed by the
gentlemen composing the committee. upon
them, when it is well known that both Col.
Zabriske and Gen. Allen, sympathized with
and supported the action of the Vigilance

ed by an unfortunate misunderstanding be-
tween them The official acts of Governor
johnson have been characterized by can.
dor and fair dealing that entities his position
to great weight in community, and all the
''astonishment'' that may be expressed by
the self constituted committee, will not
change the verdict Of an impartial public
The mildest form of that verdict will be
that the Committee misunderstood the power
conferred upon them by the Governor.

THE OVERLAND TRAvEL--Through
the enterprise of our frontier population Of
the Western States, who are now pouring
into California by the Big Tree and other
routes, our wealth is increasing. Slowly,
but surely, does our growth mature as train
after train of hardy emigrants arrive at this
haven of their rest, bringing with them
their wives and little ones, their Aocks
and their herds, from far off land to en-
JOY the pure air and continual sunshine of
our heaven-blessed land. Every train
brings thousands of dollars worth of De.
vonshire and Durham improved cattle
their horses are the strongest and feetest
to be found in the Western Prairies, and
are brought here with view of improv-
ing the mustang stock of this State One
train of such emigration, is worth whole
steamship load, of kid-gloved ballot-box
suffers and sweet-scented office-seekers, by
the ocean route. The blessings of emigra-
tion come over-land-the curses, that en-
tailed the formation of Vigilance Com
mittee, { the only plan by which murder
and ballot-box stuffing could be Justly
punished, come by the ocean routes. By
sea came the prostitute, the female charla-
tan, and their men, who are now scattered
broadcast over our fair land renegades
from the just vengeance of an outraged
people, or the edicts of the Vigilance Com
mittee. In our highways and by-ways
is presented the brazen efrontery of the
broken-down gambler, glaring with demon
eyes on the unsuspecting traveller, as ''stand
and deliver" is called out; yet that same
out-lawed rufian, was once gentleman
enaigrant,-by the steamer.


How different class are these honest
overland emigrants Their coarse, heavy
shoes and home-spun clothes seems to in
dicate want, or privation. But not SO, al
though coarsely they are comfortably clad.
We look upon these arrivals, as the har-
binger of better day for California
Those girls, have, two-thirds of the dis
tance for two thousand miles, footed it
into this State, yet they are our cherished
hope! their pride and destiny is to fulfill
a natural obligation,-to be the wives of
honest miners, farmers and mechanics;
and the mothers of noble, god-like men;
their daughters,-good well-behaved hon
est-hearted country girls,-the brightest
gem of the social circle, and Keystone of a
happy and prosperous home.

article:
MEssRs. EDIroRs:- Yesterday, being the
anniversary of the admission of California
into the Union, our city presented an unu-
sualy gay and animated appearance. The
| weather was all that could be desired; the
procession numbered about six hundred, Of
which, the Fire Department was the largest
portion. Pominent in the ranks of the De-
partment were the Monumental who
turned out some seventy men and who were
the feature of the possession.


To-day the trial of Durkee and Rand
for piracy commences in the L, S. Circuit
Court; considerable feeling has been mani
tested for some days concerning this trial and
there has been some danger of rescue by
the higher law men. Happily, wiser counsels
have prevailed and the trial will go on with
out interruption. This is as it should be-
collision between the Vigilance Committee
and the United States would be deplorable
and would compcate almost beyond remedy
the unhappy differences as yet confined to
San Francisco. 1t is to be hoped that peace
and harmony will be fully restored before the
election, for should this not be the case, the
vote of San Francisco county will be thrown
out of the canvass, being illegal while in a
state of insurrection. This, of course, is not
desirable to either party. Let us hope that
we shall get through This difficulty with safety
and taking warning 10y the past, never again
put ourselves in the same position.


We are looking with great anexiety to the
action of the Convention now in session at
Sacramento With good nominations and
with strong national ground to stand, upon
we shall go into the contest with vigor and
out of it with victory. TRUST that Amador
will be found on the side of the Union at the
coming election That she will be is pretty
certain, Judging from the immense meeting
held at jackson on the ID Yet every vote
will be wanted to carry the county and each
individual Democrat should constitute him
self committee of one to assist and perfect
the organization of the party throughout the
county. The Know Nothings here are count
ing largely on Amador for Fillmore, but |
trust that November will falsify their expec-
tations. If the Know Nothings were honest
in their principles they would drop their own
candidate and go over to Buchanan as the
only sure way to put down Black Republi-
cans. Sectionalism is now the real and only
issue before the country.

In another column will be found the Con
stitution of the Vigilance Committee. We
ask for it careful perusal.

By an arrival at New Orleans we have two weeks
later Dews from California. The Vigilance Com
mittee have executed two persons for MURDER and
still keep Judge Terry in prison. Their power
seems to be as firm as ever.

GENrLEMEN.--I have observed an arti-

ESQ, and the terms of that article call Tor
my reply. 1t is true that the heinous crime
seems to have been committed somewhere,
for it is publicly confessed by those who ap-
pear to speak by authority, but you may
be in error when you hasten TO the conclu-
sion that the crime was committed In this
city, and at my office. However, am quite
willing, and even anxious that the facts shall
be brought out, whether they implcate this
Office or any other.


The very day on which the matter was
first made public, proceeded to investigate
it, and the only success have yet met with
is simply in having traced it through two
or three informants upto the Executive
Committee of the Vigilance Committee, who
am told, were furnished copy of said in
tercepted letter. Whether that body will
dvulge the name of the criminal party, re-
mains to be ascertained.


Besides being one of the highest criminal
offences, this matter is also calculated to en-
gender suspicion against this office, and cre-
ate wide distrust of the whole mail system,
and therefore feel it my duty, to leave
nothing undone which may tend to the de-
lection of the criminal in this case The U.
S. Statute provides


"That if any person shall take any letter
or packet, not containing any article of val
ue or evidence thereof, out of Post Office,
or shall open any letter or packet, which
shall have been in Post Office, or in custc-
dy of mail carrier, before it shall have
been delivered to the person to whom it is
directed, with design to obstruct the cor
respondence. TO PRY INTO ANOTlIERS
BUSINESS OR SECRETS, such Of
fender, upon conviction, shall pay. for every
such offence, a sum not exceeding five hun
dred dollars, and be imprisoned not exceed
ing twelve months"


Finding the U. S. Statute making this so
grave and serious matter, and myself deep
ly feeling the Importance of enforcing that
statute. now announce that will pay to
the party or parties who shall secure the
conviction of the criminal in the case of the
intercepted letter herein spoken Of, one hun
dred dollars.


Very respectfully


Your Obedient servant,


c. l. WELLER,


Post Master.

Affairs at San Francisco.
article:
The excitement at San Francisco has not in the
least abated but the plot seems daily to thcken.-
What the end will be- no one can tell, nor make an
intelligent guess thereat The results thus far have
disprovcd all predictions and time alone, and the
final consummaton, will show the result of the pres
ent revolution at the Bay. 1t is deporable state
of affairs, that necessity should exist for governing
q city-the most important on the Pacific and among
the most important in the Unon-by power warm
ed into life by an uprising against the representatives
of the law, saying nothing about the means by which
they became such. The people of San Francisco
as body, the very best of its people-compose the
present power and they asseverate that the necessity
for the movement existed We will not undertake
up-countIy and interior as (thank Cod we are, to
contradict them, in the matter of the existence or
noneXstence of such necessity We know that there
was much corruption in the Bay City, and particular
ly among the city officials it is probable that the
executors of the law held their places to great ex-
tent at the pleasure of the habitua trespassers on
its provisions. Had it been otherwise we should
long ago have raised our feeble voice against the
course pursued by the organization now in power.


The Committee rose, a giant full-grown, without
or tending, and did its greatest work for its
first. Its apparent might awed the State Executive
and he constrained to become mere locker on
in Vienna powerless as the rest He did as re have
all aong-looked on, seeing that desirable end was
being attained and hoping that the excited populace
would see the dangerous precedent their course would
be in after times, and disband. The excitement
luLed and he interposed proclamation, calling upon
members of the Committee to dissolve the organza-
ton and go about their accustomed pursuits. He
also called upon law abiding citizens to enroll them
selves under his subordinates subject to his orders
and in favor of restoring tranquility to the State-
The proclamation asked nothing that might not have
been consistently complied with by the Chief Ex-
ecutive of the Vigilance Committee. He called for


quiet return to the civil stations of life, by those
who had for the time taken upon themselves re-
dress of grievances against the public The first
great purpose of the organization had been achieved
and the excitement had died. Those within and
without the halls of the Committee, who were in
favor of speedy return to the beaten path of repub
lican government, might all consistently have enrolled
themselves under the Governors call. We said at
the time, that we thought the Governor was right
We have never unsaid it,


We have not, however, at any time thought that
the Governor should make an actual armed onslaught
upon the city. High-handed and defiant as the acts
of the Vigilance Committee may appear to ga man
up tree" or in the highest civil position in the
State we say what we know to be the popular sent-
ment in the mines that no blood should be shed on
account of any act yet committed by the Vigilants
DIT = Al.
howlng-for the howlers are not the bone and sinew
of the land-but strong undercurrent is gaining
force in the public mind, and the current runneth
thus: 1.-The Vigiants must resign soon" !" If they
do not resign, and the Federal Government take any
part in the premises, not a man. nor a cent nor a
word of encouragement will ever pass from the noun
tains to our fellow-citizens at San Francisco.


Our city friends may deprecate this plain talk but
we speak from the book-our words are dictated by
careful and extensive observations among our noun
tain people, and spoken for the benefit of those
to whom they are addressed. The residents of this
part OF the State would rise almost as one man,
against movement hereafter towards making men,
oerS OF the Vigilance Committee Individually answer
able for the acts of the organization thus ar-but
they say that the Vigiants should at once break up
and let their brief career be terror to evildoers-
and not set an example of anarchy for those who are
to come after them.


We have heretofore said very little on this subject
considering the whole movement in the direction of
local reform, and that the end justified somewhat
extraordinary means. Hamlet's language expresses
our general view of the matter


nt oaled iade vnce our
Owing to somewhat apathetic temperament, the
abundance of ice, and the high price of whisky, we
have felt very little fire in our veins-but we hope
the end is nigh, and that no portion of our commu-
nifty may ever see propriety in citing the late up
rising in San Francisco as precedent on which to
build similar organizations hereafter.

Mr.. Editor:-We have long observed the

1t is needless to say that nine-tenths OF

the Vigilance Committee at the risk Of all
dear to them in life. The Vigilance Com
mittee must triumph--for they are the peo-
pie and their cause is a just one.


The public press have solemn duty to
perform at this iuncture of time--for after
all, to a great extent, they are the common
directors Of the great public mind. Hip.
hip. hurrah. for the Vigilance Committee

disement. FIRMLY gentemanly, and up
above board from the commencement have

terest.

alert for the latest news from San Francisco,

tellow-citizens the popular heart has beat but

eye on them.


Judge Shattuck's discourse to the people

munity. His motives in throwing oil Of
peace upon the troubled waters Of this com
monweaIth may be accepted for what it is

Judge Terry must be treated as any other

plary punishment. He was no more the

righteous iudg dge-sding with desperadoes and

rights Oh! Judge Terry, hadst thou lived

If Hopkins die, Terry must also die
Blood for blood is the past word here, until
the entire State is purged Of the scoundreIs
who have long usurped our dearest rights
Let the scales Of justice, Notwithstanding the
much and foul wrong done US as a people,
be equally balanced no matter who the
offender may be-


We repose our entire confidence iii the

article:
DEAR BROTHER WATSON: For fear you or some ofyour friends might con clude this to be the year to come to Texas, 1 will give you short state ment about the crops.

 1 have travelled through several counties recently, namely; Falls, Bell, Travis, Milan, Roberson, 4imestone and Freestone. There are several counties north of me and from me to the Louisiana line, in which corn can not be purchased for less than two dollars per bushel, and in great ma ny places, corn cannot be had at any price. Pork will be very high, but we are blessed here with as good beef as the world can afford and this is a very good substitute for pork. Wheat Is worth two dollars bushel.

 It is ofno use to mention the cause of the hard times here, as it is under stood that this country is seldom bless ed with rain enough to make good crops.

 Our country has been thrown into excitement in consequence of the burning of several towns and resi- dences. After examination it was found that Abolitionists had placed in the hands of the negroes great quan- tity of poisonous medicines and had the plan laid for an insurrection which was to have come off on the fourth of August.

 The plan was to poison all the melons to be taken to the Election, on the night before, and on the Election day, to burn all the houses and gran cries; kill all the women and children; then make wives of the young wom- en; then kill all the men as fast as they returned from the Election! But greatly to their disappointment, sev- eral white men have been convicted and hung! also, several negroes, and there is no telling how many more will be convicted. As the work goes on, the more there is found out. Two or three of those hung, were Metho- dist ministers: two more were me chanics from the north.

 The towns burnt are Dallas, Hen derson and Nachodoches. Those fired but extinguished are Tylor, Mar lin and Palestine. There is n Vigi- lance Committee in every county that looks into every hidden mystery and keeps the county well patroled.

 Your interesting paper comes to hand regularly.

 Yours Truly,

 J. j.. BOWDON.

 Springfield, Teras,

At meeting of the citizens of Red Fork township, Desha county, Arkansas, held in the village of Red Fork, on Saturday, January 2oth. 1S60-Upon motion, Col. D. T. Johnson was called to the chair, and l.. A. Sullivan requested to act as Secre- tary. The chairman in few appropriate, we'll timed and eloquent remarks, explained the object of the meeting to be for the pur- pose of appointing a vigilance committee to protect ourselves against the inroads of abolition emissaries. After which. mon motion, a committee of three. consistind of Dr. R. $. Parish, Calvin Stroud, and Hadley Malpass, were appointed to draft series ot resolutions, expressive of the sense ot the meeting; who, after retiring a few moments, returned and reported the following, which were unanimously adopt- ed:

 Believing that elf-protection is one of our first inherent rights, therefore, we the citi- zens of Red Fork township, Desha county, and State of Arkansas, do

 Resotpe, lsf, Considering the unsettled state of our country under the repeated northern aggressions upon southern rights, we have determined for selG-orotection, and the protection of our fellow citizens, to form vigilance committee consisting of twenty gentlemen.

 Resolped, 2nd, It shall be the duty of said vigilance committee, to arrest and ex- anime all suspicious persons in our com munty, either residing amongst us or pass ing through our neighborhood.

 Resotced, 3rd, That said vigilance com mittee shall deal with such characters as will in their judgment insure our security, and rid us of such nuisances.

 Resolped, 4M, That we pledge ourselves to stand by our vigilance committe with our persons and property, in all things they may do in furtherance of this object and under these resolutions, which they may regard as our instructions to them

EDITORS HYDRAULIC PREss.-Our town, on
last Friday night, was thrown into state of ex-
citemeflt by shooting affair which took place at
the residence of Mr.. Eder, and resulted in the
death of one man and the wounding of three
others, one of whom was q lady, the wife of Mr.
Eder. The facts of the case are as follows:


Some time ago Eder rented house to family
named Devins When the rent became DUE he
demanded it. Deyins said he was unable to pay.
The rent was afterwards repeatedly called for,
but not paid. Finally Eder ordered the family
to vacate the premises, which they refused to do.
Yesterday afternoon, Eder and another person
armed themselves, and proceeding to the house,
threatened forcibly to eject the occupants. A
difficulty ensued, which was likely to be settled
by the use of deadly weapons. However, the
entreaties of Devins wife prevented it. and Eder
and his companion left the spot. After dark,
Devins and five others, went, in spirit of retail
iation, to Elders house, and made assault
upon his family. At the time, there were in the
house Mr.. Eder, his lady and child, and man
whose name | have not learned. The parties
commenced firing, and some twelve shots in all
were exchanged. Eder was wounded in the leg.
His lady received severe wound in her thigh,
breaking the bone. The man stopping in the
family, was shot in the arm, and had the bone
fractured. One of the assauting party was
mortally wounded, the bullet entering his fore
head and lodging in the brain. His name was
Hughes. He died this morning. Immediately
after the fray, the other five assailants left and
have not since been heard from. Efforts are
being made for their arrest. Had they been
caught last night, the probabilities are, that they
would now be enjoying the society of their ruff
fanly companion, in a world not quite so bright
and beautiful as this. The formation of vigi-
lance committee has been much talked of; but
the movement encounters too much opposition
to be successful.


TWE should be pleased to hear often from
our Virginia City correspondent.

article:
The death of A. c. Forb. Esq Of
Denver City. Kansas, at the hands of a
Vigilance Committee has already been
announced. but the following particulars
of the tragedy. which correspondent of
the St. Louis Republican, writing from
Leavenworth city, under date of Octo-
Der 4th. furnishes that journal. will be
read with interest:


The death of A. c. Ford, lawyer OF


Denver city, at the hands of the Secret
Vigilance Committee, is generally
known, but the manner and circumstan-
ces have not before been made public,
owing to the secrecy in which his exc
cutioners saw fit to vail their doings
The following account from reliable au-
thority, and is no doubt, true:


Ford. at the time of his death. was a
passenger in the express coach, on his
way TO this place, either to assist in de-
Tending young Gordon or to appear as
a witness for the defence When six
miles from Denver, the coach was stop
ped by number Of men in disguise,
and Ford, was ordered to yet out He
complied, and the coach drove on. AZ
ter il was out OF sight his captors told
him their purpose, and started with him
away from the road toward the bank
the river.


Ford resisted them and showed fight;
when the leader ordered his men TO pre-
sent guns, and in u moment several fire
arms were bearing point-blank upon his
body when he concluded to submit and
proceed They carried him few miles
to the bank of The river, when he was
told to prepare to be shot. Ford, see
ing they were in earnest, requested one
of them to attend 10 some directions
conc erning the dlsoostion Of his proper
ity; and also 10 take his watch and
leave it in the hands of certain person
tin Denver. The reply to these requests
was that they would attend to no busin-
ess for him. That they would leave
his body with everything upon it, but
would pin n paper to his clothing con-
taining any directions he might wish to
leave. In a few minutes after this con-
versotion he as shot, and the party
mounting their horses, disappeared in
the direction Of Denver. When Ford
was found, his watch was untouched
and upon his coat was pinned slip Of
paper with the words Executed by the
Vigilance Commiuee. His body was
perforated by six buck-shot and one
bullet. The Vigilance Committee had
indubitable evidence that he was con-
nected with the large band OF horse
thieves and murderers who infested the
country. He hailed from Council Bluffs,
Iowa, where he had considerable prop
erty' In that place he bore very fair
character lie is buried on the left
bank Of the Platte ah~ ut six and half
miles below Denver. His grave is
known to but few, and the grass of an
other season will obIiterate all traces Of
recognition which that few may possess
the sod being carefully cut and repla
ccd over his last resting place.

EDITOR DEMoCDAT After the regular De-
mocracy of Oroyille had held their ratifca-

secession, disunon faction resolved to do
something handsome and throw everything
in the shade, and get the good peonle of
Butte county to commit themselves in favor

dingly, dark.lantern meeting was held at

raised for the purpose Of getting up a grand
affair worthy of the occasion. Flaming
handbills were stuck up on every tree and
public house in the county, private letters

was given that the great C) Breckenridge
guns, Zach Montgomery and Kirkpatrick
would appear to enlighten the political hea
thens of Oroville Behold, Saturday came
and with it the Hon. Zach, accompanied by
the editor of the Marysville Express and one
of the proprietors. But oh, my eountrymen,
what fall was there! and partly in the
language of Julius Cesar, "they came, they
saw" and they fszled Evening came, and
with it the g-r-e.a torch light procession,
so much heralded about. And the affair
commenced by thirty nine men ana boys Il

have heard this eloquent gentleman before.
am only glad there were no children pres
ent for he would have frightened them into
fits. After he had concluded, three faint

when some one called for three cheers for
Douglas, which were heartily responded to-


After which, w. II. Rhodes, Esq, the po-

have to say that this gentleman was editor

one can judge of his love of the institutions
OF his country. 1t is really ridiculous to

about half an hour, he wound up by calling

rotoriety, finished there were bet fiftv.one
persons present, not more than one third of
whom were Breckenridge. Thus ended the |
grand Boiling izzle at Oroyille.

regular Democratic nominee.

 The public generally are aware of the recent burning of towns, residences, barns, stables &c., and the poisoning of wells and springs in Texas. The people have rais- ed In their majesty-Vigilance Commit tees have hung white men and negroes ndiscriminalely wherever the evidence of their guilt was fastened upon them. As an inkling of the preconcerted plans of the Aboliionists, we publish the following which has been furnished us by c. w. Johnson, Esq, who has just returned from Texas. The same letter was published in the Austin (Texas) &ate Gazette;

 [Copy.l

 DENTON CREEK, July 3, 1860.

 DEAR SIR "A painful abscess on my right thumb is my apology for not writing at An derson. Our glorious cause is progressing finely. as far South as Brenham there part ed with Bro. Wempler; he went still further south; he will do good wherever he goes. travelled up through the frontier counties, part of the time under fictitious narne found many friends who had been initiated and understand the Mystic Red. I met with a good number of our friends near George town; we held consultation, and were unan- inously of opinion that we should be cautious of our new associates; most of them are des- perate characters, and may betray us, as there are shareholders among them, and value poor negro much higher than a horse The only good they will do us will be destroying towns, mills etc., which is our only hope in Texas at present. If we can break Southern merchants and millers, and have their places filled by honest Republicans, Texas will be an easy prey, if we only do our duty. All wanted for the time being, is control of trade. Trade, assisted by preaching and teaching, will soon control public opinion, Public opinion is mighty, and will prevail. Lincoln will cer- tainly be elected; we will then have the Indian Nation, cost what it will. Squatter sovereign ty will prevail there as it has in Kansas; that accomplished, we have at least one more step to take-but one more struggle to make-that is, free Texas. We will then have connect ed link from the Lakes to the Gulf. Slavery will then be surrounded by land and by water, and soon sting itself to death. I repeat, Texas we must have, and our only chance is to break up the present inhabitants, in whatever way we can, and it must be done. Some of us will most assuredly suffer in accomplishing our ob- iect, but our Heavenly Father will reward us for assisting him in plotting out the greatest curse on earth. It would be impossible for us to do an act that is as biasphemous in the sight of God as holding slaves We must have frequent consultations with our colored friends. Let your meetings be in the night Impress upon their clouded ntellects the bless ings of freedom, induce all to leave you can; our arrangements for their accommodation to go North are better than they have been, but not as good as 1 would like. We need more agents, both local and travelling, 1 will send out travelling agents when get home. You must appoint local agent in every neighbor- hood in your district. I will recommend a few think will do to rely upon, viz: Bros Leaze, Wood, Ives, Evans, Mir. Daniel Vierv Cole, Nugent, Shaw, White, Clifford, Ashley, Drake, Meeks, Shultz and Newman Brother LeaIe, the bearer of this, will take circuit our route, and see as many of our colored friends as he can; he also recommends diff ferent material to be used about town, etc., Our friends sent very inferior article: they emit too much smoke, and do not contain enough camphene, They are calculated to get some of our friends hurt. will send sup ply when l get home. l will have to reproye you and your co-workers for your negligence in sending funds for our agents; but few have been compensated for their trouble. Our faithful correspondent and industrious agent, Bro. Webber, has received but tri1e-not so much as apprentices wages, neither have Bro. Wilet, Mangun and others. You must call upon our colored friends for more money; they must not expect us to do al they cer- tainly will give every cent, if they knew how soon their shackles will be broken. My hand is very painful, and close.

 Yours truly, w. H. BAILEY,

About two weeks ago the body of James Case
beer, man living in the neigbborhood of Area
ia, on the Bay was found dead. 1t was believed
at the time that he had been murdered by the In
dians, which belief was afterwards confirmed by
the voluntary confession of an Indian known as
Jack" who had been arrested on suspicion
He acknowledged that another Indian, "Big
Jack, with whom be was in company at the
time, went to Casebeer's house while be was at
work in the woods, stole bis gun, and creeping
upon him shot Casebeer through the breast, then
covered him up with brush. One Tewksberry had
the first intimation of bis having been killed by
Indians, from a friendly squaw. Both Indians
were arrested and confined 10 The Humboldt Jail,
a rickety concern, on the 9th ult That same
night, after citizens became aware that the mur-
derer of Casebeer (while quietly at work on his
own premises,) had been arrested, summary pun
ishment was resolved on. The old building was
broken open and both Indians taken to eonve
nient tree and hung. In regard TO the execution
the Times says:


"We sincerely deplore such lawless proceed
ings as were enacted in this place. in The popular
execution of the two Diggers Thursday night
To allow self-convicted murderers-Diggers at
that to lie in Jail till March next, awaiting the
slow proceedings of a trial according TO the forms
OF law, was asking great deal from any CON-
munity-more particularly one situated as we are
in regard 10 Indians. Still we regret such deeds
of violence. They have baneful effect on the
morals OF our own people, and are seized upon
by those at a distance, ignorant of our situation
or the circumstances of the case, and repre- sent
ed greatly to our prejudice"


That is sound, worthy reasoning, and as little
as could possibly be said in reference to the af-
fair. For our part, we consider the punishment
an hundred times more justfable than the sum-
mary and wholesale murder of women and chill
dren which took place at the Bay several months
age. In fact we doubt whether there is COM
munity in the State which would not, under sim
liar circumstances, and with like opportunities
of resoue, have done just as the people of Arcata
did The selfaoknowledged murderer, with no
other excuse than hatred of the whites, was in
their midst, and sooner than give him an oppor-
tunity to escape from bis unsafe place OF con-
fnement, they chose to administer the deserved
punishment at once.


We do not uphold such transactions, as a gen.
eral~ thing, but If there is a community in the
State of California that may be justified in such
proceeding, it is the one where this summary ex-
ecutiOn occurred. II is the duty OF men every
where to protect their lives and property, and
and punish the murderer For near ten years
the people of Humboldt county have suffered
suoh grievances as the one above narrated, and
we cannot wonder that forbearance has ceased to
be virtue. The people who did this deed are
not as guilty as the source from which they rea-
sonably believe they should look for and receive
protection The history of that county since its
first settlement, is continuous recital of massa
ere, pilaged homes, desolated farms and Internal
barbarity and waste at the hands of these same
offenders. Even at this late day. though under
the very nose of the power 10 whom it should
look for protection, Humboldt county is not as
well protected as most of the settlements on the
extreme outskirts of civilization That is a truth
which cannot be denied. Last spring the Indians
of the Bay country were gathered up and taken |
to the Klamath reserve, and now the local paper
announces the return of nearly all again. OF
course the Reservation agent is not to blame ;
like escapades from Government Reserves are |
winked at now q, days. The Times has learned |
that on account of the small appropriation made
by Congress for the Indian service on this coast,
the agent is unable to subsst the Indians there
any longer. Nobody will have the temerity to
urge that the people of Humboldt can reasonably
blame Congress or General Government for so
trifing a matter.


Under these circumstances we see only one
course for the Bay people to pursue, that is to
protect themselves. They alone must be the
avengers If their dwellings are burned over their
heads, or their neighb0rs shot down while en-
gagged in their industrial pursuits. A hard row
the people OF that county have had TO hoe, aud
we cannot see that the end is yet

The death of A. G. Ford, a lawyer of Denver
City, at the hands of the Secret Vigilance Com.
mittee, is generally known, but the manner and
circumstances have not before been made public,
owing to the secresy in which his executoners
! saw fit to veil their doings. The following account
is from reliable authority, and is no doubt true:
Ford, at the time of his death, was passenger
in the express coach, on his way to this place,
either to assist in defending young Gordon or
to appear as witness for the defense. When
about six miles from Denver the coach was stopped
by number OF men in disguise, and Ford was
ordered to get out. He complied and the coach
drove on After it was out of sight his captors told
him their purpose, and started with him away from
the road, toward the bank Of the river


Ford resisted them, and showed fight when the
leader ordered his men to present guns, and in a
moment several fire arms were bearing point blank
upon his body, then he concluded to submit and
proceed. They carried him few miles to the
bank of the river, when he was told to prepare to
be shot. Ford, seeing they were in earnest, re-
quested one OF them to attend to some directions
| concerning the disposition of his property; and


also to take his watch and leave it in the hands of


a certain person in Denver. The reply to these re-


quests was that they would attend to no business
| for him that they would leave his body with


everything upon it, but would pin paper to his
| clothing containing any directions he might wish


to leave. In few moments after this conversation
| ne was shot, ana tne party mounting their HOfseS


disappeared in the direction of Denver. When


Ford was fouud, his watch was untouched, and


upon his coat was pinned slip of paper with the
words, Executed by the Vigilance Committee y
| His body was perforated by six buckshot and one


large bullet The Vigilance Committee had indubi-


table evidence that he was connected with the


large band of horse thieves and murderers, who in


Tested the country. He hailed from Council Bluffs
| Iowa, where he had considerable property. In


that place he bore q very fair character. He is


buried on the left bank of the Platte about six and
a half miles below Denver His grave is known to
but few, and the grass of another season will OBJ
literate all traces of recognition which that few


may possess--the sod being carefully cut and re-
| placed over his last resting place.

headline:
INCENDIARY PAPERS-THE BALTI.


MORE SUN.
article:
As no people are so profoundly interested in
the preservation Of the Union as the citizens
of the District, they will be prompt to exert
their influence in all things, great and small,
in putting down disunion. And one measure
of no small importance, will be a withdrawal,
by concerted unanimity, of all patronage
from disunion newspapers.


We have one such published in the District
ITSELF the Constitution, but as that has little
circulation here, or anywhere else, it is beyond
popular reach, and must be left to die with the
corrupt administration which sustains it.


The Baltimore Sun has a very large crcula.
ton in the District as mauy as FIVE thousand.
Our peaple are justly incensed with its daily
preaching Of disunion, all the more dangerous
for being insidious. There is, we believe, no
division Of opinion among our citizens, in rep.
ROTATING its course. And yet from Incidence,
and to avoid the trouble, although not great,
of stopping subscriptions, its circulation falls
of but little. This ought not to be so. We
have too much at stake, not to discharge so
obvious duty as the withdrawal of patronage
from sheets which, like the Sun, give daily
currency to sentiments which, if carried out,
will annihilate the value of property in this
city. Let every good citizen cease to take, or
read, the Sun, and regard himself as Vigil
ance Committee man, to admonish bis neigh
bors not to touch or handle it.

Pursuant to call, meeting of the
colored citizens of Boston was held in the
Joy-Street Church, on Monday evening,
June 18th, 1860, which was organized by
choice of John J. Smith as Chairman, and
Charles p Taylor as Secretary.


The Chairman stated the object of the
meeting to be an expression of thought and
sentiment with reference to the recent
speech in Congress, of their illustrious
Senator, Hon. Charles Sumner He then
introduced William c. Nell, who submitted
the following resolutions:


ResOlred, That true to those impulses for free
dom which were the choice inheritance of Hon.
Charles Sumner its characteristic fruits blossomed
out in his efforts for equal school rights of the col
ored children of Boston, and through many other
channels of benevolence and reform, here in his
native city, elsewhere, and in Congress culminat-


ing in that eloquent and noble speech delivered in
the United States Senate June 4th, 1860


ResOE0cd, That our past and every day experience,
both as enslayed and nomnally free colored Ameri-
cans, confirms the graphic truthfulness of said
speech-the barbarism of slavery. But passing by
the facts of Southern slavery, abundantly cited
by him in illustration, the speech has special sig
nifcance to US at the present time, inasmuch as
prominent Senators and Representatives from
Northern States, claiming Republican majorities,
directly sustaining the institution of slavery by
IL. Il. & 80
zens as a prospective feature in their party pro-
gramme; and the Executive of our own beloved
Massachusetts, nterposes a second gratuituous veto

other citizens, native and adopted while this great
speech of our distinguished Senator not only por-

slavery, but is redolent with recognitions of our
manhood and citizenshp-our equality before the
La1o'-a speech, though too radical for politicians
and parties, is loyal to humanity and God; for all
grateful homage of our hearts.


Mr.. Nell said From these resolutions,
complimentary to the living orator, he felt
that it would not be deemed an inappropri.
ate transition to award a brief tribute to a
recently departed friend, who, if now in
the flesh, would have promptly enunciated
from lips of glowing rhetoric an earnest
commentator of Mr.. Summers speech; and
he would, therefore, submit for endorsement
of the meeting resolution relative to the
late Rev. Theodore Parker.


Resolved, That in the death of the Rev. Theo
dore Parker, mourn the loss of an ever-vigilant
devoted, noble-hearted friend. Independent of his
muldfarious offerings for the good of mankind, VT
remember especially, (for how can we forget 2! hii
Herculean and complicated services in the trial
hours of 1850 Isl and 81, when the Fugitive
Slave Law established reign of terror in Boston
and throughout the country. As President of the
Boston Vigilance Committee, he as watchfu
| as Argus with his hundred eyes, and executive
as was Brareus with as many hands The scenes
consequent upon the hunting of William and Eller
Craft-the rendition Of Thomas Sims and Anthony
Burns-his words and deeds at Faneuil Hall
Music Hall, United States Court House, &c.;-ir
the highways and byways of the city and suburbs
or protecting the flying fugitive in his own house
in times of imminent personal peril. Indeed
wherever his voice or hand could assist those who
would escape, or foil the attempt of those who
would betray, there was he sure to be found, abun
dant in resources, and ready for any emergency
His letter from Rome in approval of the purposes
of John Brown and party at Harper's Ferry, COM
pleted public record consistent with his own
chosen language love my God, Father and
Mother of the white man and black; and am | tc
suffer the liberties of America to be rod under the
hoof of shareholders and slave-drivers = These
doing and saying now swell up to the surface ol
our memories, invoking the tribute due to him.
who, though dead, yet speaketh to encourage all
who would be faithful in the battle between Free
dom and Slavery,


William Wells Brown, Robert Morris, Esq,
DR.. John S. Rock, and Rev. j. Sella
Martin addressed the meeting in support OF
the resolutions-when, on motion, they
were unanimously adopted, copies ordered
addressed to Hon. Charles Sumner and
Mrs. Parker, and their publication solicited
in newspapers of this city and elsewhere.
JOHN J. SMITH, Chairman.
CHARLES P. Taylor, Secretary.

headline: The End Of the Tragedy.
article:
The man ODonnell, who assessiuated
Shields, at Pine Grove, Sierra county, on
Saturday night last, while the latter was
crossing bridge on his way home from the
more public part of the place, was taken up
10y the mob. Sunday night, and hung Shields
was man occupying very respectable po
sition, was President of the Minnesota Mining
Company, and quite popular. ODonnell sns
pected him Of having been too intimate with
his WIFE on a certain trip which the two took
to San Francisco, last winter, but swallowed
his wrath for some time and did nothing
Meeting Shields, frequently, as we are in
formed he made no attack on him whatever,
but let him pass. Finally after the lapse of
weeks, and when Shields was expecting no
attempt NJ on his life, ODonnell, with com
panion whose name has not transpired, way
laid him, and under shelter Of the night,
sprang unawares upon him and stabbed him
20 death


Had the killing been done in open day, and
in a bold and above-board manner, it is prob
dDIe tHdI hoI d hulE Vi " l'ouutll , Hedu
would have been injured As it was, he was
not at once meddled with, and had he used
discretion and fled, he would have saved his
life. But he remained, it would seem in the
midst of the excited populace, and his pres
ence increased the excitement against him.
Various representations We're Of course made
aggravating the nature of the case against
him, and, in fit of uncomfortable rage and
fury, the people rose and hung him.


1t seldom happens in these United States
that man is hung for killing the seducer Of
his wife. The law Of custom seems to be that
the husband is justified in shooting down, or
stabbing to death on sight, the destroyer of
his domestic peace, but then it must be done
in a manly way, and not by secret assassina-
tion. This is the law Of public opinion, and
yet tits difficult to see any great actual diff
ference between shooting down an uRarmed
man in the street, ns Sckes did Key, and
killing the same man in the night when he
has no opportunity to contend for his life
! If it be cowardly to take mans life under
cover Of night when he has no chance to de-
fend himself, is it any brayer to meet him on
the street when he is without weapons and
| deliberately murder him there? Yet this
kind Of killing is the kind that has been done
in the great majority of instances, in which
wronged husbands have avenged themselves
and been acquitted afterwards, for the
wounds inflicted upon their domestic honor
If there be any basis of Justification at all for
IL mans taking vengeance into his own hands
in such cases, it consists in this,-that he who
inyades the domestic circle, 20 dishonor it,
places himself beyond the pale of protection
by the laws of the land. lie is an outlaw, in
the estimation Of public opinion, so far as the
injured party is concerned, and it is not mur
der for the man he has injured to kill him
The wronged husband is under no obligation
to give him an equal chance, but may shoot
him down like dog upon the streets Ac-
cording to this doctrine, then, it makes but
little difference, where, or in what way, or at
what time, the act of vengeance is consum-
mated; whetherit be done in the day time or
night time whether it be done by steel or
bullet or 10y sweetening the gay Lothario'
tea with a little arsenic. We are speaking OF
the matter, now, as in the abstract, for we
confess that secret assassination wears a very
repuguant aspect and, another thing. it look:
like evading the responsibility of the killing
In this instance the evasion was an unhappy
one for the unfortunate ODonnell.


1t is stated that Mrs ODonnell, on hearing
of the death of Shields. started from the EN-
pire Ranch, on foot, through the snow and
mud screaming frantieally, and that she has
not since been heard from Some suppose
she was struck with insanity and that she has
perished in the wilderness. 1t is more likely
that she has stopped somewhere on the road
to take her cry out.

After lucid remarks from other gen. tlemen, the club which were now held together by union stronger than water," slowly dis solved, and mixed into their original elements. From the mixture of races and brogues represented, he is of opinion that it was one, 'tother, and both, and we humbly suggest an account of its proceedings may be sent to the Hartford Post-a paper whose influence will 20 great ways toward making the gathering re- spectable.

On her re- turn, she found the older child out of doors, with it's clothing consumed by fire, and its body burn- ed so seriously, that it survived only an hour.

GREAT ExcrrENESr.-0ur citizens were in a

force was appointed and citizens generally
formed themselves into patrol clubs, who kepta
vigilant watch all night, but no disturbance oc-
CURED.


All things considered there exists not the
least doubt in our mind but that deep laid
scheme for general revolt exists in the South,
and suggest the great propriety fthe citizens
everywhere forming vigilant committees and
keeping on the alert. No harm could possibly
arise from this proceeding, while, on the con-
trary, carelessness on the part of our citizens

cure" "Eternal vigilance is the price of liber-
