headline: Do not Despair of the Union.
article:
Do not Despair of the Union.


We are frank to say that we are not one of
those who despair of the Republic. We believe
1t is today as firmly bound together by the
bonds of patriotism, friendship and interest as
at any period of its existence. A dozen Har
4 per's Ferry raids by dozen old Browns, sent
forth from each free State against each slave
State, would not shake our confidence in the
perpetuity ofthis Union. 1t is the handiwork
of giants inspired by the Great Jehovah. and
de hath written upon it, in indellible marks
perceptibe to every patriots eye, the words
Esto Perpetua. Harpers Ferry raids, then, in
stead of lessening our confidence in the strength
of the Republic and weakening our belief in the
capacity of the people to govern themselves,
only serve to inspire US with increased conf
dence in the healthfuness of our system of gov
ernment, and in its perfect adaptabilty to secure
the utmost possible liberty to an intelent people,
with the least possible danger to society. Do
we despair of the life ofa man because of often
sive pestules upon his face or eruptions upon
his body? On the contrary, they are frequent
ly considered good evidence of health, or as the
immediate result of robust health What are
John Browns, Beechers, Garrisons, and their
sympathisers, but foul blotches upon the fair
face of a moral society, and offensive bos upon
the body polite? Thus vigilance committees,
mobs, and Harper's Ferry raids are not to be
considered as evidencing waning patriotism, or
| 1acav of tba frota
this Union of States, but rather as testifying by
their impotence and utter futiity, not less than
by the sudden destruction hurled upon them by
the strong arm of the powers that be-" the
strength and indestructibility of the Govern
ment.


Nay, we do not despair of this Republic Our
confidence in the patriotism and public virtue
of the great body of the American people is
unimpaired. We know that in every State may
be found men lacking in virtue, in patriotism
men who are fanatical, who, for lack of correct
religious teaching, or for long continued mpe-
ties, have been given over to hardness OF
heart and reprobacy of mind,'' that they might
d" believe lie." Such was the case with old
Brown and his followers. Such is the case with
all who sympathise with his cruel, murderous,
| reasonable enterprise. Believing that the negro
of the Southis groaning in chains-crying from
dungeons for liberty-that is, believing lie'
with fanatics belief-they abandon their pov-
ertystriken mothers and sisters (ride letter of
the sister. of the insurrectionist Stevens), who
are absolutely suffering for the want of food,
| and START forth n incita tba clpolS fa1
song singing negroes to revolt, slay their mas
ters and escape to a land of freedom where
they may enjoy, what ?-hunger and nakedness
along with the kindred of their deliverers We
know that such people exist, and they may a.
gain and again project Harper's Ferry raids.
But what of that? Do we not know that an
immense majority of the communities from
which they issue forth contemn and despise
them? Admit that bells were rung in some
northern towns on the day old Brown was
, hung, and Abolition meetings held-it is no
evidence that the people of the North sympa-
thised with that bloody, heartless old scoun-
drel? One Abolitionist ring bell. 4 dozen
noisy ones can always attract large crowd.
People anywhere will go to see the antics and
hear the talking of an infatuated brawler A
dog-hght or the rawlings of drunkard will
draw full house" any time. The presence
of the crowd attracted, however, does not
indicate approval of dog-fghting or drunken
ness. So with these Abolition gatherings in
Northern towns. And men who suppose they
indicate the sentiment of the body of Northern
| DeODle ipnOran nj nr aacjlv a1
Democracy of the North = T,celve Hundred
thousand strong-will at every hazard maintain
for the people of each section their constitu-
tional rights. So also will thousands of those
who have heretofore acted with the Republican
party. That party having become thoroughly
abolitonsed, these men will abandon it. and
hereafter be found battling in the ranks of the
Democracy.


Nay, never despair of the Republic, Let po-
liticians threaten. Let crazy fanatics howl
and denounce the Union as a failure, the Con-
stitution as "league with He'll" and an sabomi-
nation" They have done the same from the
beginning. When this Government came fresh
from the hands of its inspired makers, fanatics
sought to destroy it. But even then, when it
was like vessel green from the hands of the
potter, it was sufficiently strong to bear unin-
jured the assaults Of its enemies Shall we
then fear for it now that it has been hardening
for more than half a century in the genial rays
of the sun of prosperity?


y The American people know that the North
and South are mutually dependent upon each
other None save Abelitionists and fre-eaters
desire dissolution of the Union. They consti-
tute but contemplate minority of the whole
people. But if sef-interest and patriotism did
not fasten together the North and the South as
with hoOkx steel, the numberless glorious
memories With cluster around and warm eve
ry American heart, and like halo encircle the
American fag-the " stars and stripesn-would
of themselves forever render dissolution impos-
sible.

article: FROM PIKE's PEAK.-Late arrivals from Pike's Peak state that crime and vio- lence still prevail there. Three sporting men. Carl Wood, George Steele and John Rocker in state of intoxicatlon, entered the office of the Rocky Mountain News, at Denver, seized Wm. H. Byers, editor, braEdishing cooked revolvers, and threat ened to kill him instantly, or any one who should attempt to interfere, and forced him to accompany them to the Criterion saloon, where they became more violent in their threats and demonstrations. Edward Jumps, proprietor of the saloon, succeeded in getting their attention, while Byers was taken out the back entrance and escorted to his office. article:
We notice that the editor of the Go1dsboro'
Rough Notes who says that he is in posses
sion of alarming facts alludes to plot which
has been detected in which 100 negroes and
90 white men are engaged, in New Hanover
County for an nsurrection on next Saturday,
the 22nd instant This is indeed a startling
rnnlor, and one that if it really have founda-
ton in fact, will call for increased vigilance
throughout the State.


We are glad to learn that our town authori-
ties have determined to tnrn out citizens
r1atch during next week of Sc instead of 10
anen This is right, and we would suggest
further that they befurnished with instruments
which would enable them to suppress an out
break should one occur. We have not heard
a word that is calculated to cause us to fear an
outbreak In this locality-we have good mas
ters and good servants-but then owing to the
alarming condition Of affairs and the rumors of
contemplated rebellion elsewhere it behoves us
to be vigiIant We owe this to ourselves
and we owe it to our slaves, for while they re-
quire watching and increased vigilance on the
part of their owners and by communities they
also require protection While we are clearly
for Furnishing, with death, every white man or
slave who may be detected la an attempt to
get up insurreetjon or cause rebellion We are
for protecting the slaves against public excite
1Aeat or undue violence when found to be in
nocent And we are confident, il their own
e1s will discharge properly their daty, and the
community can be purged of all improper and
dangerous white persons, there is No trouble
to be apprehended from our slaves


Then let us increase our vigilance let each
and every man who owns or has slaves about
him establish and maintain most rigid dis
cipline-let tbe creatures be treated mildly but
firmly Let al license that may by any posi-
bilty have an evil tendency be withdrawn du-
ring the coming holidays. All intercourse
between the slave and the free colored popular
ton should be suppressed as far as possible,
and a most rigid police should be applied to the
latter class Let those Of Ghr good citizens
who have been in the habit Of suffering their
slaves to hire their own time, to live off to
themselves and to so about contracting and
doing work On their own account the same as
freemen. ia violation Of all law, realize that
the practice is not only wrong but dangerous
TO all classes OF our people; and II such prac-
tice be not abandoned let the law be enforced
against every offender


The times are pregnant with troubles; the
rumors which we fear are but too we'll foun-
ded which reach us from the Cape Fear are in
deed alarming, and We know not what day
or an hour may bring forth. Hence we renew
our suggestion that Vigilance Committee be
at established by our citizens to act in con-
junction with the public authorities for the
grntection of llfe and property, should their ser
vices be required aad for the further purpose
of riddng the community Of all suspected and
dangerous persons We would suggest to our
friends throughout the county also to form
their Vigilance Committees in the different
precincts We may be standing on volcano
which may burst forth at any moment scatter
ing ruin and destruction in every direction
Nothing Is to be lost by vigilance. Let us be
on the watch then.

SHASTA COURIER.

CoAAUSICAIED-
The Slave Code.
article:
What is it? Most of the Abolition and Re-
publican papers in the State are making great
ado about the Slave Code, as they call it, and by
asserting that the National Administration Dem.
ocracy are in favor of a slave code, and that
slave code is legislation in favor of slavery in
the Territories. seek to frighten men from the
support of Governor Wise, of Virginia, and all
the politicians and statesmen of his political
views on this subject They further say, and in
shis many Douglas Democrats join that by ad-
yocating what they term the slave code the
supporters of Wise are placing themselves in the
same position that the Abolition party occupy


This, to the mind of your correspondent, is
the most reckless and false position which could
possibly be assumed. The position which the
opposition assume on this subject is this:-they
impledly admit that by the Constitution, and
under the compromise of the Union, slavery or
slave property could go into the Territories in
their territorial state, and by legislation seek to
keep it out. Hence the Missouri restriction
hence the Wilmot Proyiso-hence the present
Abolition doctrine.


The Administration Democracy, on the other
hand, claim that since under the Constitution
slave property can go to the Territories, Con-
gress having control over the Territories-hav-
ing the right to pass all needful rules and reg
ulations in regard to the Territories and other
property-having power and exercising the
power to establish Courts-and the Constitution
recognizing slaves as property, that the owners
OF such property should be protected in its en-
joyment, until the people, in their sovereign
capacity, when about to form State govern
ment, say that slavery shall not exist in the
State to be formed. This is what is meant by
slave code for the Territories and it is but ex-
ercisinga protectorate over the common proper
~ of the nation. Whether such legislation is
needed depends altogether upon the fact whe-
ther the Kansas-Nebraska Act intended to give
the first halfdozen who put foot on new terrific
ry the right to pass " unfriendly legislation in
regard to this species of property, or whether it
is an act of State Sovereignty alone which can
do it.


If the Interpretation which the President and
his followers place upon that act be adopted as
the policy of the country in the future, there is
no necessity for legislation upon the subject, but
If it be true, as Mr.. Douglas and his followers
assert, that the people, whether many or few,
can legislate unfriendly" then the Federal
Government should interfere, and assert its do
minion over the Territory, and protect her cit
liens in the enjoyment of a common property.


In no case can any one who really and truly
wishes even-handed justice meted out to all the
citizens of the Union, object to legislation on
this subject, nor can any object to Governor
Wise because of his advocacy of this doctrine
An accidental majority may make law, and if
we admit that majoritiss are always right we
must admit that even the San Francisco Vigi-
lance Committee was right and that the law
which said " Thou shalt not murder" was alto
gether too old fogyish to be considered a safe
rule of action. Legislation in aid of just law
as defined by the Constitution is the object of
the followers of Governor Wise whilst the Alb
oiitionists, ct id omns genus, propose by legsla-
tion to keep the people of position of the
Union from enjoying what with their blood and
treasure they aided to procure. In this i, the
difference one seeks to do justice, the others
seek to perpetrate frGrd.


These thoughts are thrown out hurriedly, but
may be eliminated further should have leisure
in future number of the Courier


Your correspondent cares little whether we
have slave code by Congress, or whether the
people are restricted in the expression of leg
islative opinion on the subject of slavery until
they form State Constitution.


In conclusion permit me to say that Daniel S.
Dickinson, Of New York, is, | believe, the most
available candidate for the Presidency, and en-
tirely acceptable to ne, but that Gev. Wise's
" slave code" is the least of all possible objec-
tons, in the opinion of your subscriber, which
should be urged against him by honest, right
thinking men. Respectfully,

headline:
Collision between the State and City


Officers at San Francisco.
article:
Officers at San Francisco.


From the general tone of the San
Francisco papers, we infer that the people
are greatly exasperated at the unwarrant-
able stretch of authority on the part of
Judge Wells, of the Supreme Court, in
summarily ordering a gang Of villains to
be turned loose in the city without even
coming to trial. We learn from the
Courier, that the Vigilance committee
are about establishing their tribunal,
which was formerly the only conservator
of life and property in that city. San
Francisco has always been cursed by
herds ofthe most brutalized convicts from
the British penal colonies, as we'll as the
skillers" and assassins of theAtlantic cities;
| AID if they are to be protected by judicial
functionaries, the people of the mountains
will visit the Bay City as seldom as posi-
bic. The whole matter will be understood
from the following statement from the
Times & Transcript.


| On Friday afternoon an application was
made to the Police Office for some officers
to arrest some persons who were engaged
in creating disturbance at the Mercantile
Hotel. Sergeant Towle, and officers Haven
and Wall were sent down, and upon their
arrival were attacked by the party in the
room and severely beaten. Hearing that
the officers were likely to be overpowered,
an additional force proceeded to the spot,
headed by Captain North; they succeeded
in taking James Turner, William Carr and
James Casey to the station house. Warrants
were then issued for the arrest of other
persons who were in the party, and Sergeant
Towle and officers Dolan, Black and Wall,
proceeded to the bark Zoraida, laying out
in the stream, to arrest them As before, a
desperate resistance was made, and Ser
geant Towle was knocked down and badly
bruised, but for all that stuck manfully to
his prisoner, though there were fifty of his
! friends present. the vessel being bound to
Guaymas. and with the officers with him,
succeeded in arresting three men, named
Gallagher, Lewis and Perry, and bringing
! them to the station house. Some dozen
others were arrested. At the station house
! the prisoners behaved in most disorderly
manner, making terrible threats, and abusing
and assaulting the officers. Capt. North,
of the Police, was thrown down and some
what injured. Application was made by
their counsel, Mr.. Kewen, to the Recorder,
to release the parties Oh bail, but he declined
doing So though it is also stated that he
said he would accept bail if satisfactory
The same application was made to Judge
| Wells, of the Supreme Court. who issued
| tl.af j Il


''In the matter Of the application of
James z. Casey, Willim Lewis. William
Carr, James Turner, Martin Gallagher,
Thos. Perry, ct al.-Hajeas Corpus.
| Let writ of Habcas issue; and it is
| further Ordered that the petitioners be
discharged from close confinement, until
IL o clock tomorrow, 18th instant.


ALEXANDER. WELLS,
Associate Justice Of the Supreme Court.
Feb. 18th 1851"


| Capt. North at first refused to obey the
| order. and sent it back to the Marshal; the
Marshal gave the order, and Capt. North
released the prisoners, much against his will.
1t was understood that the Recorder was of
opinion that the order was Illegal but
considered the Marshal the proper person
to decide upon it; and the Marshal consider
ing that the Judge Of the Supreme Court
knew what was legal, did not feel at liberty
to disregard it. On Saturday morning a
writ Of habeas corpus was served upon the
Marshal. requiring him to show by what
authority he held them in custody; upon
which, he made the following return
'The within named parties are not in my
custody, having been discharged by Justice
Wells, of the Supreme Court of the State
of California, some twelve hours since. +"
The accused persons, however, made their
appearance of their own accord, but the
District Attorney being employed in an
other Court, and the City Attorney not
making his appearance, they were dismissed
by the following order


ssSAN Francisco Feb. 18, 1854.


A writ of habeas corpus having been
issued upon the petition of James P. Casey,
VIM. Carr, VIM. Hamilton, VIM. Lewis.
Martin Gallagher, and John Perry, and no
person appearing against them or either of
them, and no good cause being shown for
their detention, it is ordered that inasmuch
as such detention is illegal and without
authority, that they and each of them be
discharged from custody.


ALEXANDER WELLS,


Associate justice of the Supreme Court"


The Recoder had previously declined
having anything to do with the case, con-
sidering that it was taken ont Of his hands
by Judge Wells. We understand that it is
the intention of Mr.. Byrne, the District
Attorney, to bring the whole matter
; before the Grand Jury.

article:
On the afternoon of Friday, the 18th, party
OF the fraternity which governs the elections in
San Francisco-the shoulder strikers-entered
the Mercantile Hotel in that city, and com
menced demolishing the bar room furniture,
preparatory to personal attack upon the pro-
prietors. Several Police Officers happening in
at the time, endeavored as was their sworn
duty to quell the row, but were severely beaten
by the desperadoes. a reinforcement then be-
ing furnished from the Marshalls office, the
ringleaders after hard contest, were arrested
and carried to the Station House. The same
evening, on failing to be liberated without
giving the proper bail to secure their appear
ance before the Recorder the following
morning, they applied through their friends to
Judge Wells, to be liberated OH IA habeas corpus
Accordingly that judicial officer took the respon-
sibility to interfere with the Police in the regu-
lar and lawful performance of their ordinary du-
ties, and released the rowdes not only from
confinement, but from the civil authorities of
the city, by issuing the following order:


g In the matter of the appli-)


cation of James F. Casey, VIM.


Lewis, Wm. Carr, James Tur- Habeas Corpus
ner, Martin Gallagher, Thorn


Perry. et al.


Let Writ of Habeas Corpus issue, and it is
further ordered that the petitioners be discharged
IRON close confinement until eleven O'Clock to-
morrow, 18th instant, ALEX. WELLS,


Associate Justice of the Supreme Court.


Feb. 18th, 1854


Thus it will be seen, the Judge went step
further than even the audacity of the brawlers
haI Ir,1u 70 IL I'll IL,
once upon their mere parol of honor, the writ
of habeas corpus not having issued until the fol-
lowing morning. The law-breakers however,
appeared before Jedge Wells of their own ac-
cord on Saturday morning The city authori-
ties having been so unlawfully interfered with
by the Supreme Court, while endeavoring to
preserve the peace of the city, and protect the
property and persons of their fellow citizens,
refused to have anything more to do with the
matter, and the prisoners were accordingly let
loose to repeat their high handed ourages.-
Soon after their liberation they went to the
Mercatile Hotel, and intimated to the propre-
tors that they would shortly again be visited by
them. They also took occasion to insult Mayor
Garrison, Marshal Seguine, and Capt. North of
the Police, being induced to do so. no doubt by
the pleasing consciousness that they were un-
der the special protection of Judge Wells.


The San Francisco papers, with the exception
of the Ledger and Adrertiser. in their animad-
versions upon this unparalleled outrage on the
part of Judge Wells, exhibit greater degree of
severity and indignation than has ever been
called forth by any act heretofore committed
by an official. Indeed the whole community
was tremendously excited, and strong proba-
bility existed that the Vigilance Committee
would re-assemble, for the purpose of protec-
ting the citizens against the rowdies, and their
abettor and protector, Judge Wells.

thing available to them, they forced his daughter
to join them, tearing her from beneath the roof
where her murdered father lay weltering in his
blood, and making her the victim of crimes too
horrible to be told. From the house of Mr..
Harrington they proceeded up Red river to the
mouth of the Cocodra, where was then living a
Mr. Todd, with his wife and child, who kept a
small store to supply raftsmen.


"At that time the two negroes were armed,
one with double-barrel gun and knife, and
the other with rifle and pistol. They de-
manded food and liquor, which he gave them.
After satisfying their appetites, they demanded
a free pass. He pretended to comply, and
wrote an account of what had transpired at his
house, stating his belief that they intended to
murder him. They did murder him by beat
ing out his brains. They then departed, TAX
ing with them his child, and his wife, whom
they made the victim of the same horrible
crimes to which they had devoted the innocent
young girl whom they had ruthlessly torn from
the home of a murdered father. Miss Herring
ton seemed to have lost her reason, but Mrs.
Todd it seems, was woman of great strength
of mind, and knowing that so soon as the muir
ders and abductions became known, the
neighbors would be ont in pursuit, she endea
vored to mark a trail for the pursuers, by leav
ing shreds of her dress on the bushes as they
passed, and making her little child walk in the
mud of the swamp at times, that its little track
might afford indubitabe proof of the course of
these savage hends and their unhappy victims.


"In week or ten days, while the party were
at halt, about three miles back of Union
point, which is on the Mississippi river, about
thirty.fve miles below Natchez, the two negro
men feel asleep, one of them with his head in
Mrs. Todd's lap. and the negro woman keeping
guard. Suddenly Mrs. Todd perceived the ap-
proach of the armed pursners. She, with admi-
rable presence of mind, motoned to them to be
cautious. They advanced silently, and when
she thought them sufficiently near, she sprang
up with shrek of deirious Joy, and rushed
towards them. The negroes sprung to their
feet; one was captured, the other escaped, sew
eral shots having been fred at him as he fed.


"The party were then taken to Union Point.
Many of the neighbors were collected. Miss
Harrington was maniac, but the mind OF Mrs.
Todd was clear and unclouded. She told her
story with remarkable clearness and consist
ency. 1t was enough to make men weep tears
of blood-a series of crimes black enough to
be execrated by devils. The people assembled
did not need long to deliberate. A summary
execution was resolved upon. The captured
negro was tied to tree. fagots were placed
around him, and Mrs. Todd herself set fire to
his funeral pile II aeas the one acho had mur-
dered her husband, and first outraged herself!


"About one week afterwards, the other negro
was captured and met similar fate. The ne
gro woman was not executed, Mrs. Todd stating
that she had saved the lives Of Miss Herring
ton and herself several times from these savage
fends.


"This is as accurate history of the trans
action as can be given at this lapse OF time
without reference to old files of newspapers,
which we have not been able to obtain. 1t is
drawn from the narrative of several old citi-
zens of that neighborhood, and in part from a
gentleman who witnessed the execution, and
heard Mrs. Todds tragic and heart-rending
story.


".Both the negroes made full confession of
their horrible crimes. They confessed further,
that they had lurked around the plantation Of
another planter of the neighborhood, for the
purpose Of numbering him also, and of obtain
ng'possession of his wife. We have seen and
conversed with highly respectable and intel
ligent planter of the neighborhood, who wit
messed the execution of the second negro, and
was opposed to it, thinking it best that the law
should take its course. He conversed with the
negro from whom he heard full confession.
The same gentleman also informs us that the
negroes assembled were far more anxious for
the execution than the whites, and that it was
with difficulty, after they heard of the crimes
he had committed, that they could be restrain
ed from tearing him to pieces; that he him
self addressed them to prevent them from
taking vengence themselves on the unhuman
fend."


The monsters described in the foregoing ex-
tract from the Free Trader are the prosecuted
saints over whose sad fate the Tribune and its
righteous allies shed their tears. That they
deserved the punishment they received, no
right-minded man can deny. It is not because
they were negroes we say this. Far from it.
Had they been white men, they would have
merited greater torments.


We are not accustomed to deal with such
subjects in our columns. They are disagreea-
bic subjects; but the present condition of
affairs renders it proper that such gross frauds
and falsehoods as those to which the Tribune
and its kindred journals have given currency
should be exposed. We might say much more,
but we forbear.

Another Great Outrage in Boston Co

 lOred Man Carried off to Bondage.
article:
The Boston Times, of the 27th, gives us some of the particulars of the abduction of another colored man and his being carried off in- to bondage, despite the strongest efforts of the patriotic FOSTER and ABBY KELLY! The man was taken off in irons, and this was suffered in broad daylight right under the shadow of the cradle of liberty!" The poor fellows name is WARREN VICTOR, and what name is Nsat, to go bound hand and foot into gnominious sla- very Warren, for one of the most illustrous American patriots, and Victor, for the result of our great revolutionary struggles! Our blood is chilled, even with the thermometer at 94, and we have no heart to write more-the Bos- ton Times must tell the rest:

 Victor is a notorious New York scoundrel and burglar, and has been practicing his profession in different parts. of the country for some time past He broke jail in town in Pennsylvania, where two indictments stand against him for burglary; and he also escaped from jail in Kingston, Canada West. Five indictments ex- ist against him for robbery in Elmira On these he was arrested, and was being conveyed to Elmira, but managed to slip the irons from his wrists, and, with the assistance of some "fugi- tive" rescuers, escaped. His friends put him on the track for this eastern "land of the free and home of the brave," and on his arrival in Portland, he was taken charge of by the noto- rious aboltionist Foster, husband of Abby Kel- ly Foster, and was enjoying the touching air of "Old Folks at Home," played with exquisite sweetness by sympathizing young lady for the amusement of the unfortunate "fugitive" himself, when deputy marshal Brady entered and presentation of steel bracelets soon after took place with interesting ceremonies, to the no little astonishment of most of those present We have already given an account of the ex- citement that ensued when it became noised about Portland that colored man had been ar- rested on charge of burglary, which was be- lieved to be but a feint to cover the arrest of fugitive slave; but the vigilance committee" of the city finally became satisfied that he vas rascal, and then they suffered the law to be executed without obstruction. On his person, when arrested, there were found set of ske- Teton keys, of unusually nice mechanism, re- volver, pistol-balls, caps slugs, etc., and $500 in money.

headline: Vigilance Committee.
article:
THs unearthing of q gang Of thieves and
vagabonds last week has led to the organi-
Sation Of q Vigilance Committee, for the
better preservation Of life and property.
We sincerely hope that this committee
will never attempt to take upon them
selves authority to execute summary JUS
tice, or what they conceive to be such, in
dependent Of the authority Of the officers
whose duty it is to see that the laws arc
executed. In times of unusual excite
ment. when every one Is fred with indig-
nation at some unwonted outrage, the de-
cision of this dreadful tribunal, backed up
by the populace, is greatly to be feared.
The history of the Regulators in the South
West causes one to shudder at the enormi-
ties committed under misguided zeal for
the public welfare. But there was q ne
cessity for an organization of this sort in
thiuly populated country where horse
thieves and murderers preyed upon tho
community at will. In this place we can
see no necessity for anything more than
secret police. We have no reason to
complain Of the officers whose duty it is to
keep the peace. Neither money, influence
rcr friends Gun avail the criminal when
his guilt appears, and any interference on
the part of the citizens would only cause
confusion and lack of confidence in the
administration of justice.


The names of the members of the Com.
mittee of Safety, place of meeting, and
manner of proceeding are of course kept
secret, and we know nothing Of them ex-
cept that such organization exists. We
presume, however, that their object is to
watch the movements of suspicious char
acters, who are always seen lounging
about the streets in mountain towns, with
no visible means of support, always well
dressed yet never seen at work, or in any
sort of employment.


If the Committee act as an auxiliary in
bringing to justice offenders who must
otherwise escape, aud abstain from all in
reference with the duties of the authori-
ties, it will be an additional safeguard to
life and property. There are often cases
where the guilt of parties is apparent to
every one, but proof cannot be obtained to
justify commitment. In such cases
secret police might succeed in ferreting
out offenders who are constantly on the
lookout for the known officers of Justice;
and when one Of the gang is apprehended,
his accomplices, often respectable looking
enough, are ready to swear him out ofthe
custody of the officers.


Every year, at the commencement of
the business season, the mining towns in
the mountains are visited by hocks of Jail
birds who have been driven out of the
lower cities, after becoming too well known
to the police to operate with salty to
themselves. There is less chance of de-
lection, here and we have them. Now
and then one is detected and sum-
marily dealt with, but while be is under
going trial, his accomplices are watching
for an opportunity to commit depreda-
tions next door. Their operations have
already commenced, and the vigilance Of
every one is required to protect his
property.

The Vigilance Committee composed principally Of
Americans, at Aspiuwa had at last accounts compelled
notorious thieves leave that place. and lad also
forced the authorities TO send several desperate criminals
confined in Jail to Carhagena. One Of the Alcades de-
termned to resist the committee had armed fty or
sixty Carthagenians employed the Panama Railroad


but fortunately by the interference Of Col Toten and
some Of the authorities, collision was preyented -.

have always had passion for theatricals, and

ace had, that, although they might see, they must
''touch not taste not handle not" 1t was bad

When my eye turned to his fingers which worked

headline: Meeting of the Democracy.
article:
On Tuesday evening when Mr.. Marshall ad-
dressed the citizens of Bdwell, Mr.. Mont
gomery of Marysville was present, and was
prepared to answer Mr. Marshall, or to discuss
with him the principles of their parties. But
Mr.. Marshall was entirely unwilling, and ao-
solutely refused to make any argument,whlch
Mr.. Montgomery would have an opportunity
of answering After some talk about the
matter Mr. Marshall told Mr.. Montgomery
that he (Marshall) considered it as his meeting
that he looked upon Mr.. Montgomery In the
light of an intruder, and if he spoke at all, 1t
was at the sufferance of Mr.. Marshall and his
friends This closed at once, all conference on
the subject, and Mr.. Marshall had the whole
evening to himself By permission, Mr.. Mont
gomery remained until Wednesday evening,
when he took upon himself the answering of
Mr. Marshalrs speech of the evening previous.
1t was very soon evident, even to the kye-Eyes
themselves, why Ned was so unwilling to meet
lack He dare not do it. He actually feared
to meet the sledge hammer blows, with which
Zack scattered, like chaff before the wind, all
his fine drawn sophisms, and well turned
periods We had never heard Mr.. Montgomery
speak, and to tell the truth, we felt some doubt
of his success in answering sOur Ned" The
Kye- Eyes themselves stood around anticipat-
ing q splendid failure. But as he opened his
address and began warming with his subject,
our own fears began to tighten, and the faces
of the Kye- Eyes to lengthen. One by one, he
took up Mr.. Marshall's propositions of the
evening before, examined the argument made
in support of them, then attacked and de-
molished them. sometimes with a single blow
as utterly as the foot of an elephant would the
cob house of school boy. Mr.. Marshalfs
own past action with the Democratic party,
and his present position, was shown up i'll so
unenvable light, that even the Kye-Eyes
felt ashamed of their present champion, and
one by one, with down cast eyes, sneaked away
from the crowd that hung around the speaker.
The speaker having finished the speech of Mr..
Marshall, then paid his respects to the Secret
Order" itself. he understood his subject, and
was capable of handling it. Mr. Marshall
asked no quarter, and Mr. Montgomery showed
no mercy, and gave US the most triumphant
vindication of Democracy, and the most sue
cessful expose and refutation of Kye-Eyelsm
we have heard during the campaign. The
difference between the two speakers is soon
summed up. Mr. Marshalls forte is jest, Mr.
Montgomery's is argument; the former makes
assertions, the latter produces the record
the former deals in brilliant fancies, the latter
in solid facts--the one raises laugh, the
other heartfelt cheer, the one pleases, the
other eonvinces--the former abandoned the
Democratic party, when, from his own state
ment it was much purer than 1t had formerly
been, the latter joined the party for the same
reason--the former abandoned his party when
he believed it to be in a minority, at the same
time confessing that its principles were the
best ever presented to the American people,
the latter joined it at the same time. believing
that the principles and policy of the Demo-
cratic party are better calculated to preserve
the Union, and to maintain in it's purity the
supremacy of Republicanism, than those of
Kye -Eyeism.


We most heartily tender the sincere thanks
of the Democracy of Bidwell, to Mr. Mont
gomery, for his visit and address

article:
YANKEE JIM's, Dec. 9Th, 1855.


Mr.. EHtor: | notice a correspondent in
the Ioaca Hill News of Nov. oath, who uses
three KS as signature, and purports to
write from this place as one of its citizens, is
out in favor Of division of the county


1t is no doubt quite convenient to use
Yankee Jim's as starting point for this
move, the better to hide the real object of
the move and at the same time give charac
ter to it. But the communication in ques-
ton, as we'll as the very lengthy one of the
subsequent issue, reminds me too forcibly Of
the style of certain Senator, who is said to
have obtained his nomination from the Know
Nothing county convention by pledging his
support to the Iowa Hill Office seekers, in ia
vor of this measure, to establish any great
degree of confidence in the good intentions
Of the. author, hereabouts.


Perhaps the Honorable gentlemen fancies
that inasmuch as Iowa Hill influence pro-
cured him the unmerited nomination, he is
bound to 90 into the Legislative body for the
sole purpose of representing the X. Ms Of
that flourishing village, and like statesman
of enlarged views, he is by means of these
anonymous epistles preparing the public
mind for this great measure of internal
policy.


The editor, in commenting upon the first
communication, very modestlv observes that
The subject of division of the county and
the want of a new county seat Of reasonably
convenient access to a large portion of the
people of Placer County, as ercittng some at
tepfion among those Who are most nconrep-
ienced Jy tie present arrangement" The
young man has barely heard of it, but it is
only exciting some attention among those
who are the most inconpenienccd by the pres
ent arrangement. This present arrangement,
| suppose must Inconvenience the proprie-
tors of the -Ne,cs, to the extent Of certain
official patronage, which they snuff in the
distance. Being entirely disintercsted in the
matter, he condescendingly remarks that he
has mo objection to making room for fur
ther communications upon the subject All
this is done contessedly as starter, in a
scheme, in which the tayern-keepers, four or
five incipient county judges and some twenty
would be Sheriffs, of our neighboring village
are the real parties in interest. 1t has been
discovered that debt of some forty or fifty
thousand dollars is of incalculable advantage
to new county. and the aggregate of mile
age will be infinitely less if this division
takes place. A plan of salvation, for all the
evils old Placer is laI oring under, has been
conceived: yea, more. from the fruitful brain
of this giant legislator, this new county has
burst upon the planetary system, all glowing
with harmonised organization, and its name
is Uashingtoni


Now, Mr.. Editor, I'm Il plain blunt man,
and quite willing to admit that there are
some convenences to be enioved at the
county seat which we do not have who live
out of it-among which is the exquisite priv
iege of sueing and being sued, with great
er degree of facility, and Of being jerked up
to settle other peoples difficulties, every few
days, as Juror. None Of which Injuries
am | particularly DESTROYS of, but as my
neighbors rather envy Auburn on that ac-
count, | could wish for their accommodation
that every town in the county was a county
seat. | am not willing, however, as one Of
the tax payers to 90 into this speculation
merely to CRAFTY this whim of our neighbor,
when taken in connection with the expense,
which any sensible man must be convinced
would necessarily follow in the train of a
new county organizaton-the purchase of
books, Court House. Jail, the salaries of Off
GERS, to say nothing of the annoyance arising
from the crowds of the hungry attorneys
that would flow in upon us. | do not find
it any further from Y Yankee Jim's to Auburn
now, than it was three years ago, and the IA
cities of travel much better and all the
time being improved; and, if am obliged to
90 to the county seat as a witness or juror,
shall exact my mileage and per diem, and if
as a suitor, | shall consider it as an evil that
a new county would be more likely to in
crease than diminish. | have another objec-
ton to this move, which will mention and
then close this hurried communication, viz:
We now live in a county of some Importance,
some weight politically, say about the fourth
in political magnitude in the State as we
now stand we can make ourselves felt in our
legislative bodies, but divide us up. as the KS
propose, and we shall have two counties
perhaps three, for God knows where these
things will stop when once commenccd),
neither of which will support itself, or have
the necessary weight in legislative matters.


From this state of insigniicance, good
Lord remoye-from the contemplate bck-
erings about county seats, and the small fry
ambition for petty office-good Lord remove
me and all my respectable fellow citizens


YANKEE JIM'S.

REPORT OF THE GRAND JURY.-The report of
the late Grand Jury We are unable to give entire
in to-day's paper, and We therefore content our
self with brief reference to its most important
items. They report to the Court eleven true
bills, as follows: grand larceny, l. assault with
intent to kill, 3 ASSAULT with intent to commit
great bodily injury, 2; rape, /; improper and
criminal use of deadly weapons 4. The Grand
Jury deprecate the too frequent use of deadly
weapons in our streets and public assemblies, and
urge our officers to prevent it. They also call
upon the good citizens of the county to use their


influence in disbanding the Vigilance Commit
tees. They allude to the unsatifactory service
and School Marshals, and state that it has cost
the county $500 to get hold of 5000 due us
from the school fund There are at present ten
school districts in the county. The Jail Is re-
ported clean aud orderly, but the building unfit
to be used. The erection of a new stone edifce
is advised. The hospital of Drs. Kendall &
Browne, in which are lodged the INDECENT sick of
the county, is fatteringly alluded to-the sick
well attended, and every thing pertaining to the
establishment admirably adapted for the purposes
intended, SO far as examined, the books OF the
various county officers are kept in a workman.
like manner" They recommend more vigilance
in the collection of poll and foreign miners tax
and advise that the proceedings of the Board of
Supervisors be published in the papers of the
county. They call the attention of road superv
vors to the bad condition of many roads and
bridges, and recommend to the authorities the
enforcement of the law against noisy and barba-
rous amusements on the Sabbath, and the sup
preston of houses of ill-fame.

Much complaint has lately been made by ,he
Mexican population in our midst, in reference 70
the action of certain parties who claim to be
invested with authority as members of Com.
mittees of Vigilance. We confess we have given
the subject too little attention, satisfied as VA
are that wrong has been inflicted upon innocent
persons in the name of that sort Of justice which
| is appeased by violence. The undisguised FEEL
| ing which prevails to great extent among oar
mining population against all foreigners does not
stop to consider that the Mexican people held
rights and interest here long before cur laws were
| substituted for theirs; and although we boast Of
the freedom we brought to the Pacific shores the
| occupants we found here often have just cause
! TO complain Of our encroachments end our in.
| tolerance. The genuine American feeling should
| pride itself On its liberality and magnanimity,
instead of exercising disposition to override awe.
and crush the weak. The rights Of the humblest,
as well as the greatest, should be held alike Sa-
cred. That there are bad Mexicans, their own
people know, and frankly confess, yet let them
be held amenable Ia the law. Ii is not Of the
law, but of violence, the Mexicans complain
and who in any community, whose boast is tho
supremacy of civil law, does not alike deprecate
violence We are not Of those who recognize
either the right or the proprety of any selEcon.
stituted committee to step forward as judges and
executioner The mob may sometimes be right
and there are instances of fragrant outrage where
popular opinion will support it; yet the prece,
dent is perncous one, and the spirit, ii un.
checked is dangerous to liberty, and disastrous
to the peace Of society.


In the La Cromica, of the 30th ult., we find
petition of our Mexican citizens addressed to
the Deputy Mexican Consul at San Francisco,
on this subject. Mr.. Bolton has referred the
matter to the Mexican Minister at Washington


The petitioners above alluded to, after recur-
ring to the many illegal arrests of their country.
men by selfconstituted conservators of the pub.
lice peace, say: 1--WE do not ask that these Grim
inals should be pardoned. We do not assert that
they are not guilty of crime All we require is
law and order; and we believe We have perfect
right to demand that our citizens be delivered to
the proper authorities, that their cause may bc
publicly judged according to the laws. If in this
country we are never to have any guarantee to
life or property; if we are not to live beneath
the protection of the authorities and the laws,
it would be better that they fix Gpon some time
for our entire expulsion and the world will then
know which is the guarantee that the foreigner
has in this country, aud the manner in which trea-
ties made with friendly foreign nations are COM
piled with.


I" In the commerce, mining, agriculture and
arts are daily seen by innumerabe number Of
Mexicans assisting although perhaps on small
scale, to develope the riches of this country;
but none are free Ono matter how well known
their occupation may be- from the danger of being
sacrificed by Lynch Law or from being the nnno-
cent victims of the simple will of any member Of
the vigilance committee, who, deying the authori-
ties, commit sweeping vengance upon the help
less"

A terrible tragedy occurred in the Tread
water neighborhood twelve miles north OF
Princeton. last Friday. Jesse Williams, a
man over fifty years of age, was found hang
ing to a tree in the road near his house. He
and his family had been a terror to the
neighborhood for years on account of their
desperate character, and were suspected of
having instigated the murder of Mr.. Stevens
few months ago They also figured in a
horrible outrage on two of their negroes very
lately an account of which we published
The family had started to Princeton to wit
ness the release of young Williams from the
Jail, and found the old man hanging by the
neck on the way. The most terrible rumors
are afoat throughout the community as to
various murders perpetrated by this family,
which have now been exposed by the ne
groes. 1t is rumored that six skeletons have
been found in cave near Williams house.
The people are wild with excitement. and
have raised a vigilance committee, who are
resolved to exterminate the offenders. The
young Williamses have fled and are hotly
pursued. The Williamses are one of the
wealthest families in the country, and are
believed TO have used foul means to add to
their treasures for many years.

The philadelphia North American, speaking

Here Is Senator Of the United States hunt

cry owner OF q bullet Not that he ruined the


fair fame of man. woman or child; not that he

fore his constituents, where all public men meet

commeAted upon the sayings and dongs Of the


party inpppesition TO him, and more particu-
larly the Politicians by whom it was led. Up


to the beginning Of this canvass he had borne


in silence contunely and reproach compared
with which all that1we here know Of political
SANDER must be regarded as child's play. Such


was the effect OF fhiA that when Broderck was
elected to the Senate and came on 10 take his
scat, men were surptised TO find him decent,


good-natured, kind and courteous gentleman,


Of dignifed bearing, and not the low vagabond


he had been represented. During the reign of
the last Vigilance Committee in San Francisco,


the feroeity of his enemies went to such lengths

ernment patronage was added to the faction of

and McKibbin attempted to make head They

ing everywhere. 1t had been SO long said that

ed himself and attacked his enemies with inf

The Senator could not refuse a Judge Of the

from the existence of Chinese population

great mass of the American miners in Shasta
county are composed of industrious, intelligent

Pdcifc NetAoaist denies that Californians are
generally infdel to Christianity, as many
have asserted; they are too busy to be pious:


"Californians are earnest people, and upon
this element of their character we predicate
our most sanguine hopes with regard to their
religious future. Whatever they do, is done
with all their might. Whether engaged in
boring tunnels, washing down mountains,
huming gorges, canvassing for political hon
ors, building cities, or fighting one another,
they throw themselves into what they un-
dertake with all their souls and all their
strength Intensity is their distinguishing
characteristic. They surrender themselves
to the excitement of the hour with almost
Partisan abandon. Hydraulic mining, quartz,
city lots, ranching, politics, vigilance COM
mittees, Gold Lake and Frazer river have
each in their turn had their day. Religion
will have its day yet-and when that day
shall come most thrilling chapter will be
added to the history of Christianity"

The State election is now progressing There

Ward are blockaded with rowdies. and the po-
lice are doing nothing to hinder them.


In the Tenth Ward the Reform Judge of elee-
tion WAS intimidated and compelled to leave his
post. Hinsley. who was appointed by the act
ing Mayor and rejected by the Council has been

en- Off

ness at SO, Hanover street, and Reformer, has

dition, bis brother G. ii. Kyle, who came to his
rescue, was also shot and is dangerously
wounded.


In the Fourteenth Ward desperate struggle
occurred, aud the Reformers were resisted with
arms. Sonny White, alias James johnson, q
notorious rowdy, run an awl into Reformer,
aud was shot dead with pistol ball. Two 9TH
er rowdies named Harris and Duffy, were shot

Richardson, however, managed to escape,


Judge Giles, OF the United States District

Accounts given by Texas papers in regard
to the storming of Brownsville are contra
dictory. An extra of the Corpus Christi
Ranchero of Nov. 7th, contains a statement of
NJ. w. j. Miller, to the effect that Browns.
vile was taken on the 3lst of October, by
Cortinas, after hard fight The Ranchero
says Miller was in the fight The following
is a portion of the statements


Cortinas attacking party consisted of about
four hundred men, and he has in all proba-
blity two hundred men patroling the coun
try to prevent communication with the city,


In all told we had about fifty white men
under arms, and these were aided by one
hundred and fifty Mexcans, sent from Mata-
moras, Col Maranco. Commander of this
force. | can form no idea of the number of
men killed on either side. The cry of the
Mexicans, was, Death to the Americans I"
mo quarter" and such is truly the case, as
is proved by the death of every man Corti-
mas has taken prisoner


On Tuesday morning Cortnas had entire
possession of Brownsville.


The Corpus Christi Rancho of Nov. 18th,
has intelligence showing that Brownsville,
not been taken on the 3lst of October. The
town still held out up to the 7th or Sth of
Nov. San Antonio papers of the 18th and
10th of Nov, contain the following:


The different accounts of the state of af-
fairs at Brownsville are so conflicting as to
dates and circumstances, that it is impossible
to ascertain the exact truth. We refer our
readers to the extra of the Ranehero, and the
extract from the N. 0. Crescent. The Gal
weston News of the Sth publishes letter
from l. B. Bigelow, dated Brownsville, the
lst inst, which mentions several attempts
upon the town, but not word about its fall.
The report of its being taken on the 3lst
ult, was therefore premature. In all proba-
bility, it has since fallen.


The Ranchero says that by authentic re-
ports Cortinas is stated to have two forces.
amounting together to about 700 men.


We observe that the Governor had sent a
special message to the House on the subject
of the Rio Grande difficulties. 1t was re-
ferred to a select committee.


We have been shown letter from a relia.
be citizen of lndianola to one of our mer-
chants in town. 1t is dated the llth instant
and states that an express had Just arrived at
lndianola with the news of the fall of Browns
vile, after a gallant defense of five hours
hard fighting. 1t says also that Cortinas had
greatly increased his forces, and that he had
scouting parties between the Rio Grande and
the Nueces, robbing the ranches. Parties
from Corpus Corpus Christi were at Browns.
vile to procure arms and munitions. but
could not be supplied. They state that Cor
vaial is said to be at the bottom of the move.
ment.


The Corpus Christi Ranchero says:


On the 4th instant n party of armed men
had crossed from Mexico to this side, about
six miles below Rio Grande city, surprising
'fandango party" killing two aud taking
twenty-siX prisoners with all of whom the
invaders again recrossed the river


That paper also stated that the people Of
Corpus Christi were preparing for the defense
of their town, being fearful that it would be
attacked by Cortinas


The following from San Antonio paper
shows that the people were apprehensive o.
an attack


1t is not by any means beyond the bounds
of possibility that San Antonio may be Wis
ted by Cortnas. We believe, except officers.
the number of soldiers at present stationed
IN San Antonio does not exceed twenty.tbree
Would it not be as well that our citizens
should take measures for the defense of this
place in case such a contingency should arise?
we think it would be advisable, more par
ueularly as there are many among the low
est class of Mexicens who are not to be de-
pended upon. Numbers of them we be-
lieve, would join Cortinas if they had an
opportunity to do so. They have not for
gotten the operations of the Vigilance Com
mittee and the Last War.

From the following which we find in the

tits our very unpleasant duty to report
a total suspension of the railway works at
this place, arising from some dissatisfaction
on the part Of the carpenters and laborers at
the manner in which they were boarded. as
also because Of the carpenters demanding,
and being refused, an advance in their wages

OF two dollars a day.


wv are the last person in the community,

thing calculated to act EMPLOYERS and EN-
ployees by the ears; but Justice compels us
to declare that the contractors have misman
aged the business, have acted, indeed. yerv

The laborers were hired at S26 a month
and board. If the weather proved too wet
for the men to work, the DAYS wages were
stopped, and moreover one dollar each was
scored against them for she food eaten on that
idle day. On Sundays all hands were oblig
ed to keep a belly Sabbath during dinner
time, for they never got more than two meals
on that day-which was established, it seems.
according to tie contractors rules, although
we must confess the custom is new to us
The material of the table of those hospitable
contractors consisted Of ships pork, and beef
unfit for use-old junk which circumnaviga-
ted Cape Horn, and bought as old stores, in
San Francisco at three cents pound But
ter, the refuse Of all San Francisco mix
ture between lard and confectioners grease,
which served very long at the table, for no
body touched it.


"On Sunday evening last, the laborers out

ed the contractor for their third meal-call

mon instinct, formed themselves into a vigi-
lance committee of some kind-took posses

/ ton, Judge Lynch and a rope, with which

citation was at end. The sword of Alexan.
der was thrown into the balance. The men

ed off to the mines in the Sierra Mountains

mutability of the human stomach"

ing Company keeps ap appearances of doing

The close attention of the special police, appointed during the Fair last week, had the effect to intimidate these gentry, and keep them in their proper place. We have class among us who it is known 'Ffol- low no visible vocation" for Livelihood they live, nobody knows how-except that now and then some one is feeced at Ca little game," and that Tom, Dick or Harry won his money. These things are all wrong, and a stop should be put to all such operations. Men who do not earn livelihood by some visible calling should be avoided and eschewed by the working and business men of com munity. Thus far, until recently, Des Arc has been, comparatively, free from this class, and exertions should be used to keep the fair fame of our town untarnished by the blasting and destroying influence of the thief, loafer and professional gambler.

 Eden into pandemonium, have imported into our midst lewd women and whereas, also, from what we have seen and learn, we believe there are Aboltionists in our midst, persons unfriendly to the institution of sla- very as we have it, and who are tampering with our slaves. endeavoring to instil into minds evil principles, and whereas, we look upon this class (abolitionists) as thieves, hypocrites, cut-throats, incendia- ries, false to themselves, traitors to their country, hypocrites in religion, and false in everything and untrue to everything save the devil and his service; and as we believe "self-preservation to be ''the first law of nature," and as the exigency of our situa- tion is not such as to permit us to await the tardy and uncertain relief of the law therefore be it resolved:

article: Over the northern States and especially over their cities, dark cloud is lowering. Should they succeed in crippling the south, upon whose products the greater part of their prosperity depends, the result would be to close their factories, bankrupt their importing firms and destroy their com merce. Independent of this, there is a spirit of agrarianism abroad among them that will, some day, consume much that is valuable. The result is that labor starves. yet is unwilling to be employed Domes tic labor in the families of the north is diff ficult to procure, yet thousands are unem. ployed. The employers refuse to give any. thing bnt scanty wages, and the employees prefer short life of vice to a long, finger. ing one of ill requited labor to wind up with death in hospital Society is de- moralized the most foul and corrupt isms flourish like willows by the water-courses and worse than all there is growing an- tagonism between the rich and the poor The fanatics who are waring upon the south will find to their cost, ere long, that the white slaves of the north are mere to bo dreaded by them, than the black slaves here are to be feared by us. When mobs of hun. gry men and women are sacking and pilag- ing, demanding food and fuel, and initiating the Parisians of the first revolution they may learn that charity should begin at home as a matter of policy. The growing agrarian- ism, the breaking up of all ties, the de- moralization of society at the north will all produce their bitter fruits. Whether the present winter will witness one of these outbreaks, will depend good deal on the severity of the season. Fortunately, bread stuffs are yet low priced and there is no commercial panic. seems that the standard of rebellion has been
raised, by the Gentiles in Carson Valley-re-
bellion not against Brigham Young but
against Gov. Cummings the legitimate Chic

misguided individuals assembled, on the 18th
of December, at the "Clear Creek House, ,

Let every lover Of onr common country be in
attendance.


This meeting was to second one of the kind
held in the valley, and proceeded, with all
due deliberation, to follow up the unfinished
work on hand. From what we can gather
from the scanty information before us, we
should judge that the meeting was called by
a sort of Vigilance Committee, which moi
only assumes to act as court for the tria
and punishment Of criminal offences but ac
tually aspires to regulate the entire munich
pal affairs of that region.


1t seems that a man named Child has beer
appointed by Gov. Cummings Probate Judge

rial statutes county to be called Carsor
county. He proceeded in October last to tn,
exercise of his power; called sn election OF

Sheriff one County Recorder, one County

men, and one Justice of the Peace and one
Constable for the several precincts The

But the meeting whose proceedings we are
considering, assumes to say that the Probate
Judge was appointed contrary to the wishes
of majority of the people of Carson's Val
ley, and that, in the matter of regulating the
voting, &c, DC, he did not do the fair thing
The meeting thereupon resolves, that the
people of the different valleys on the East
ern Slope of the Sierra Nevada have no other
body to be governed by but the one Of their
own appointing, and gives due notice to Judge
Child that it will be prudent for him to
withhold from action in attempting to en-
force laws repugnant to a majority of the
citizens. The second resolution reads as fol-
lows;


mat we, the Committee, believing and know

tain this action OF ours to the contrary of all
courts organized under Mormon Statutes"
The next resolve is that if Judge Child at.
tempts to enforce the laws he shall be dealt
with as the Committee sees fit. This gives
the Committee power, we suppose, to hang
or Danish him, at discretion. A Committee
was next appointed and commissioned to go
to the regularly elected Recorder of Carson
county, and demand from him the delivery of
all the records and papers, affecting the citi-
zens of Carson Valley, in order that they
might be put into the possession of some
competent person" for safe keeping, until
some Recorder, who would give satisfaction,
could be elected the person having the re-
cords and papers in charge, to act as Record
er until that time.


The meeting then gave man named Olds,
who was obnoxious to the Committee, one
month in which to make his exit from the
Valley, and after other business, adjourned,
thinking no doubt that they had done won
ders.


A more high. handed course of proceedings
could scarcely have been engaged in under
any civilized government, and, if persisted in
to the end, should enttle the participators to
the summary punishment which is due to
rebels and traitors. Whether there be any
Justice in the complaints made by this meet

larly constituted authorities, wherever there

tered how long will it be before complete
anarchy prevails? If our own American
citizens in Utah will not obey the authority

Territorial officers with what sort of grace
can we talk about putting down the rebel
lious Mormons." and all that? The General
Government has trouble enough with the de-
luded followers of Brigham Young, without
being annoyed by those who are supposed to
be something better than Mormons. The
people of the remotely western portions OF
the United States are becoming altogether
too fond of taking governmt Mt into their own
hands, establishing Vigilance Committees

or the evil will grow to the most formidable
proportions.

At preliminary meeting of the cltl' zens of Des Arc, on Monday Afternoon, committee was appointed to report by preamble and resolutions.

 On yesterday morning at 9 o'clock the citizens again assembled, when the fol- lowing preamble and resolutions were adopted unanimously. They speak for themselves:

 WHEREAS, Des Arc has heretofore been the most quiet, peaceable and orderly town on

 White river or the West, and her citizens had the reputation far and near of being civil, courteous, industrious and moral {; and whereas, recently our quiet condition has been broken by the fierce feuds, strife and quarrel of strangers, and we have heard in every direction, horrid .oaths from the dirty mouths of this basphemous set, and seen the bowie knife and pistol constantly brandished by this set of outlaws, out-casts, frequenters of gambling he'll and fiends incarnate. And

 WHEREAS, We believe that this class, con- sisting of gamblers. and all manner of pu- tridity from the filthy sewers of cities and towns, which have been driven off by the fierce torrent of public opinion and ont ragged decency, from other places, are be- ginning to congregate here, and make this their head quarters, and for the purpose of accomplishing more effectually their dia- bolical purposes, pursuing more successfully their hellsh practices, and converting our Eden into a pandemonium, have imported into our midst lewd women and whereas, also, from what we have seen and learn, we believe there are Abolitionists in our midst, persons unfriendly to the institution of sa- very as we have it, and who are tampering with our slaves, endeavoring to instil into minds evil principles, and whereas, we look upon this class (abolitionists) as thieves, hypocrites, cut-throats, incendia- ries, false to themselves, traitors to their Icountry, hypocrites in religion, and false in feverything and untrue to everything save the devil and his service and as we believe "self- preservation to be ''the first law of nature," and as the exigency of our situa- tion is not such as to permit us to await the tardy and uncertain relief of the law therefore be it resolved:

 1. That all gamblers are hereby notified to leave Des Arc within 24 hours after the ap- pearance of this resolution in print, or they will be dealt with summarily by the vigilance committee

 9. That all lewd women, and women of lll-fame, are nereDy notlned to leave DeS Arc within 24 hours after the appearance of this resolution in print, or they will be summarly dealt with by the vigilance comittee.

 3. That all abolitionists, or persons inimi- cal to the institution of slavery,sor who do not believe that African slavery as it exists among us, is right, and all persons who asso- ciate with, keep company with, and put them selves upon an equality with our slaves. be notified to leave Des Arc within 24 hours after the appearance of this resolution in print, or they will be summarily dealt with by the vigilance committee.

 4. That each and every member of this meeting bind themselves to keep profound secret the actings and doings of the vigilance committee, that we will divulge nothing that is done by the vigilance committee under any circumstances, nor any information commu- nicated to the vigilance committee by any of it's sub-commitiees.

 5. That we hold ourselves in readiness to support the vigilance committee in everything and upon the shortest notice, and we pledge ourselves not only to support the vigilance committee, but to support one another in every thing pertaining to the good of the town.

 6. That the names composing the vigilance committee be published.

article:
l THE IRREPRESSlbLE CUNfLlCI.

 MR. EpIToR. the outbreak at Harper's Ferry, we ought to learn a les son, seeing as we do to what end the "lrre- pressible Conflict" doctrines of Seward and his colaborers are tending. If it be true as asserted by MT. Seward, that there is an "irrepressible conflict" between slave labor and free labor; and as asserted by others of that school, "that slavery can only be exterminated by force," then we may look upon the Harper's Ferry diff culty as only the "beginning of the end" ," We of the South should begin to set our house in order. "In time of peace pre- pare for war;" is maxim not less true than old. The war has been commenced

 the ''irrepressible conflict" is being waged; why stand we here idle Shall we be still till our enemies have compassed us about, bound us hand and foot, and led us captives into the victors camp. God forbid. Seeing as we do, that we are not treated as equals in the Union-that our rights under the Constitution are not respected, and are in danger of having civil war thrust upon us, 1t behooves us to see that all is right l in our midst-and all who do not sympa- thise with us, or who are opposed to the institution of slavery, should be given a reasonable time to leave-and should they fail to do so, within that time, should be treated to Q coat of tar and feathers, and made to leave forcibly. l know this proposition of mine will be objected to by some who are good southerners, because they will say it is contravenng that right which under the Constitution every man has to go from one part of the Union to any other without fear or molestaton. - To such reply, that self.preservation is the first law of nature. And to shield ourselves from danger is the first duty we owe 10 ourselves and the country in which we live. The evidences before us and in our possession, are that every part of the slave states is prosecuted by the agents of the aboltionists. They are among us as ministers of the gospel, school teachers, pedlars, gypsies, drummers, Sc. Strange faces are constantly among us-they ap- pear to have no particular business-are not seen doing any thing-are not heard to inquire after business. They are here but short time and disappear, we know not whence they come or whither they goeth. Strangers have been seen in our town looking around negro houses and kitchens. Strangers have been seen at unusual hours of the night, in the out skirts of the town. To my mind bis is a suspicious circumstance and one that should pu. us upon our guard, and which it seems to me would justify us in taking some steps to ascertain the business of those who are now, and who may come among us, doing nothing and asking no employment, and who are strangers. It is certainly time for us to be up and doing. No halfway measures will do. l recom-

 mend that the citizens of Des Arc hold meeting, that resolutions be passed re- questing all persons inimical to the nssi- tuition of slavery to leave by certain time-,hat vigilance committee be form- ed that the town authorities increase the city police with power in said police to deal summarily with all persons found in suspicious positions, and in such manner as may seem best 10 said police. That the vigilance committee have the same power and be requested to act in concert. |

 Something of this sort should be done, and done soon. It is no time now to be quiet or sing the old song of "materly in- activiiy" Union, glorious Union." The glory of the Union now is in a united South. We have shown our pluck upon battle fields in distant lands-let us show some of the same spirit at home in the protection of our homes, our rights, altars and fresides. Now Is the accepted time the day of preservation is at hand.

Jacques" who writes for the N. Y

midnight pastime in Kansas. Instead ol

State government, it would be far better
to enforce whatever of statutory law there
is, and protect the legal rights of every
man, though he be the vilest criminal thai

is more notoriously unsafe than mob law
nor more unreliable than the mob-spirit
The very men who to-day may extort by
the halter confession of guilt, and hang

vengeance on moral men who attempt tc

the rod of terror, in many localities, which

Criminal Jurisprudence presupposes the
innocence of the accused until proven
guilty, and even requires doubt as to the
guilt of the prisoner to be construed III
his favor. Lynch law metes out its judg-
ment, on suspicion, ex-parte testimony, OIL

The pleas set up that the laws cannot be

termined to enforce them. Government
here has not relapsed into the hands OF
desperadoes similar to those who cursed
California, hence the precedent sought to
be borrowed from the shores of the Pacific
docs not apply.


If Kansas is to retain fame for any
thing noble and just, her citizens should
disown lynch law, be law-abiding, and
prove by their acts that the problem of
Territorial self-government without the
intervention of Congress, has been salts
factorily solved in this Territory.

headline: Death of Senator Broderick.
article:
one of Californas United States Senators, from
a wound received at the hands of Judge Terry,
in duel which took place in small valley
near San Francisco, on Monday morning last
His death occurred 20 minutes alter o'clock
yesterday friday morning.


Mr.. Broderck's seconds were Hon. Jos. c.
McKibben and Gen. D. D. Cotton; the seconds
of Judge Terry were Calhoun Benham and Thos
Hays The distance fought was ten PAGES


The S. F. Times says:


Each held his pistol in his hand, pointed to
the ground. Each was dressed in black clothes,
and wore slouched Palo Alto hat. Mr. Brod-
erick stood erect, but with his head rather down
lie pulled the rim of his hat down about his
eyes, as if to shade them from the light. The
positions OF the two were somewhat different
Judge Terry maintained that of practced
dueliSt, presenting only the edge of his person
to his antagonist, and keeping his left hand and
shoulder well behind him. Mr.. Broderick, on the
contrary, though at first assuming a position
/ somewhat similar 10 that of the other seemed
to prefer more careless and less constrained
one, and gradually presented more of his body
to the fire of his opponent. His pistol he held
in his hand rather awkwardly, and seeming to
!
wrist of his pistol-arm to the right with his left
hand as though endeavoring to comply with
some prescribed directions previously given him.
He took one good look at his antagonist, ran
his eye rapidly along the ground from him to
his own position, as If drawing bee-line be-
tween them. From that time he did not raise
his eyes until the word was given to fire. Once
his right foot got fraction beyond the line
when Mr.. McKibben STEPPED forward and replaced
it


Both men were perfectly cool, and manifested
no uneasiness malicious rumor, character
stcally malignant, and as base as it is possible
to conceive, that Mr.. Broderick was nervous
and lost his presence of mind, is utterly false
Not the slightest shade of trepidation marked
his conduct from first to last. The same cour-
ageous adamantine man he has ever shown him
/ self to be, he was on this occasion We have
given the mnutest details of the bearing of both
gentlemen that no mistake may possibly obtain
| in this respect. The rumor of Mr. Broderick's S
nervousness" is utterly false, and is based up
on his occasional motions to observe those pre-
scribed positions of hand and arm which his Sc
conds had enioned upon him. The bearing of
Judge Terry, though he assumed more prac-
tlced and motionlesS attitude was not one lot
more that of an iron-nerved man than was that
OF Mr. Broderick. AT quarter before seven
o'clock, Mr. Cotton pronounced the words


care you ready ?"


"Ready," responded Judge Terry, and Rea-
dy" was uttered by Mr. Broderick Immediately
after.


Fire One! Two !" pronounced in mod
erately quick time


Mr.. Broderick raised his pistol (botb weapons
were set with hair triggers) and had scarcely
brought it to an angle of forty-fve degrees from
its downward position and in bee line towards
his opponent, when, owing to the delicacy of the
hair trigger, it was discharged the ball entering
the ground about four PAGES in advance of him.
Judge Terry fred few instants later taking
deliberate aim. There was a perceptible inter-
val in the two reports. At that instant Mr..
Broderick was observed to clap his left hand to
the right side of his breast when it was seen
that he wounded He reeled slowly to the
left, and before his seconds could reach him, he
fell mot heavily to the ground, with his right
leg doubled under him, and still grasping his
weapon. Judge Terry, upon discharging his
pistol, Immediately folded his arms, holding the
pistol still smoking in his hand, but did not
move from his position.


The circumstance of Mr. Broderick's losing his
shot is accounted for in the fact that the choice
OF weapons fell to Judge Terry, who selected his
own dueiling pistols. These have the hair trig-
ger so senstivey set that sudden jerk of the
weapon would serve to cause its discharge Mr.





pons, and by the slightest touch of his finger
produced the discharge. A similar cause pro-
duced the accident which occurred to Henry
Clay in his famous duel with John Randolph.


The challenge came from Judge Terry. The
occasion for the challenge is this: Before the
last Democratic State Convention Judge Terry
made a speech in which he spoke of the Anti
Lecomptonites as the followers OF one man, the
personal chattels of a single individual, whom
they are ashamed of. They belong, heart, SOUL
body and breeches, to David c. Broderck They
yet ashamed to acknowledge their master
and are calling themselves, aye, forsooth, Doug
las Democrats. Perhaps
they do sail under the flag Of Douglas, but it is
the banner of the black Douglas, whose name is
Frederick, not Stephen"


Mr.. Broderick had read this, and, says the
Sacramento Bee, while at breakfast one morn
ing, at the International Hotel, San Francisco,
entered into conversation with those near him
on the subject, and stated that he had once ex-
pressed the opinion that " Judge Terry was the
only upright man upon the Supreme Bench, but
he believed he would now have to take that
back"


Some further remarks were made, and Brod-
erick in the heat of the moment, expressed his
sorrow that the Vigilance Committee did not
hang Terry when it had him in custody.


The receipt of the sad intelligence that the
soul of Mr.. Broderick had passed away from
earth, occasioned universal regret in this COM
nunty. His bitterest political opponents ex-
press sorrow at his violent and untimely death


We learn by private telegraph from Gen. Col
ton, that Mr. Broderick's funeral will take place
on Monday next.

EDITOR TRUE DEMOCRAT

 From facts recently brought to light in this community, there can be no doubt that Arkansas river was embraced, as a part of the general plan, in the Harper's Ferry in surrection. Several negroes were seized and vigorously examined, under circum- stances which precluded the possibility of communication; and so strongly did their statements corroborate each other, that most of our citizens were sufficiently arous- ed to form themselves into vigilance com mittee, for the protection of life and pro- perty.

 Their plan seems 10 have been as fol- lows: The free negroes that have just left our county, were to encamp, one part in southern Kansas, the other in western Texas; and i'll these localities wait for the slaves The latter, meanwhile, were to have every thing ready for insurrection, and in a certain night in March next, as one of the negroes said, but many think much earller, our town was to be set on fire, our citizens to-, be slaughtered, and such arms, ammunition and property were to be seized on III 5 Tt Dc uccllcu HtccSSalN, ana then Tn two divisions they were to join the free ne- groes Tn Kansas and Texas, and thus make thelr way, one part to New Mexico, the other 10 Indiana or Illinois. Whatever may be thought of the wisdom of this ar. engagement, or the possibility of it's execu- ton, one thing, we think, is tQlerabIv certain; 1t was never originated by negroes. Several iiHle circumstances, which we deem It improper to mention, taken in connection with negro testimony, go to establish, at least strong presumption, that some half dozen white men right here in our midst, are deeply implicated in this ugly affair." Their names, with other important parti cnlars, we at present, for good reasons, withhold. Should future developments. however, establish the .tact of their oom plicity, it might be prudent for these gen tlemen to look around for other and more comfortable quarters.
