headline: Molony and the Vigilance Committee.
article:
The New York Times, of April 5th has
the followingin reference to the case Of Mo-
lony VS.. Dows, arising out of the expulsion of
Molony from San Francisco by the Vigilance
Committee, of which the defendant was a
member. The Judge of the Court in which
the case was tried decided that he had no
iursnction:


The case of Molony VS. Dows, which has
been in progress here for some days, sud
denly terminated yesterday by its being flung
out of Court-virtually another case of ex-
pulsion. The ground for this was want of
jurisdiction.


1t will be seen by card published else
where from Molony, that he has determined
to appeal from this decision and carry it to
another Court.


1t is no part of our duty to advise in this
matter, though were we called upon to do
SO we should recommend him to cry quits
and let the matter rest.


The whole difficulty grew out of state
of affairs which are not likely to occur soon,
if ever again, and whatever might have been
his particular case, or the acts of the Vigil
ance Committee toward him, he probably
will not deny that the action toward many
of those with whom he was at the time as
sociated, was just. Such, at least, is the
judgment of the world, and whether such
conclusion is arrived at through a want Of
information, the force of prejudice or some
thing else, that judgment stands, and is not
likely to be reversed by any Court in the
country. Hence it is that we suggest to Mr..
Molony to let the subject rest, to save his
time and money, forget the wrongs he fan
cies have been done to him, and by course
of life, the propriety of which cannot be
questioned, convince the world that he is,
what he meant to prove himself before our
courts, to be, worthy and good citizen.
This will be to him a higher and a safer rec
ord than any which could be awarded him
by any Court of law, and if prejudice wrong
fully exist it is the true way to dissipate it.

We were visited on yesterday by Gen. G. D
Mitchell. Agent for the the above named institu
ton. Gen. Mitchell informs us that the Coleg,
has opened its fourth session under more favora
bic auspices and with larger number of students
than ever before. The Institution is under thu
Presidency of the Rev. DR.. Thomas II. Capers
nephew of the late Bishop Capers, of South Caro-
lima, assisted by Rev. DR.. D. F. Capers, brother
of the late Bishop Capers, as Vice President
The Mathematical Department is in charge o
Professor j I. Hicks, graduate of Chapel Hill
North Carolina and unsurpassed in his depart
ment by any professor of Mathematics in thu
South. The Musical Department is under tn,
charge of Dr. Elwig, Of Germany, one of the bes
educated and thorough musicians in the Unite,
States, aided by competent assistants


The Institution is entirely Southern in its charac
ter-located in the north east corner of Claiborne
county, Miss, in one of the most healthy regions
Of the State-in the midst of an intelligent ant
wealthy population-away from all towns, ant
exempt from the usual temptations to extrava
ganee, folly and fashion.


1t has the largest and finest apparatus for the
illustration of Astronomy, Chemistry, Botany
Physiology and History, with the largest and
finest Telescope Of any Female Institution in the
United States.


The object of Gen, Mitchclrs agency is to col.
lect females sufficient to enlarge the Buildings &C
as to accommodate three hundred and fifty
students, instead Of one hundred, as at present
and to furnish the institution with q complete
library, sc.


Gen. Mitchell assures us, that having been d
teacher himself for twenty years, and having thor
Oughly examined the rules regulations and dici-
pline of the Southern Female College, he can,
with perfect confidence, recommend it to the
Southern people as worthy of their patronage,
and its faculty unequdlcd by any female institu-
ton in the United States.


Gen. Mitchell will remain in tfis city for few
days, and cnll upon our citizens in whose liberal
ty he has entire confidence 10 solicit donations
for the objects above stated. THE cause of edu-
cation, and especially of female education in the
South, should meet with encouragement at the
hands of all true southern men, and we know of
no opportunity more appropriate for its exhibi
ton than by subscribing in aid Of the Southern
Female College.

him there to die. That ravine, should be
the bed of his glory.


But gathering around him, a guard Of
breasts and steel-while two of their
lumber bore him tenderly along-those
men of Kentucky fought round their fall
en- hero, and as retreatiLg step by step,
hey launched their swords and bayonets
nto the faces of the foe, they said with
every blow-"HENRY Clay


1t was wonderful to see how that name
lerved their arms, and called smile to
.he face of the dying hero. How it
would have made the heart of the old
man at Ashland throb, to have heard his
name yelling as battle cry, down the
shadows of that lonly pass


Along the ravine, and up this lonely
path! The hero bleeds as they bear him
on and tracks the way with his blood
Faster and thicker the Mexicans swarm
they see the circle around the fallen
man, even see his pale face, uplifted as a
smile crosses its fading lineaments, and
Ikea pack of wolves scenting the frozen
traveller at dead of night, they come
howIng up the rocks, and charge the
devoied band with one dense mass of bay
onets


Up and on. The light shines yonder,
on tne topmost rocks of the ravine. 1t is
the light of the setting sun. Old Taylor's
eye is upon that rock, and there we will
fight pur way, and die in the old mans
sight.


1t Was murderous way, that path up
the step bank of the ravine! Uttered
with lead, slippery with blood, it grew
black tr every moment with swarming
Mexitans, and the defenders of the
wouDled heto, fell one by one, into the
chasn yawning all around.


A last they reach the light, the swords
and bayonets glitter in sight of the con-
tending armies, and the bloody contest
-oars towards the topmost rock.


Then 1t was, that gathering up his dy-
ing frame-armed with supernatural Wig
or-young Clay started from the arms of
his supporters, and stood with outstretch-
ed hand, in the light of the setting sun.
1t was glorious sight he saw there,
amid the rolling battle clouds; Santa An
mas formidable array hurled back into the
ravine and gorge. by Taylor's little band.


But more glorious thing it was to see
that dying man, standing for the last time,
in the light of that sun, which never
shall rise for him again!


"Leave me-. he shrieked as he fell back
on the sod-"I must die and 1 will die
here. Peril your lives no longer for me!
Go! There is work for you yonder.'
The Mcxicano crowding. on hungry for
blood. Even as he spoke, their bayonets,
by hundreds, We're levelled at the throats
of the devoted band. BY the mere force
/ of their overwhelming numbers, they
crushed them back from the side Of the
dying Clay.


| One only fingered; a brave man who
had known the brave and chivalric Sol
der, and loved him long; he stood there,
and covered as he was with blood, heard
these last words:


"7'eH myJatAer hoao I died, and gire
linn these Pistols"


F. Lifting his ashy face into the light, he
turned his eyes, upon his comrades face
placed the pistols in his hand-and fell
back to his death.


That Comrade, with the pistols in his
grasp, fought his way alone to the top
most rock of the path, and only once look
ed back. He saw quivering form, can
opied by bayonets--he saw those out
stretch hands graphing with points of
steel--he saw pale face lifted once in
the light, and then darkness, rushed upon
the life of young HENRY CLAY.

headline: THE DEMOCRACY ORGANIZING.
article:
On Wednesday night last, as will be seen by the
proceedings below, the Democrats Of this City had
a rousing and enthusiastic Meeting. A Cass and
Butler Club was organized and interesting speeches
were delivered by Messrs McRae, Bledsoe, Hover
ton, of Halifax, Va, and Busbee. We can assure
friends at distance that the right spirit is at
work here at the centre-every Democrat in Wake
County is determined to do his whole duty. We
hope Cass and Butler Clubs will be formed in every
Captains District in the State 1t is only by organ
zation, by meeting the Federaeaders boldly and ex
posing their demagogueism and misrepresentation,
and by laying principles clearly before the peo
pie, that we can hope to triumph. Let do this,
and victory must and will crown our banner. -
.:.-... CASS AND BUTLER CLUB. -ez-reI


The Democracy of this city assembled in the Court
House, after few hours notice, on the evening of


Duncan K. McRae, Esq, was called to the Chair,
who, in few well-timed remarks, explained the OBJ
ject of the Meeting. ...r-.
: On motion of W. w. Holden, ESQ.,. a committee
of three, consisting of Messrs. Perrin Busbee James
T. Marriott and w. w. Holden, was appointed by
the Chairman to reports Constitution and ByeLaws,
for the government of the Club who retired for that
purpose. ,.'.. saw


In the absence of the Committee, a call was made
for Moses A. Bledsoe, ESQ.,, who received with
rapturous applause. He was Unexpectedly called
upon, did he appear there to take active part





would say, however, that heretofore he had been
actor in the Whig ranks-he confessed it; but,
where was that party at this time1 They had for
saken their standard, thrown away their principles,
and running after Gen. aylor, the no-party,
no-prnciple candidate They had principles to
contend for-the Democrats did, and therefore, he
poused the cause of Cass and Butler, whose princi
Piles he admired and upon whose success the happi-
ness of our country depended Mr.. Bledsoe took his
seat amid thunders of applause.


VIM. M. Howerton, Esq, of Halifax, Va, being
present, was called for. He came forward, and in
strain of eoquence-facts and arguments, he enter
tanned the Club in speech of thirty minutes. He
handled the Taylorites with govesso sof"-he dealt
very tenderly with General Fillmore, reserving the
1" fun for the 9TH of November. He brought gori-
news from the Old Dominion all was right there
she had always stood by the Democracy of North
Carolina-had never forsaken them, and neUer aUOuH
forsake them. And, the day of election, the De-
mocracy of Virginia would not be found hesitating,
whether to vote for Taylor Cass, but they would
be found hesitating whether they will give Cass and
Butler IO,or 10000 majority! (Great applause.)


The Committee then made the following report
through Mr.. Holden:


This Club is organized for the purpose of advanc-
ing democratic principles, and the members Of it
pledge themselves to all fair and honorable
to promote the election of Cass and Butler.


The Officers of this Club shall be President, two
Vice Presidents, Corresponding Secretary, Re-
cording Secretary, and Treasurer.


In the absence of the President one of the Vice
Presidents shall call the members to order and pre-
side.

ty and Vigilance, Committee Documents and
useful publications, and Committee of Reception
and Arrangements.

Vigilance to guard the Democratic generally
to defend it and its champions against all unjust and
false charges, and to devote themselves, especially

Democratic vote.

information.

at the National Theater, on the night of

headline: Gen. Denver to Brigham Ye-ns.
article:
Gen. Denver, Commissioner of Indian Affairs,
has written letter to Brigham Young, in reply
to one from that functionary in which he exco-
rates that old villain for the improper manner
of his administration of Indian superintendency
in Utah. He tells Brigham Young that he has
exceeded the appropriations for him by more
than S3l 900, and that he has no reason to COM
plain of his drafts not being paid. Gen. Denver
adds:


so far from encouraging amicable relations,
you have studiously endeavored to impress upon
the minds of the Indians that the Mormons are
their friends, and the people of the States are
their enemies"


The rule is to withhold annuites from hostile
Indians, and Gen. D. knows no reason why it
should not be applied to Young
In reply to Young's objection to the presence
of troops, Gen. Denver says:


If it is your intention to preserve peace the
troops will not interfere with you but if you
intend otherwise, then it is necessary that the
troops should be on the ground to enforce it,"


He tells Brigham that his claim for double
salary is against law but that if it shall be as
certaincd that his expenditures were properly
made, he will be paid should Congress make an
appropriation for that purpose.


He concludes by saying that the Executive
has no alternative but to crush out rebellion,
and that for that purpose all the powers ofAthe
government are placed under his control


After reading the letter of the Indian Com
missioner, Brigham will doubtless feel like the
individual of old, who went out after wool and
came back shorn.

ostensbly in discussing the provisions of Mr..
Lees Bill, for the suppression of mobs, in
surrections etc, but in reality in reviewing
the acts of the Vigilance Committee and in
resurrecting the unpleasant "reminiscences
connected Herewith. There seems to be
an anxiety on the part Of members to set
themselves right on the record, either for or
against Vigilantism, which savors more of
buncombe than any other quality. If Lees

rakng up the unfortunate acts of the past,

ready9 But If the laws at present upon our
statutes, are strang enough, if enforced, to

If this wide and useless discussion could

tee, and remove the vivid and bitter recollec-

headline: From an Occasional Correspondent.
article:
Editor Herald:-The anniversary of our
national independence has come and gone
the noisy squbs and crackers of patriotic
Young America have subsidized into silence
dullness has resumed its reign in San Fran
cisco, and aching heads and real pain, are
all that remain to testify to the spiritually in
cined, that the 4th was not all dream
And yet it was considerable of sham, our
City Fathers to their shame be it said "Carv-
ed not bone, raised not dime" In honor
of the day, "But left it alone in its glory"


The Old Guard fired the usual salute, and
the Monumental Engine Company spread
collation. in the engine house, to which the
Maryland boys did ample justice, and there
after followed sundry speeches and patriotic
sentiments. Sundry individuals celebrated
on their own hook, but the City Fathers,
like Frazer river, did not show the color; and
like it all men pronounce them bumbug.


Your county, learn has been sadly de-
pleted by the Northern exodus. think this
folly has reached its height, and many who
are now here, will bless what they considered
their i'll luck, in not being able to get off.
Nearly 10000 people have left our shores
for this modern Utopia, and now wait not
for the troubling, but for the falling of the
waters; while hard fare, exposure, and fabu-
fous prices for the common necessaries, are
wasting their health and strength and ex-
hausting their means They will come back,
if they ever do come back, like famished
wolves, and if they wreaked their vengeance
upon those who have deceived them, land
some think that the Pacific Mail Steamship
Co. are not as innocent as babies in this mat
tpr,) it would be righteous retaliation upon
the authors of yet untold misery.


We have had exceedingly cold weather,
and there is not blood enough circulating in
our city to keep the body polite warm. The
harvest is pretty much over-Alamda has
cut its barley, and there will be no lack of
malt liquor if the brewers get hold Of it, A
plentiful crop of smut has rewarded the
labors Of the husbandmen in the upper val
ley of the Sacramento; but Napa, beautiful
Napa, reigns in her golden fields, where
whea: from $4,000 acres, averages from 25
to 80 bushels to the acre. Come back, We
gold hunters. and cultivate the soil, it will
yield more than the twelve feet square { just
big enough for burial lot,) given you bv
the British Fur Company, at the bottom of
Frazer river.


In the way Of politics there is not much
doing. Douglas stock is not quoted on
change, and the Bears have it all their own
way. l noticed in montgomery street the
other day, another man who was a candi-
date for the Presidency. l forget his name,
but it wasn't Fillmore nor Buchanan, but
remember he parted his hair in the middle.


Shall we have a war with England is the
question? | think not-there will be much
ink split, and fine spun negotiations. till the
original issue is forgotten. Louis Napoleon
has nearly half million of soldiers who
grow impatient for action. They are ready
to pounce upon "Perfidious Albion" bu. that
the latter power shrewdIy gets up show of
fight with US, and diverts the Gallic Eagle
to this new scene. while in the mean time,
Europe SINNERS over the fires of revelation,
and something may turn up and develop
a new plan Of operations. But should we
have war, how defenseless is our city. Some
80 men at the Presidio, at Fort Point all
silent is the half finished work-and a forty
gun trigate would have rare sport in sending
hot shot into our wooden city


BY the news from China, you will see
that the Celestials refuse to treat, and the
Four Powers refuse to retreat, so we shall
have more fighting, and more blood of the
Fowry Empire.


We wait anxiously for the news by the
next steamer Of the announcement of the
Vigilance Committee of New Orleans, and
the inception of one at New York The
latter would make glorious scattering of
rasca's VIATOR.

meaner rounds of cunning arti6ce. Many
a man with abilities below dull medioc-
rity, has managed in few years to ac-
eumulate decent modicum of political
reputation, by adroitly addressing him.
self to the prejudices of mankind. Per
haps some of those gentlemen who have
been amusing the ladies on "crowded
galleries" for the past fortnight in the
House at Sacramento, are trailing on this
scent. If so, what mistake! The
hound that mistook the skunk trail for
fox's, was not more sadly disappointed
than they will be. The prejudices of the
people run in another direction; and if
these eloquent representatives had taken
half the pains to study the sense of their
constituents that they exhausted in the
preparation of their phillipics, they would
have run longer and treed nobler game
than their present wild route will lead
them to. We speak this in all kindness
for the time has passed when it is either
wise or profitable to measure an adversary
with violence, in this argument.


Whilst the people of America are as
strong in their attachment to their Consti-
tutions and laws as any people upon the
earth; slow to move towards the violation
or suspension of either, whether in spirit
or letter, they are as radical as the Giron-
dins in their Interpretation of liberty,
and their right to rise superior to all law,
when an extraordinary emergency de-
mands it for the good of the whole
And we do not indite this as an apology
for anv miserable band of wretches, who,
urged on by blood-thirsty nature, be-
come their own judges, jurors and exc
cutioners, merely because the weak and
defenceless are their victims. Not at all
but because the history of the nation
the history of the race proves it. We
need not refer to particulars; but. we
would humbly suggest to Legislators who
may be little wrong now and then, as
well as other men, in their ideas upon
government, the perusal of that part Of
English history which dates from the be-
ginning of Charles /, to the Protectorate
and, also, that portion of our own which
begins with the destruction of cargo of
tea in Boston harbor and ends at York
town. If the perusal results in no other
good, it may at least serve to convince
them that the Anglo Saxon race, however
humbly they may bear with abuse and
tyranny, when the eliminating point is
reached, well know where the real soyer-
eighty lies. 1t is to this bold character
istic of the race that the English of to-day
are indebted for their Bill of Rights -

ceeded the calm. Last week all was
bright, genial and sunlight; this week all
is gloomy, forbidding and dismal-only,
however, by way of antithesis-for the
stormy weather that makes us wear oul

our slouch hat and cotton umbrella, is just
the sort of thing we want to set the coun-
try going California is like clock,

order, it does not keep time.


Half of Sacramento is afoat-that is

The new experimental macadamization is
rather creamy, the houses are little more
discolored by the rain than usual, and
more coal is used for domestic purposes
but there is just about the same steady
amount of business doing. The Courts
are in session, which, with other matters,
mentioned or implied, tend to enliven ou1
city at the present moment, with much OF
briskness of appearance, in spite of dis
NAL atmospheric influences.


The one absorbing topics of this week,
has been the Insurrection Act, or "Mob
Bill" Debates, loud and long, have ia
ken place on the subject in the legisla-
ture, that, as specimens of oratory, would
have done honor to the efforts of MANY
Cambyses or Demosthenes. Day and
night has the torrent of eloquence been
poured out in session, with vigor and
tenacity of purpose, that shows this great
question to be one of position-just kind
of stand-up fight for the sake of bump
tiousness and dogmatism. Such are the
kind of men we want-well led and di-
rected-men who now are consuming the
peoples money for nothing. The same
amount of money that is now being con-
sumed in daily pay of members, on this
question, laid out in a better cause, in
direct appliance, would have made one
half of the people of the State joyful,
and the country would have been just as
safe as it is likely to be under the stu
pendous idea of arming the Executive
with tyrannical powers, to govern peo-
pie, ever willing, in the mass, to do right,
and to aid and see that it is done.


Amongst other lodges that pro parties

The city is full of questionable char
acters. Manifestations of violence, con-
nected with the subjectof Vigilance, have
more than once exhibited themselves
Have we the seeds of disorganization

Calmer reason and right principles, tenn
pered with moderation will prevail. 1t is
allowed that this vexing bill, so uncalled
for, will not pass, or if so, it will never
be carried out to affect the community
The ordinary powers of the law are known
to be sufficient If this law pass, we
must erect Heidelberg or Bastile, to
complete its spirit to the letter, and adopt
a passport system. We shall be worse
than the worst of Autocracies of Europe


The Archey" slave case has attracted

1t is thought to be at once an interpreta-

ence to its Constitutionality, and a contra

Terry's conclusions are considered the

There has been a little squabbling about
the incorrectness of reported Legislative
speeches in the newspapers. Members,
it is asserted, are made to say things 9TH
erwise than as spoken. 1t is, we think,
merely a question of small potatoes, in
volving difference between tweedle dunn
and tweedle dee The scene enjoined,
believe is admitted to be rendered with
general accuracy: Fancy phrases. to catch
the imagination and dazzle the under
standing, when transposed into common
sense, or ill-constructed sentences, well
enough, perhaps, if spoken with proper
emphasis, do not, generally speaking, ap-
pear so graceful to the judgment of their
author, when arranged by others in a
business-like way, on paper. That naught
can be charged against the fairness of
newspaper reporters, in wilfully misrep-
resenting, is the universal opinion.

Since the decision of the Supreme Court re-

II. Stovall, he has been kept at Stockton. He
was taken to Oakland last Thursday night, and
on Friday conveyed to Angel Island, for the
purpose of placing him on board the steamer
Orizaba, which sailed for Panama that day.
The steamer neared the island about ono o'clock
and Archy, by means of a boat which contain
ed Stovall and two or three OF his friends. was
placed on board. The colored people of San
Francisco, however, had taken efficient measure
to prevent Arohy from being taken off, They
had procured a writ Of habeas corpus from

steamer previous TO her leaving the wharf. AS

party got into a boat and went on Shore

manded by him to the county Jail, until Monday

thronged around the Court house in great num-

scheme knew no bounds. At last accounts, the
darkies were having their own way at the Bay
and there was some talk of their getting up
vigilance committee to dispense justice, &c,
cording to their ideas.

 'We will furnish the True Democrat year to any mechanic, or other person, who will fur nish the outlines of the plan of such building for publication"

 If some poor architect, who thirsteth after knowledge don't take up with that magnani- nous offer, he's green, that's all. Just think of the pleasure and profit to be derived from reading the Democrat whole year, and all for little job of work worth only obout fifty dol lars,

 Now we increase our proposition. We add, that, if the person furnishing such plan will signify it as his wish, we will also furnish him with a copy of the Ouachta Herald for one year. We assert that no man can carefully read the two papers for a year without becom- ing generally informed, and it is surely worth fifty dollars to become a man of general infor- nation. The Herald will see what an oppor- tunity is offered us of writing about the bane, Chat is, the Herald and the antidote (the True Democrat going together, but we will not write it and hope our forbearance will be noted and appreciated.

The hanging of young man in Noble coun- tv, Indiana, few q TVS since by virtue of the authority of body of regulators, was terrible aff,r. The cause of the excitement, which resulted in the assem- blaze of so formidable oody of citizens, to un- lawfully take the life of a man, Is thus given by a correspondent of the Indianapolis Journal

 s'For several years there has been a regularly organized band of horse thieves, blacklegs, coun- tereiters and murderers, whose range extended from Chicago to Toledo. The swamps and oak barrens of Noble and adjacent counties have been their head quarters and pricpal hiding places. At last their numbers became 50 great, and their villanous deeds so bold and daring, that it was unsafe for a stranger, or any one who 1t was supposed to have money, to pass along the public highways with any degree of safety Within the last few months there have been several highway robberies and attempts to con- init murder. At length the better portion of the citizens in Noble and adjoining counties or ganized themselves into vigilance committees, horse companies. etc, to See if they could not ferret out some of the leaders,

 Recently the regulators caught counterfeit CT, who had on hand heavy assortment of bo- gus coin. He was hanged until he confessed

 

 nected. He was then put in jail, and arrests made, some twety-tive persons being taken in custody, and lodged in the iails of Noble, La Grange and De Kalb counties. One of the leaders of the scoundres was taken before the executive committee of the regulators, and sen fenced to die. He had many aliases, but was best known by the name of Gregory McDougal. | He was twenty-seven years old, Canadian by | birth and leaves wife and child. The corres- pondent Of the Journal says:

 After the verdict of the regulators about five hundred horsemen from his and adjoining counties formed procession, with their prisoner in d wagon in the lead slowly and solemnly to the place of execution, romantic spot about five miles out from Ligner near small lake, The procession arrived at the selected spot about three o'clock, and after some preliminary ar rangementS the wagOn-contauing the prisoner and his cotfin-was driven under an oak tree, from a branch of which the fatal rope dangled.  A Rev. Mr. Wirt' made feeling prayer" the prisoner made speech, little thought he would ever cong to this," hoped the Lord would have mercy on his soul" and was strung up and hung until dead. The correspondent we quote says:

 About fifteen hundred horSemen from all over the country, were in town yesterday, and about five hundred went out to the place of execution to-day, and formed circle around the wagon. article:
Law and Order.


A bill was passed in the Assembly on Friday
last. authorizing the Board Of Examiners to
audit and allow the claims of the volunteers
called out by order Of Governor johnson, in
1856, to suppress the insurreetion in San Fran
cisco. The sum Of fifty thousand dollars is ap-
propr lated for The payment of the claims. The
Republican members from San Francisco op-
posed the bill. Their opposition was expected;
one Of the principal planks in the platform Of
that party in this State has been to approve
the acts of the San Francisco vigilance commit
tee. They have always contended that the tur-
bulent Inhabitants have right to rebel against
the government and set the laws ct defiance,
and that the calling cut Of troops to suppress
insurrsction, in accordance with the plain pro-
visions Of law, is an assumption Of power on
the part Of the Executive. Fer this reason they
object to paying the volunteers, who answered
to the call Of the Governor and enrolled them
selves to suppress the insurrection in San Fran
cisco.


A number of Democrats in the Assembly also
objected to the bill, on the ground that the
Board of Examiners ID net the proper body to
audit the claims. They centended that the ac-
counts should be submitted to the committee on
claims and be audited and allowed by the Leg
islaturs. This position is doubtless correct,
and the fact that the proper form Of allowing
the accounts was disregardsd induced number
of Democrats to vote against the bill. We re-
gard il, however, as Of little consequence what
particular form Is adopted in settling the claims.
The volunteers should be paid for the time they
were actually in the service Of the State, and
we have NO doubt the Board Of Examiners will
take good care that unjust claims are net al
lowed. Let the Senate pass the bill, not only
Is an act Of justice 10 volunteers, but as an ex-
ample for what may be expected Ia future. Wig
ilantes will then think twice before they attempt
again to set the laws ct defiance and should
occasion ever again require, there will be no
lack Of volunteers to answer the call Of the Ex-
eoutive for the suppression Of mobs and insur-
rections,


We well remember when vigilanceism was at
its height, and the Governor was endeavoring
to enlist volunteers to suppress the rebellion,
that every vigilance paper In the state was
warning people against enrolling themselves
with tho volunteers; telling them that they
would never even be thanked for their services.
These representations no doubt had their effect,
and the few whe turned out in obedience to
the call Of the Governor, did so more for the
purpose Of maintaining the supremacy Of the
laws than from any expectation OF being re-
warded for their services. Their services II is
true were of no avail, but that was not their
fault nor is 1t any reason that they should not
be paid what is justly due them. Let the Leg
islature recognize the justice Of the claim and
precedent will be set which cannot fail TO
have beneficial effect in preventing mob vio-
lence and instructions hereafter; while the law
as It stands on our statute book will be equiva-
lent to o seal OF condemnation placed by the
people Of the State upon the proceedings which
occasionsd its enactment.

prevent the numerous depredations commit

hotels, and obtaining their liquors by force.

Committee. Should the present state of
things be quietly submitted to by our citi-
zens, we will soon have reputation abroad
that will do discredit to the fair name our
quiet cities have already earned. Something
must be done. VANoNDALE.

wont aforetime to emphasize still more
ponderous sentences of denunciation

the most chivalrous manner strikes a
very peaceablc reporter while attending
to his business and utterly unprepared
for the assault. This occurrence hap
pened in the Assembly hall on. Saturday
morning last, and a more wanton and
cowardly assault never disgraced the
Legislative halls of the State. The
cause of the dartardly act is alleged to
be as follows: ALLIGATOR" Stakes and

Friday last in expounding the character

bly,. Mr.. Sumner, employed by the

war-of words only-between these two
bellicose individuals. At the culminat-
ing point in the twitting match, Mr.. Lee

gator" and sung out that Horse" was
armed. The reporter said Lee "neruous-
ty' calculated the announcement
Whereupon, on the following morning.
Mr.. Lee inquired of Mr.. Sumner if he

dividual who never gets nervous struck
the reporter severe blow in the face.


We have carefully studied the mean

porter, and are bound to believe there
were other inducements for blows than
the word in question. We are led to
this belief by the assurance of gentle
men who know Mr.. Lee that he re-
ally has a little sense and discretion.
To say Mr.. Lee is so nervous as to be
put out of sorts at the bare mention of
nervousness, is an imputation that Mr..
Lee will not stand. 1t will drive him to
more blows. The probability is, Mr..
Lees little sense and discretion taught

porter, amiable withal, and unarmed,

himself the pink of chivalry; and,
like Mr.. Brooks, perhaps, the fellow
thought go days at $40 day having
expired) he could wAale Sumner over

be sent to Congress- consummation

headline: Trial of Marion Whithurst.
article:
The San Francisco correspondent of the
Sacramento Union says of this case, that the
testimony was brought to close on Tuesday
evening, before Judg Hager, in the Fourth
District Court.


At the conclusion of the evidence, Mr.
Thomas, District Attorney of Placer county,
addressed the jury on the part of the people,
stating the several grades homicide is classi-
fed by our statute. He reviewed the facts
disclosed by the evidence, and charged on the
prisoner the commission Of a cowardly, ma
lignant, diabolical murder. He disclaimed
any feeling on his part towards the prisoner,
and would be satisfied with whatever verdict
the jury would render. He said the people
of Placer county were anxiously looking for
the result of this trial. and it was for them
to say whether Vigilance Committees and
mob laws would be justfiable, and it be made
necessary to cast the statutes into the fire by
allowing prisoners to go unpunished. He
was very severe in his denuncations of the
prisoner and some of the witnesses for the
defense. Mr.. Thomas was followed by Mr..
Mills in behalf of the prisoner He referred
to the serious responsibility the jury were
called upon to meet and the fact that the
existence of human being depended upon
the issue. He called attention to fact
which might be considered strange-that
the prisoner and his counsel should have
selected San Francisco as place for his
trial. 1t was known this city had been con-
vulsed by revolution, recently, and it was
reasonable to suppose the greatest prejudice
would exist against, and the least favor
would be shown the prisoner. The reason
was, because he trusted TO the justice Of his
cause, and did not fear to entrust his fate to
the honesty and conscience of a jury in San
Francisco. He reviewed the testimony, and
contended the evidence showed the prisoner
to be guitless of the otfense charged against
him, and that the jury,if free from prejudice,
as he was satisfied they were, would render
a verdict of acquittal. Mr.. Latham occu-
cupied the attention of the jury this morning
in a brilliant speech for the defence, and was
followed by Mr.. Nunes, in an argumentative
address for the prosecution. :.

menced yesterday at noon, was kept up all the

we puOllSncd sOmetnln6 or the tragedy referred to below, yesterday but further and interesting particulars are here given, and, as moral that ought to be needed everywhere is in volved in it, we publish the following account of the transaction from the Abbeville (Parish of Vermilion) Me- radaonaI of the 25th ut. The three persons charged with killing Lebleu, it has already been stated, were taken to Opelousas by a change of venue granted by the District Court of Cal casieu Parish, and the next day after their arrival were set a liberty--we presume by competent authority:

 Bloody Tragedy- Tardy but Retrlbutive Justice.-A great crim- inal offender, Paulin c. Lebleu--the cold blooded murderer of Ewing and Parsons--the cold-hearted wife se- ducer and kidnapper-the lawless des , perado of the parish of Calcasieu, who once dared and did force his own ne- gro slave to sit on the bench of the District Court of that parish during Court time, and in derision of the pre- siding Judge-has at last met with that fate he so richly deserved. As to the particulars of his death, we are indebted to the politeness of S. Bel den, Esq, who has just returned from the Court of that parish /; and we here give them as communicated to us by that gentleman.

 On Monday, the 18th instant, the District Court commenced its regular session at Lake Charles, the seat of Justice in the parish of Calcasieu.-- Everything about town indicated that deep under current was at work for some purpose unknown to strangers :; for the Western wing of the hotel dis played in fine order and good keeping many double barreled guns, pistols, and bowie knives. Like implements of warfare were also conspicuously visible in the Courtroom. Things remained in that state until Wednes- day morning, at which time Paulin c. Lebleu, coming in from the country, rode up to the rack of the hotel, descended from his mule, and started towards the house with a pair of heavy dragoon pistols across his left arm, besides a repeater and bowie knife in his belt. He had almost reached the steps of the west wing of the hotel, when he was shot from the front of the very same steps, four different times, by man named Eugene Foux and several others, who all had been the victims of tho lust and other de- pravities of Lebleu. Each discharge was deadly. His right arm was aw- fully mangled four buck shot pene- trated through his neck, one through his right breast, one through the lower part of his abdomen, and the balance -as he turned at the first fre-took effect in this shoulders and back. It appears that he received from thirty five to forty buck shot through the most vital portions of his person.

 Lebleu expired almost instantly.- And thus closed the life of one whose earthly career has been stained with blood and ruin, all of which could have been prevented, if those intrusted with the administration of justice in that parish had only performed their duty fearlessly and regardless of conse- quences. We are told that from his early manhood Lebleu prided himself in the violation of the laws of his country in the most outrageous man. ner, and that none ever dared to ar rest him for doing so. Probably some immaculate officials will look upon this assertion as libelous but we care not. And we say boldly, although with re- gret, that whenever criminals are per mitted to escape, either through the leniency of the juries, technical defects in the indictments, absence of the wit nesses, and many other means-then let popular justice be done.

The following particulars were brought by

The people of San LUIS, Opispo county,
are just now in q state Of great excitement,
owing to the discovery among them Of regu
larly organized banditti. who for several years
past have been engaged In assassination and
robbing whomsoever they suspected Of having
money or valuables that could be stolen
The massacre Of two Frenchmen, Messrs
Barate and Borel, on the San Juan Capis-
trano ranch, forty-iive miles from San Luis.
ON the 10Th of May, aroused the people of
the county, who organized themselves into a
Vigilance Committee, and set about detect
ing the assassins. -Four Of them were caught,
and summarily executed at different places.
They were al native California Spanard>,
who, in that part of the State, seem to think
it no sin to wage a kind of private war of
rohho~,- al raf;nr - IT.. Wit rcigh
bors. The noted JACK Powers, an Ameri-
can, is said to be the chief of this gang of
bandits. The people of San Luis threaten
q war of extet mination against them. Sevc-
raj of the Williams executed are fugitive Grim
inals, for whose capture large rewards have
been offered by the Governor, and other re-
wards by the citizens. The people preferred
to hang them up to turning them over to the
authorities and claiming the rewards.


Following close after this excitement in the
South, comes the news OF similar explosion
in Carson Valley. Some time ago, poor
Frenchman, named Henri Galdere, was mur-
dered and robbed in Honey Lake Valley. 4
man named Snow was seized by the people
there, and the circumstances proved against
him showed too plainly that he was concerned
in the crime. TO save his life, he confessed
that he belonged to regular band OF robbers
gave their secret signs and passwords, and
named number of his confederates. 1t was
given out that Snow had been hung,and means
taken to capture the entire gang Of assassins
with certainty. These proved successful, and
on Monday. the 18th of June, seven of these
scoundrels were suddenly seized by an armed
band of citizens, at Genoa, Calson Valley
and, were, at latest accounts, being tried for
their lives by an dmprompu jury; and it is
thought that three of them, w. b. Thornton,
l.. Olds, and one Edwards would certainly
be hung. Edwards murdered Mr.. Smelling,
last Fall, at Snelling's ranch, Merced county
and reward of ST. 500 was offered for his
apprehension by the neighbors of his victim.
He undoubtedly deserves death. The people
in the sparsely settled region OF Carson Val
ley, which is outside of the limits of the State
of California, were, of course, much excited
by these events.

article:
FENCING OUT SINNERs.-The Pacific newspaper
condemns Bishop Kip for confirming an actress,
Mrs. 1Iayne,, to membership in the Episcopal
church. We like this sort of exclusive piety it
will be particularly popular with the saints al
ready in heaven, as il would prevent them from
being crowded. We think, however, this man is
swinging his internal fre-brand outside the gates
of heaven without authority he is little more
vigilant that his Master requires him to be, and he
may, possibly, frighten people away who, but for
him, would make very good citizens of the king
dom. He reminds US OF very severe old minis
ter we once knew. At communion occasion the
old man went through with process which he
called fencing the table, He drew a line so
near the Holy of Holes that there was no room
for a soul to stand between. His requistions of
holiness were so severe that the Beloved Disciple
himself could have hardly passed muster. Then
alter terrifying his congregation with imm edate
accommodation, with one'blow of the ccclesi-
astical beetle he knocked down the bars, and
crying come unto me all ye that are heavy laden
cd permitted all to partake of the ordinance.


Sentiments like that uttered by the Pacific are
what makes men and women hesitate to join th e
Christian Church. Such interpreters of scripture
make the Supreme Being an implacable, revenge
ful fury, and Christians themselves company Of
wo-begone, fearful pilgrims through valley fill
cd with instruments of eternal torture, by river
of fire nnquenchable. When they shall have end
cd their pilgrimage and secured their seats in
Heaven, out of reach of the communicating pres
once Of those whom they warn of from the Ark o

tude coming from the North, South, East and
West, and from the uttermost parts Of the earth
whom the Board of Equalization will place be
side them. century hence their decimatinl
theology will live among the thumb screws ant
broken racks and constructing iron-crowns of tht
dark ages.

pie, too, are beginning to ask questions

The most important news by the Stephens
is that in reference to the British outrages
in the Gulf and the action of Congress and
the Government thereon, and the organza
ton and success of Vigilance Committee
in the city Of New Orleans.


The British cruisers, at last accounts, had
not abated their activity in overharling
American vessels, and it is even reported
that they had fired into one ship and killed a
seaman. Altogether 81 vessels have been
visited and searched. The most intense ex-
element prevails in the Atlantic States at
these repeated outrages, and public meetings
held in various cities of the Union, have
spoken out in the strongest terms against
these high-handed acts. The Government
has ordered the entire home squadron mount
ing l63 guns to the Cult, to stop these de
predations, if necessary with cannon balls;
and the British Government has been called
on to stop and disavow the disgraceful acts
of their cruisers. The next news from the
East will bring us something more definite
and if it be that British insolence bas been
checked 10y American broadsides the act will
meet heartfelt response from every man
who cherishes his country's honor But
there will not be war-acts Of retaliation
there may be-but the intimate commercial
relations Of the two countries forbid this
difficulty to be pushed to extremes. Wise
councils will prevail in bringing about an
amicable settlement in which, we doubt not,
the British Government will relinqush the
long claimed right OF search.


New Orleans has followed the example Of
San Francisco, and the people have risen in
their strength to punish criminals that the
law and it's officers could or would not reach
The result will be to purge the Crescent City
Of the desperadocs WHO have for years defed
all legal authority and who have been guilty
Of the most daruning acts Of outrage and
murder.

steamer news does not present ATTY other
features Of absorbing interest.

fact is, it is generally understood at Wash.
ington. that Stebbens, White 6 Co. have no
real. binding contract with the Nicaragua


Government, giving them any right what,


ever to open the Nicaragua Transit They


did once have such a contract, but they for


foited all the rights acquired in it. Nicara-
qua granted TO them in 1857 the privilege to
establish Transit Communication between
the two shores, but with the promise that
they were to have the work performed
within given time. That time passed, and
the Company asked for an extension. Itwas
given. The time granted again expired, and
they asked for still another extension which
was granted. After two or three ex-
tensions Of this kind, the Nicaragua Govern
ment became tired of extension, and refused
to give the Company any further time
Nevertheless, the Company set up claim,
on the ground Of the original contract, to
the opening Of the route, and desire to have


the American Government back them up in


it. The latter seems disposed to favor the


views OF the Company to this extent that it
will consider their interests in the negotia-
tions now pending with Nicaragua 1t is
understood that the Nicaragua Minister,
Yrissarri, is interested in this Stebbens,
White Company. Such being the case, he
will do all in his power to negotiate matters
fayorably for the Company. One thing is
certain, however, the United States will not
permit the claims of any private parties to
interfere with the negotiations to such an ex-
tent as to impede the speedy settlement of all
pending questions and the opening of the
route. The fact is, no existing association,
whether headed by Webster or Garrison or
Vanderbilt or Stebbens White, has, so far
as we can see, any valid claim at all upon
Nicaragua. Whatever claims they may
have had have been forfeited by their own
acts. Nicaragua, then, is perfectly free to
give the franchise TO any person or persons
that she may choose, and oil that our Gov
ernment need contend for is, that the route
be opened by somebody There has been so
much diily-dallying about the opening of
this much talked of route, all on account Of
the conflicting claims of American citizens.
that the whole world is becoming sick of it
In the meantime, we are suffering, here
in California, all the evil results of the
crushing monopoly which owes its impunity
to the simple fact that the Nicaragua transit


is closed and there is no opposition.


The announcement Of the establishment of
a newspaper at Salt Lake, to be devoted to
the interests of the Gentle population, is
the forerunner of great changes in that re-
gion. 1t is prophetic of the doom of Nor
monism The very fact that paper can be
tolerated in Utah, which would dare to dis
pute the doctrines which, in the sight of his |
followers, hedges Brigham Young,is evidence |
that the light Of Mormonism is beginning to
grow dim, and that it is soon Comparatively /
speaking) to be utterly oxtinguished-at any
rate, in its present locality A year ago, I.
and Gentle newspaper would have been
burnt up at Salt Lake and its editor giLbet |
ed. But the presence of the United States
army, and the protection which Brigham |
Young well knows that the Government is |
now going to extend over the rights of every
man, woman and child in Utah Territory. has
had marvellous effect upon the great "Pan-
jandorum." There is no doubt that there
will soon be almost as many Gentiles as Nor
mons in that Territory. Hundreds have
been anxious to throw off the thraldom of
the Apostles" for a long time, and they
will certainly avail themselves of the pres
ent opportunity. Add to these the hundreds
who will come in, with the telegraph and
railroad to say nothing of those now COM

The State Senate seem unwilling to aban-
don the Democratic doctrine of popular
sovereignty, so decidedly repudiated by the
Assembly. At last accounts they had taken
no action upon the concurrent resolution of
the Assembly. In caucus. it appears that
but thirteen of the Democratic Senators
Of California we're willing to caucus away
the vital principle of free government, and
one which has given national vitality, life
aud success to the Democratic party. The
justness of that principle has boon recog-
nized in every portion of the Union, and it
was justly reasoned and well.understood
that those who opposed it denied the right
Of the people Of q State to form their own
institutions, but claimed that Congress had
Jurisdiction over them, and power to say
what institutions should be adopted in new
States or retained in the old. This was de-
MED by the National Democratic Conven.
ton, and by the Democratic conventions Of
every State in the Union. 1t was, and still
is asserted by the Republicans and extrem-
lists Of the South-who desired Congress to
exercise arbitrary power over new States,
and bring them into the Union with such in
stitutions as their respective sections might
desire. An abandonment of the Democratic
platform leads to the adoption of sectional
views and motives, and to the exercise Of a
power by Congress, which the nation, In the
election Of Mr.. Buchanan, decided as belong
ing to the people of the States or territories.


Notwithstanding the reservations Of Pres
ident Buchanan in favor of the doctrine OF
popular sovereignty. while recommending
Congress to force an obnoxious fundamental
law upon the people Of Kansas, the debates
in Congress have shown that the warmest
supporters Of his arbitrary and anti.demo-
cratic policy. are bitterly opposed to and
utterly repudiate the doctrine that, the peo-
people Of sovereign State have the power
to form their own institutions Notwith-
standing the reservations of those in Cali.
fornia, who sustain the Kansas policy of the
administration, and oppose and denounce
the Presidents Nicaragua policy, to the con-
trary, itappears that they, too, are opposed
to the doctrine of popular sovereignty. A
letter in the State Journal, of Friday, dis.
closes the real position and hypocrisy of
this class Of unprincipled politicians. That
letter ridicules tho doctrine of popular
sovereignty" and compares it to the San
Francisco Vigilance Committee, and says
that "such is tho popular sovereignty
Douglas desires the President to get down
upon his knees and acknowledge The
letter sneers at the declaration of our con-
stitution that government is instituted for
the protection Of the people" We mention
these points to show the position of these
traitors to Democratic principles, and the
estimation in which they hold intelligent
freemen, and the contempt with which they
compare the legitimate exercise of the elect
i've franchis with the action Of a mob


This is the position which the Assembly
have instructed our Federal Representatives
to occupy! The Senate may we'll pause be-
fore concurring in such outrageous senti.
mcnts.


The letter was not designed for publica.
ton; but the Journal could "not withhold
IL from" their "readers" 1t is an old
adagc that "Children fools sometimes speak
the truth"

blyman, Mr.. Street. upon the bill to allow the
sum of $4,000 to tire Anti-Mob Army for serv-

Mr.. STREEY-Sir, would be recreant TO my
duty here a legislator were | to remain silent
i'll my seat and allow, what conceive to be
gross wrong and outrage upon the people of this
state, to be perpetrated without entering my
solemn protest against it. AS said on a former
occasion, stand ready at any time to vote for
| the payment of such services as were rendered
| by the law and order troops in San Francisco;
whenever a legitimate committee of the Legis-
lature have aeertained the services, and the
amount legally aud justly due, and reported the
same to the House. We would have control
over the action of that committee and its report,
and standing as guardians of the public enterest
and the public honor, do justice to the claim
ants and justice to the State. But what does
this bill propose 10 do? 1t authorizes a Board
of Commissioners tribunal outside of and
Independent of the Legisature-to examine
these claims and allow them, and to issue bonds
to the amount Of $4,000 to pay them. The
Constitution imposes us, the legislative de-
partment of Government the duty of ascertain
ing claims and then providing for their payment.
This bill provides, without reserve for the issue
of fifty thousand dollars worth of State indebt-
edness for the payment of these claims before
single dollars worth of services has been ass
certained and established to be legally and just
ly due. Is this the way to do business? Is this
the way that as business men we manage our
own financial affaifs Do we pay first and
then ascertain the amount due? Why such
a course would be absurd in an individual, and
is equally absurd in the State. The power to
adiudicate and ascertain all claims is in us and
hold we cannot delegate that power to any
outside Board of Commissioners, irresponsible
to US, and beyond our control, without violat-
ing our duty and our constitutional oath to pro-
tect the interest of the State. We, and we alone
are responsible to our constituents for the per-
| forrnance of that duty; which belongs to u.s. and
! TO no one else We are told that in opposing
this bill we call in question the integrity of the
| Board of Commissioners. That is not so have
| the highest confidence in the proposed Board.
| Gentlemen may draw their own differences as to
the motives of others but, for one, | have be-
fore disclaimed any imputation on the honor
and integrity of the men who compose the pro-
posed Board and any who charges me with
questioning the integrity of the proposed Board,
| charges that which is false. There is no such
issue. l am contending for a principle, that, if
departed from in this instance, will open wide
the door to fraud and rascality in the future.
am contendng for those rights and powers con-
ferred on me by the Constitution, as one of the
guardians of the treasury and will never sur
render those powers, and delegate them to any
other tribunal; though that tribunal might be
] composed of saints in the courts of Heaven not
even if Jesus Christ himself were one of them.
| Weare told by gentlemen who voted against this
$4,000 appropriation the other day, that this is
different bill. A species of sophistry and sub
terfuge is resorted to, in order to quiet the
sciences of tender-footed members What is
the difference in the bills Z? Why, one provided
for the payment of $4,000 in cash; the other
provides for the issue of State bonds that must
eventually be paid in cash and, of the two
modes, prefer that of the first bill. If anything
is due, pay it in cash, not in paper, and run the
State deeper in debt. The House took sensi-
BILE view of this question in the commencement,
and by a heavy majority, defeated the bill APP
| propriating $4,000 to pay claims before they
were ascertained. In that, they acted like hon
est, sensible Legislators but they reconsidered.
Yes, they reeonsidcrcd. And why did they re-
consider? Were there any new facts elected
Was there any new light thrown on the subject?
And if so. from whence has it come? Without
imputing against honorable men who enrolled
themselves against the Vigilance Committee,
know that this Capital has been besieged with
law and order soldiers. Has this greedy army
manufactured public sentiment and legislative
| sentiment7 | would remind legislators that
there is a power behind the lobby-the masses
of the people the Woodworking, over-taxed
people OF TINS State-and that their sentiments
may be at war with the contaminating, corrup-
ting influences that hang around this hall. We
are urged to pass this bill as Democratic mea-
sure. The member from Amador. who says he
has always warred against the Democratic party,
is one of its noblest champions. He introduced
the first bill. He has been consistent from the
first and has ably advocated the measure.
think that if he wanted to strike blow at the
Democratic pasty, he could not do better than
fasten on its shoulders this law and order ap-
preparation of $4,000. | believe its passage
will be stab at the Democratic party; and
mill stone hung around the neck of every DEM
ocrat that votes for it, which will sink him down
to the lowest pits of political datnnation. If
anything could rcvvfy and galvanize into life
the dry bones of his party, this bold and reck-
less onslaught on the State Treasury by DEM
ocratic Legislature would do it.

SACRAMENTO, Feb. 10th, 1858.


MR. EDITOR Il visited the Assem-
bly, for a few hours to-day. and listened
for short time to the debate upon the
bill of Mr.. Lee of Ell Dorado, the
popularity called Vigilance
Bill" | was unable to listen to the
whole debate, as the San Francisco boat
left at ? O. o'elock, and 1 was compelled to
leave on the boat.


Mr.. Mccoy of Santa Clara, took the
floor after the house had resolved Itself
into committee of the whole upon the
special order of the day. and spoke
about an hour in opposition to the bill.
He is slow and deliberate speaker, but
highly effective, and often eloquent.
He referred to the state of things
well-known to exist for period of some
years in San Francisco before the out
break, and drew very strong picture
of the ballot-box stuffing, by which men
who had not even been known as candi-
dates, and they infamous, were elected
of the host of political lunch eaters,
that governed the city for years, where
by all law was overridden, juries pack
ed, and crimes of all species passed
unpunished He stated the fact that
thirteen hundred murders had been COM
mitted in San Francisco, and but four of
the murderers brought to suffer the ex-
treme penalty of the law. That the
tools of the murderers were in office,
and thus the authors of these outrages,
disgraceful to authorities, had an unfail-
lug screen. Such a state of things he
thought palliated the organization and
acts of the committee, though they did
not fully justify them. chad not been
and was not now vigilance" man.
He deprecated the introduction of the
bill as divided and distracting the Der
ocratic party, He also exposed the
tyranny of the bill-its opposition to
the principles of republican liberty, and
as fayoring the way to the ascendancy
of the Republican party. He showed
that the bill repealed the homestead
law, and in the matter of venue, grand
juries, and in other features, reversed
the whole criminal practice, which had
been built up as protection to the inno-
cent as we'll as the punishment of the
guilty. He held up to merited contempt
and censue the provision by which a
man might be dragged, without means
to get his witnesses from Shasta to San
Diego, to answer an Indictment suddenly
trumped mp against him.


Mr. Buel of Ell Dorado, followed up
on the same side. He repudiated the
idea that this bill was test of democra-
cy He was opposed to the bill, and
also the Vigilance Committee. But the
people had something to say about these
tests. Besides, even if the people gen
orally were opposed to the Vigilance
Committee, they would not sanction
such an outrage as the bill before the
House


Thinking your readers might like to
know the tone of Legislature upon this
point, send you the above. Violent
speeches have been made in favor of the
law. But the general opinion is that it
cannot pass. There is too much good
sense in the Legislature. apparently, to
pass an odous law like the proposed
one-odious not, perhaps, to many that
vote against it because it is directed
against the Vigilance Committee, but
because its provisions are so framed that
our liberties are more in danger from
the law than from such committees.

The arrival Of the Prometheus brings Us fifteen
days later intelligence from California, by way Of

The prominent, and by far the most conspicuous
feature of the California news is the prevalence Of
what would be called on this side Of the continent
the supreme authority Of Judge Lynch. In san
Fran .isco IL s the execution Of the decrees Of the
Vigilance Committee of Eve hundred, (not quite so

servation Of law and order. Strange as il may

n horse thief, burglar, an ircend diary, a common

Our columns include to-day, part of our foreign
intelligence received by the Africa, several leading
articles from the most prominent English journals,


illustrative of English views of the recent startling
events in the island Of Cuba. They will repay an
attentive reading.


II was anticipated that the late reckless invasion
Of Lopez, the disastrous conseq quences attending
and succeeding it, and the momeRtous questions OF
International character involved, would create
sensation in Europe. However grave and perplex-
ing the affairs Of the British islands, or Of the con-
tinental powers, the foray of Lopez-suspected o
covering some ul.erior design Of annexation to the
United States-wss affair Of an import too start
ling to escape the loyal indignation of our trans
atlantic neighbo.s. We were quite prepared there
fore, for the lugubrious commentaries Of the Eng
ish journals received by the late steamers and fol-
their badly confessed apprehensions of the progress
sive tendencies Of this country in the enlargement
OF its boundaries. All their oarping and forced
constructions Of bad faith against the American
people, however, may be overlooked when
such an unbounded respect for the government
OF the United States is avowed, that when i.
ceases to be capable of sustaining itself, II must
be sustained by the Intervention Of England





more has q guarantee of protection against
the flttnst1os AID their sympathizers, which will
certainly secure his administration, hereafter, from
the discomfcrts Of all marauding expeditions, Of
any kind, against the island of Cuba.


But this suggestion of the London Times, coun-
selling the interposition of England and France to
aid this government in vndicating its neutrality,
though extremely absurd and amusing, is entitled
10 ha uifb tha Wit L
been advanced II was uttered when the termna-
ton of the revolutionary movement upon Cuba was
yet unknown in England, and probably in anticipl
tion offormidable renforcemen to Lopez from the
United States and the consequent probabilities of


fierce ard doubtful struggle. In view of such con-
tngencies, the recommendation of English and
French aid to this & )vernment must have been se-
riously intended for good advice. We are satisfied,
indeed, from our last European exchanges, that such
would have been the policy of the government of
France, and, most probably, of England, had Lopez
made and maintained anything like dangerous
footing to the sovereign y of the island The CHI ain
of immediate consequences would then have been
most comprehensive and momentous in their electr
cal re action. No doubt, had Lopez excited for
midable insurrection, reinsorcements by thousands
would have reached him, or attempted to reach him.
from our shores. 1t is difficult to imagine how, with
such state Of things existing, and With a COM
hined Spanish, English, and French protective
squadron round the island how all collisions could
be avoided calculated to embroil all parties in the
war. The popular opinion of this country-so
lightly esteemed and so little understood in Europe
would not permit our government to acquiesce in
the aid of foreign powers in det aiming, capturing
or destroying American citizens and their property
on the high seas, from mere picion of their de-
signs. Briefly, it is perhaps we'll for our peace
with England and France-the best for them and
for the peace of Eurepe-that this experimental
invasion Of Lopez was so speedily extingushed.
The summary execution Of the fifty prisoners at
Havana-but particularly the mutilation inflicted
by the rabble Of the city upon their lifeless re-
mains-had excited just that state of feeling
throughout this Unicn which only required con.
tinued active hostile position in the island of Cuba,
to be maintained by Lopez a month, to secure him
reinforcements by Thousands. late article in
the London Chromicle takes the proper view of the
effect Of the summary execution Of Crittenden and
his command, upon the popular mind Of this country.
II was infamed to truly dangerous pitch Of
excitement and the immediate steps taken for ven-
geance, were sufficiently alarming to justify the
impression of the immediate seizure Of the island
by . single blow. But the subsequent acts OF
clemency and kindness Of the Captain General to
the remaining prisoners, and the information that
he was forced into the execution of those fifty at
Havana, by An overruling military tribunal, have
done much to appesse the publ, indignation. Al
together, he has proved that he is not only man o
promptnes and efficiency, but Of intelligence.
ssgacity, and humanity The alarm-the panic
created at Havana by the invasion of Lopez-the
pop ular phrenzy against the frst detachment. of
prisoners brought in-the fact that they were out
lawed by the President, and that the Captain
General had nothing to do with the atrocities Of
the rsbble, must be taken into consideration before
condemning this summary judgment sf the island
executive. At all events, he may congratulate
himself and his sovereign that affairs have turned
out no worse; and that BY the judicious policy Of
humanity which he has subsequently enforced, he
has done much to secure the future peace Of the
colony entrusted to his keeping.


With regard to the maintenance Of the neutrality
of the United Stste, the least interference Of for
eign squadrons for that object the better, for an
accidental collision might result in general war.
But the affair is over and the sauadrons Of England
and France may move about in peace.

headline: Farewell soiree to George Thompson.
article:
1he friends OF this distinguished phianthropist on
Monday evening last sat down TO sumptuous supper
IN Assembly Hall, Boston. The vast room was
crowded to It's utmost capacity, and hundreds from
the country were unable to obtain tickets Of adms-
sion. Edmund Quincy presided, with the guest of
the evening on his right, and Hon. Mr. Keyes of
Dedham, on his left. Mr.. Quincy in the chair, dis
plays an ease, and elictous humor, which gave in
hnlte zest to such festive occasion.


MIR. Garrison was first introduced, and in behalf of
the assembly, read an address to Mr.. Thompson; it
bore the usual plain straightforward character of its
author, and was enthusiastically received. A very
appropriate quotation from one of Mr.. Thompson's
antl-corn law speeches was introduced, in which the
orator welcomed the aid of America in the great
work OF English reform. Mr. Thompson responded,
and on rising, was greeted with loud and prolonged
cheering; the enthusiasm was irrepressble and al
most without limit. We have not room or ability 10
sketch his address 1t was appropriate to the occa
sion, equal to the subject, and to the orators own
great fame.


A toast, upon the progressive character and final
success OF the antsavery enterprise was responded
to briefly, by Wendell Phillips 1t is not necessary


to tell those who have heard this eloquent speaker.
how nobly he acquitted himself


Charles L. Remond was then called for, and in the
name OF his fellow Of Africa he rose and thank
ed Mr. Thomson for his generous devotion to the
colored race, and his freedom from the prejudice
against color, by which too manysprofesscd phlan-
tfTopists are tainted


A sentiment, in honor of the Old Bay State, was
offered, and the chair called upon Hon. Edward L.
heyes to respond. The few remarks made by this
gentleman were in the happiest spirit The hostili-
ty to the mission of George Thompson, he attributed
to selfish political motive the part of our wire
pullers, who sought to conceal, under show in
dlgnaton against foreigner, their real opposition 10
the ant-slavery cause. He defended Mr.. It. from
the charge of oicous interference, and hoped that
as we were sending missionaries on crusade against
the sins ofother lands, our kind intentions woud he
fully reciprocated


toast in honor ofthe fidelity and zeal of the
Boston Vigilance Committee, was responded TO by
Theodore Parker. The Reverend gentleman,s
mrthfu passages with the chair, upon rising, were
exceedingly amusing; and to attempt collection of
them would be as absurd as saving up store of
glances, smiles, and laughter. The speech was
Enthusiastically able and spirited


James Bufum, of Lynn, related an anecdote of
the courtesy of Boston officials Mr.. B. when visit
ing the u S. Court, desired to sit within the mvstc
circle usually appropriated by the legal profession.
and as there were many seats vacant, stepped for
"afd to.occuPy one; but pompous tipstaff forbade
nm' Mr., B.retired after some pareying, when as
ne was leaving, John Caphart entered, and was
bowed to the most eligible seat, by the same funkey
who had elected him. 81 thought the seats were
for the bar;' said Mr. B. 'sBut we reserve some
seats for distinguished strangers p said the official


Thus, it seems, that man, whom no high. minded
slave holder would allow at his table, is to be toadied
by our officers, while our own citizens are kicked
out of the court!


Hon. Rodney French and Rev. Mr.. Mathews, re-
Gently immersed in new baptism by his lay brethren
in Christ, in Kentucky, spoke briefly, but we have
not further space to notice their efforts


Mr. Thompson then addressed the audience mos
feelngly, and announced his desire and hope to bet
permitted to return tolabor in the AntSIayery cause
hereafter.


We have not given anything more than a mere
outline fthe meeting, which lasted till one O'Clock
There was such perpetual intellectual feast, that
our recoection except of few salient points, is as
confused as that Of boy who beholds an exhibition
of fire works-corruscatio dazzling, unique, and
in endless variety succeeded in such rapdity that
the whole seems urevew like glorious dream A
safe return to England, and then new welcome to
George Thompson.

article:
10 O'Clock A. NJ. The Cherokee has made the
most rapid passage ever accomplished by the
Chagres route. She has $2,OOo.O GOO on freight,
and $500, goo in The hands of passengers.


Letters from California give the most hatter-
ing accounts of the mining interests, and the yield
of the mines the present year,is estimated at over
seventy millions.


Among the passengers are Hon. Thomas Lar
kin, of California, and Col, Green, of the Pana-
ma Herald.


The Cherokee brings the mail.


A large portion of the goods forwarded by Ad-
ans 81 Co., were left behind at Cruces


The Alta California gives some accounts of the
tragedy on board the Challenge, but nothing of
more definite character than has been already
published, from the news by the Alabama.


Capt. Cressy, of the clipper Flying Cloud,
died when the vessel was two days out from San
Francisco, on her voyage to China.


Trade with the Sandwich Islands and Oregon
is increasing daily.


Quartz mining continues to attract great at
tention Some 70 machines are already in ope-
ration, or in process of construction, throughout
the State.


The vigilance committees are fast becoming
extinct, and the machinery ofestabshed govern
mentis running more smoothly


Convention in favor of division of the
State, has been held at San Francisco, and res
olutions recommending the same, adopted though
not without considerable opposition as 10 the
manner in which it should be done.


The ship Deadalus, sent out by the British
Government, to search for Franklin, arrived at
San Francisco, Oct. 22d No trace ofthe expe-
dition had been discovered, and it is the opinion
of the officers, that all further attempts to find
traces OF those discoveries would prove fiuitless

18th. letter states that the u S. government
has entered into new bargain with the New Grana-
dian government, by which the latter yields up its
original contract for Transportation Of U. S. mails
across the Isthmus, and contract has been formed
for that purpose, between the u S. and the Panama
R. r. Co. BY this arrangement it is expected that
the mails will be carried through from San Francisco
TO N. York in the short space of "a DAYS time.


From San Juan de SUI we learn that everything
is in state Of anarchy and confusion Gen. Munose
had collected large force, well supplied with arms
and ammunition, aud was preventing the landing Of
passengers by Vanderbt's line. About 100 Ameri-
cans had joined his forces.

The following proceedings of interest to our cti- zens, were had at the last meeting of the Board of Aldermen.

 The following was received from Common Coun- cl and c0ncurred in by this board.

 Whereas, 1t is conducive to the health of the city that the wild weeds be pulled out of the vacant and other lots in the city, and that all nusances be aba ted immediately ,therefore be it.

 Resolved, That the Marshal and Deputy Marshas be required to give immediate notice to the different agents owners of lots in their respective wards to abate all nuisance and all sorts of wild weeds to be pulled and carted away, according the ord,- of the city made and provided in such case, and all person or persons refusing to comply with said notice within ten days from time of serving said notice, the Marshal Deputies are hereby required to have them brought before the Recorder to nfict such fines required by law.

 Be it further Resolved, That the street committee be requested to have all weeds growing in the streets pulled and carried away, and that the Mayor be re- quested appoint three of the citizens of each ward to inspect all yards lands, and alleys, and to report all nuisance not sbated according to law.

 The following resolution was received from Com mon Council and concurrsd in by this board:

 Resolved That the street committee be empower cd to hire three additional case they deem it necessary for the purpose ofactatng the repairs of the streets, &c

 The following report from the board of Common COunCll was read ana on motion, cOncurred, Tn

 The Police Committee beg leave to report that in consequence of the recent fires which have occurred and the alarm expressed generally by the citizens they have under the resolution of June last made an ap- pointnent of the following citizens to act with the Police Committee Wig ance Committee: J. K. Collins, Doct. Fearn, H. Myers, D. NJ. Riggs, c. Cullum, P. B. Taylor, Sidney Smith, F. Sheffield, Geo. Higgins, R. H. Redwood.

 That under the approval of this Vigilance Com- mtee they have accepted for patroe duty the services of the City Troop, State Artillery, Mobile Rife Company. and Washington Light Infantry, and are obtaining the services of citizens to complete the patroe for every night of the week to be called out as long as the Vigilance Committee may deem neces- sary.

 The committee recommend that the boards orga- mise the guards under such regulations as the com mtee may adopt, and that the Mayor be required to give notice to the citizens that such guard is es- ablished, and require that all slaves shall be at home by the ringing of the market bell at night, and that all slaves who may be found after that hour without special permit from thelr owners agents or guardians will be committed to the Guard House. The committee recommend that the Police committee have power to employ for the present additional city guard if they may deem it necessary, not exceeding ten. y.W. ROPER. Com.

The citizens of Humboldt county have
protested against the law authorizing the
location of School Land Warrants, by the
adoption of the following resolutions:


Resolued, That we view the law passed
by the Legislature of California, respect
ing the sale and location of School War
rants, unjust and contrary to all laws pas
sed by Congress, as it gives the speculator
the right of purchasing and holding any
quantity of land, while the actual settler
can pre-empt one quarter section only,
and is compelled to occupy the same.


ReSolued, That we will aid and protect
all pre-emptors in maintaining possess
sion of any public lands elonging to the
United States, although they may have
been covered previously by School War
rants, unless the owner of such School
Warrants holds but one quarter section
and occupies the same.


Resoieed, That the Vigilance Commit
tee be instructed to stop all further loca-
cation of School Warrants in Union
Township, and that our fellow-citizens
OF humboldt county and the State gene
rally, be requested to act in concert with
us IN putting an end to the location of
School Warrants.


Resoleed, That the Secretary of the
meeting should prepare copies of these
resolutions and send them to every set
element on this Bay, and also to the lead
ing papers of San Francisco, to arouse
the Indignation of every farmer, settler
and wei l-wisher to California against the
encroachment of land monopoly, which
will retard the settlement of its arabic
lands.


Resotced, That a petition should be
circulated IN the county for signatures,
praying Congress not to sanction the law
passed by the Legislature of California
creating School Warrants, and laying
them ndiscriminateIy on the Public Lands
throughout California.

the meeting that listened to Messrs Wells

Judge Wells did not discuss Biglerism
