of the state generally, and this one partic-
ularly +; Sd, defending his recent decision
that we charged was to be employed as an
entering wedge for the sale of the mineral
lands.


With reference to the first, if judge
cannot show himself on the bench as an
upright man, and thus win the confidence
of the people, he will not better the matter
by assuming the airs of demagogue.


AS to the second, if the judiciary would
be little less abusive of the press, we dare
say the press would save the necessity for
such whining about abuse of the Judiciary.
1t is well known that corruptions Of every
name at one time infested the whole system
of justice in the larger cities, especially in
that of criminal jurisdiction, so that the
spirit of justice departed from the dead
form of law, till resurrection was effected
though vigilance committees. For up
holding the selfdefensive action of these
committees, judge Wells assailed the press,
and thus identified himself with the cor
ruptions those committees eradicated.


The third point requires further refer
ence. The learned judge complains the
Journal cited no law, and then set the ex-
ample by quoting law. He told what
Blackstone and older English authorities
of the common law eXpounded as relating
to the case, and then ruled them all out
Although judge Wells, in his slavish re-
gard for precedent, quotes in nearly every
decision these very authorities, and bases
his judgment upon them, when it suits his
purpose to make a little capital he is per-
fectly oblivious to their application. Af
ter quoting so much law against his deci.
sion he referred to certain statutes passed
in New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia
assuming the control of the mines within
their borders. But he forget to tell his
audience that the government of the Uni
ted States never owned one foot of the land
thus taken-that there was no similarity
between the ownership of lands by the
state government and by the United States
as affecting the right of sovereignty. II
he had told them this it would at once have
upset his decision. No state has ever at
tempted to control the lands of the United
States of any character, and if California
does it, misled by this glaringly false and
stupid decision, it will be enacting sheer
notification.


But as we said in our first article on this
subject, the weight of the decision is moth
/ ing beside the motives that influenced it.
We charged that the design was to estab-
lish the fact or the impression that the
mineral land were in the control of the
Legislature, and that these spectators
would scheme and fight for their possess
ion, regardless of the rights of humble mi
ners. Judge Wells denied the impeach-
ment, and asked where was the motive for
it. He forgot himself presently, and told
the motive. He boasted of the vast wealth
''this decision, if sustained would bestow
upon the state!" But is wealth to accrue
to the state from the freedom of the mines
more than when in the hands of the gener-
al government? The only way the boas-
ted revenue can be derived is by sale or
lease of these lands-both destructive of
existing rights and prosperity. He COW
cred his track with all his skill, but the
snakes eyes peeped out in spite of him. He
has struck the first blow towards turning
these mines over to scheme for vast state
revenues, and we all know where California
revenues go to ! The Bigler faction sup
mort this man and are thuS identified with

MEXICAN NEws.--By the arrival of the Jno.
L. Stephens, we are IN possession OF full files
Of Mexican papers. up to December 3 ; fourteen
days later than last advices. Manuel Gandara
Governor of Sonora, is making vigorous pre-
parations to receive the F'illibusters with mark
ed attention. A large number of Mexicans
and Yacki Indians, who are his personal de-
pendants, were busy at work fortifying the port
of Guaymas, and a considerable body of troops
were in march for Sonora, and were to be COM
manded by General Yanez, who had no doubt
arrived in that State ere this.


Santa Anna had offered the grand cross of
the new Order of Guadalupe to Seneres Juan
B. Ceballos,and Marcelino Castenado, Judges
of the Supreme COnrt; but. those gentlemen
had refused the intended honor under the plea
that their circumstances would not allow them
to bear the necessary expenses accompanying
it. The Dictator, thereupon, deprived them of
their offices, saying, if they were so poor that
they could not accept the honor, they were also
too poor to maintain their posts Of Supreme
Judges with dignity.


A pronunciamento had been issued in Quad
alupe making Santa Anna, Dictator for life,
with the title of Captain General, and the right
to appoint his successor. Several other states
had followed the example, and Santa Anna had
been slavored with the most fulsOme fattery in
the public prints.


Punishment and summary executions were
numerous, among the victims was Don Luis de
La Rosa, formerly Minister at Washington,
who was shot without even the form Of trial


1t is rumored that Mr.. Gadsden, our Minis
ter, is making terms with the Mexican Gov
ernment for the purchase of Chihuahua and
Sonora, and is likely to succeed in his desire.
Such an event would be of much benefit to
both countries


The Mexican papers are filed with accounts
of Indian depredations on their northern from
tier but apart from DEGREES and circulars, the
government seems to be perfectly Indifferent
on the subject.

We learn from the Marysville Express

ries and murders in that city, and are de-

terribly

ORGANIZATION OF VIGILANCE COM
MIrTEE.--In view of long series Of out
RACES which have been committed in this
vicinity, and which the arm Of Civil Law
has proved itself powerless to punish, and
in view cf the fact that there is no adequate
protection to life or property in our midst,
the inhabitants of Mokelumne Hill, pur-
suant to general notice, convened on Satur-
day afternoon last, at the Franklin House,
to organize COMMITTEES OF VIGILANCE.
The meeting was composed of property
holders and miners, and stern detcrmina-
tion evinced that crime should not go un-
punished, and especially that assassination
and murder in our streets should be follow
ed by netting out to the offenders summary
and exemplary justice. A Constitu ton
was reported and adopted, setting forth in
brief the causes that imperatively demand
the institution of such society, regular
officers tosen and large Executive Com
mittee pointed to carry into effect the
purrr the association. We are happy
to annou nee that large numbers Of our pO-
pulati have come forward, signed the
Constitution, manifested their sympathy
with the objects of the society, and pro-
missed their hearty cooperation.


Subsequently, meeting of the Executive
Committee was held and plan Of opera
tions organized. A room for the permanent
meetings of the Committee was engaged, an
Alarm Signal for the assembling of the ge-
neral Vigilance Committee agreed upon,
and arrangements made for the instanta-
neous trial Of criminals, by fair and i'm
partial jury of twelve men. for deciding the
mode and amount of punishment and for
putting the same into speedy execution.
Among the measures adopted for preserv-
ing the peace and quiet of the Camp, was
an agreement, on the part of the members
Of the Committee, to refrain from the dis
charge of firearms after sunset unless in
cases of self-defence Officers were ap.
pointed for taking command Of the mem
bers of the Vigilance Committee in cases o.
emergency, and a reward of Three Hun
dred Dollars offered for the apprehension

headline: Correspondence.
article:
THE TRIAL OF JAMES CAMPBELL.-JHr.
Editor-I crave portion Of your columns
for the purpose of personal vindica tien,
and desire, ut the same time to give q true
history of certain events that have lately
very much occupied the public mind in the
neighborhood Of Mokelumne Hill.


[Mr. G. Campbell here gives clear and
succint account of the tragedy, and de-
scribes the proceedings of the trial with
great minuteness, differing in no particular
from what appeared in our last. We are
sorry our limits prevent US giving this
weIl-written letter at length. Mr.. G. H.
Campbell was elected judge, and his duties
prescribed, namely, to see the case t1'Tty
tried. He thus continues j


During the whole Of these proceedings
great excitement was manifested by the
audieaee, and twice a considerable move
ment was made toward the prisoner. Each
time, endeavored to persuade the crowd
to keep back. and do whatever was to be
done in an orderly manner; and once de-
clared (holding pencil, and not pistol, as
has been reported) that the prisoner should
not be taken from the stand except by the
committee elected TO have custody Of him,
while lived.


do not wish to go behind the verdict of
the jury to inquire whether the prisoner
was guilty Of murder or not; but wish
to vindicate myself from certain charges,
which, since the day of trial, have passed
from mouth to mouth in the community.


1st. That being relative Of the prisoner,
was biased in his favor.


II onc~rou dooloro khok Lun- of NO
relationship existing between US, and do
not know that l ever saw James Campbell
before the day Of trial.


ID. That l was bribed to show him favor


have only to say in reply, that if any
one innocently thinks have received q
bribe from anywhere, he is quite in error !;
and if any enc make such an assertion,
usIgu0lifedly pronounce him liar.
| 3D. That feared should offend the
gamblers if took course that would en-
sure the execution Of the prisoner
do not, Mr.. Editor, boast of any very
great degree of bravery, but if any one de-
sire it, let him produce the occasion for the
test, and "we shall see what we shall see. !"
So far from having any particular fear of
gamblers, as o class. have never known
them to act more bravely than other people,
and as I have not risked dollar upon any
game during the last ten years, am sure I
shall not be suspected of any sympathy for
their profession.


The truth is that when the jury that had
convicted Campbell, were seen coming to-
wards the Empire, his friends at once rush
ed into the room. They demanded the ver-
dict, and do not know what an impartial
man could have done except to read it. Mo-
tions, duly seconded, followed the reading
of the verdict, and / have never before
heard that it was unfair for the presiding
officer Of meeting to put questions so
brought up. l did feel it my duty to use
nv influence in protecting, as much as pos
sible, the prisoner from the hands of any
set Of men that might attempt to force him
from the room, for whatever purpose, until
he should have been delivered over to
the hands Of the committee elected to take
charge Of him, and therefore acted as did
in that matter.


Some persons have inquired why we did
not, as judges, sentence the prisoner to suf-
fer death, after the jury had pronounced
him guilty Of murder. | can only say in
reply that we were not elected to pronounce
sentence, and if we had been, there was a
large majority Of persons in the room at
the time opposed to his execution, as their
vote to deliver him over to the civil autho-
rites shows. So far as observed, the au-
dience generally were pretty well armed,
and such course would doubtless have
resulted in general fight, in which the
chances were that the prisoner would have
been rescued, and much innocent blood
spilled, for no good purpose


In conclusion, deny that I acted with
any prejudice in the matter, and further
more, am still of opinion that under simi-
lar circumstances, should again do as did
then. 1t was not my business to refuse to
read the verdict Of the jury when it was
called for; and aside from the unfairness
of such refusal, have no doubt it would
have resulted in the rescue Of the prisoner,
and probably bloodshed Pronouncing of
q sentence Of death would probably have
had similar result


l have, Mr.. Editor, been present at se-
veral similar meetings since first arrived
in California, and have invariably found
that the gamblers exercise perseverance,
when one of their number is in danger,
worthy of q better calling, while it has
formerly been almost invariably the case
that other classes Of the community ne
glect to carry out those wholesome regula-
tlons that would ensure good order. I am
happy to know, however, that Vigilance
Committee has been organized that will
probably act energetically and efficiently !;
and they have adopted such regulations as
will ensure the execution of any person
whom jury shall say is guilty of murder


By publishing the above, you will doubt
less correct some false impressions rife in
the community. GEO. II. CAMPBELL.

by the Populace.
article:
by the Populace.


We copy the annexed account of the
hanging Of two men at Coloma, on the
18th inst, from the correspondence of
the Union.


Coloma has this day been the scene
of great and unusual excitement. Two
men, the one white man of the name
of Henry George, said to be from Sidney,
and the other a negro named VIM. Mil
ler-- were forcibly taken from our Jail
and hung by mob, composed of the
citizens of this vicinity, in conjunction
with several members Of the Vigilance
Committee of Placerville. The white
man was charged with having stolen
about $4,000 from q miner on Granite
Creek near this place and the negro
with having stolen about $4,000 from
Mr.. David Martin, who resides at Co.
lumbia, near Kelsey's Diggings. Our
Court of Sessions was in session at the
time these men were arrested, and the
regular Grand Jury had.been discharg-
cd The court proceeded at once to
empannel special Grand Jury for the
purpose of enquiring into these cases.
An Indictment for grand larceny was
found and presented on yesterday even
ing against George, and another for the
same crime against the negro, was pre-
sented this morning. But before either
of them could be brought to trial, and
while our Sheriff was absent for the pur-
pose of summoning jury, the mob col
lected from different parts of the coun-
ty, to the number of some two or three
hundred, and demanded Of the iailor
the negro boy Miller The jailor, after
q fruitless attempt to persuade the mob
to desist from their purpose and dis
perse, complied with their demand.
Miller was taken about two hundred
yards from the Jail and hung which was
no sooner done, than the mob returned
to the Jail, demanded and had delivered
to them the prisoner George, whom they
took and hung to the same tree. They
then returned Immediately to the Jail,
and demanded prisoner of the name
of Dougherty, who had been indicted
for grand lafcency, on a charge of steal





submitted to petit jury On yesterday,
who had not agreed upon IL verdict.
About this time the Sheriff made his
appearance ut the Jail, and informed
the mob that jury of their country
men was then deliberating upon the
case of Dougherty, and requested them
to defer further action, until they should
s,k Al,
appointed committee of three to wait
upon the jury and inform them that un-
less they agreed upon verdict in ff-
teen minutes, Dougherty would be hung


The committee proceeded directly to
the jury room, and in about fifteen min
utes returned and reported that the
jury had agreed upon verdict The
crowd then rushed to the court house,
which was very soon filed and crowded
to overAowing. Dougherty was brought
in, and the jury delivered their verdict,
which was, that the defendant was gui.-
ty, and the punishment ten years i'm
prisonment in the penitentiary. This,
however, was not satisfactory to the
mob, and the cry of bring him outn and
hang him." again resounded through
the crowd.


At this crisis, Thos. Robertson, Esq,
who had assisted in prosecuting Doug
herty, appeared. and by means of very
effective and eloquent address to the
crowd, succeeded in soothing the feel
ing and allaying the excitement that
prevailed at the time; and it was there
upon resolved, that the crowd disperse,
and allow the law to take its course
with the prisoner Doughertv.

article:
We have received an extra from the
Office Of the Calaveras Chronicle, giving
an account Of the arrest and execution
of one Carlos Esla,a. by the Vigilance
Committee, at Mokelumne Hill, on
Thursday last. For some time previous
robberies to IN alarming extent had
been committed at Mokelumne Hill and
vicinity Tents were cut open and
robbed when least expected, and when
the owners were but short distance
from them. At length circumstances es
tended to attract attention to Eslava, who
was several times seen in rather sus-
picious proximity to tents and houses
that had been robbed, upon which occa-
sions he managed to get off by pretend
ing to be drunk. lie was arrested on
ednesday afternoon, by the Vigilance
Committee, charged with having COM
mitted several robberes, among the
rest, of purse containing $500, which
was stolen from a MIR. Perkins, on Corral
Flat, Tuesday morning.


The committee proceeded to try the
prisoner, who still pretended to be drunk
until his guilt was proven by unequivo-
cal testimony, when he threw off his
disguise, and confessed the truth of every
charge that had been substantiated
Every effort was made by the commit
tee to obtain information in relation to
his accomplices, but he remained obsti-
nately silent upon every point that might
tend to implicate others. After q long
and tedious trial. which lasted until
near three o'clock on Thursday morning,
he was sentenced to be hung. He ex-
hibited throughout the utmost coolness
and indifference. The sentence was
carried into execution on Thursday af-
ternoon in presence of between eight
hundred and thousand per.ons.


"The rope having been adjusted, at
exactly five minutes of three, the sig
nal was given, and the scaffold being
suddenly pulled from under him, Eslava
was launched into eternity. He dropped
about three and half feet, but not
withstanding this his neck was not bro
ken. He struggled violently for some
moments, and, pinioned as were his
arms, he reached up and caught hold of
the rope above the knot, evidently try
ing to release himself Vain hope, how
ever, he only drew the rope tighter round
his neck, Fastening thus his own death.
At quarter past three, the physicians
pronounced him dead, but it was deci-
ded to let him hang ten minutes longer.
At the end of this time, a committee of
Eve were appointed to take charge of
the body and bury it, which was done
at the base of Stockton Hill. Thus
ended tragedy which, however much
some may deprecate it, was perhaps alb
solutely necessary to the well being of
our citizens and the community at large.
Every thing went off with the Utmost
quiet No excitement existed, nor did
Eslava seem to have single friend who
had sufficient moral courage 10 come
forward and condole with him in his
emergency, or even to bid him good bye.
He was native Of Sonora in Mexico"
